entries.meaning: Not present where it was supposed to be — and, in the extended use, not to be found in a text, a list, or an argument.
examples: Two jurors were absent from the courtroom when the verdict came in.
Any mention of the earlier settlement is absent from the report.
She has been absent from work since Thursday.
Warmth was conspicuously absent from his reply.
That name is absent from every version of the guest list I've seen.
entries.русский: отсутствующий где-л. — не быть там, где ожидалось; не встречаться в тексте или списке
entries.register: neutral, tilting formal; the everyday word is missing
entries.complement: noun phrase or pronoun naming a place, an occasion, or a body of work (absent from school, absent from the record) — never a gerund and never a clause. There is no ✗ absent from being there.
entries.pattern: be absent from [place/event] · [noun] absent from [noun] · conspicuously / notably / entirely absent from [noun]
entries.variants: missing from is the neutral everyday equivalent and takes the same complement. Away from covers only the physical sense.
entries.contrast: ✗ absent of and ✗ absent in are errors here — the fixed preposition is from. Do not confuse the adjective with the marginal preposition absent meaning "in the absence of" (absent a court order, the file stays sealed), which takes a noun with no from at all and is a different word; see absent. Against away from, which reports a body somewhere else, absent from reports a gap where something was expected.
entries.see also: free of, short of, lacking in, from

entries.meaning: Obliged to explain and justify — to whoever may demand it, and for whatever falls inside your charge.
examples: The commissioner is accountable to a board of five elected members.
Every site manager is accountable for the safety of the crew on shift.
Somebody is going to be held accountable for losing the original file.
In a co-op, the staff are accountable to the residents, not to a landlord.
She is accountable to the state for every dollar of the grant.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /əˈkaʊntəbəl tə/ and /əˈkaʊntəbəl fər/ — in running speech the whole tail flattens to "uh-KOWN-tuh-bul-tuh" and "uh-KOWN-tuh-bul-fur"
entries.русский: подотчётный кому-л. (to), ответственный за что-л. (for)
entries.register: neutral to formal; the standard word in management, government, and journalism about both
entries.complement: after to, a person or body that can demand the explanation — a noun or pronoun only, never a gerund (✗ accountable to hiring); after for, the thing you must explain — a noun phrase or a gerund (accountable for keeping the receipts), and never a to-infinitive (✗ accountable for to keep the receipts). No that-clause attaches to either.
entries.pattern: be accountable to [person / body] · be accountable for [thing / verb-ing] · hold [someone] accountable for [thing] · accountable to [person] for [thing] — both slots at once · directly / ultimately / personally accountable
entries.variants: answerable to and answerable for split exactly the same way and are the slightly more formal, British-leaning twins. Responsible to / responsible for is the everyday pair and divides identically.
entries.contrast: To names the one who can demand an accounting; for names the thing accounted for. She is accountable to the board says who can call her in; She is accountable for the shortfall says what she will be asked about. The two slots can be filled at once — accountable to Congress for every dollar — which is the clearest proof they are not alternatives. Against responsible for, which can mean merely "caused it," accountable for always implies somebody is entitled to an explanation. ✗ accountable of and ✗ accountable with are errors.
entries.see also: answerable to, responsible for, liable for, liable to, subject to, to

entries.meaning: Used to something by repetition, so that it no longer registers as strange or difficult.
examples: She's accustomed to the noise from the freeway and sleeps right through it.
Crews here are accustomed to working in twenty below.
It took a month to get accustomed to the new software.
He is not accustomed to being interrupted.
Passengers accustomed to the old schedule kept showing up an hour early.
entries.русский: привыкший к — после to герундий, не инфинитив
entries.register: neutral to formal; used to is the everyday version
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (accustomed to working late) — never a to-infinitive. ✗ accustomed to work late is the classic error; the to here is a preposition, not an infinitive marker, which the noun test proves: accustomed to the work ✓. A that-clause is impossible.
entries.pattern: be accustomed to [noun / verb-ing] · become / grow / get accustomed to [noun / verb-ing] · accustom [someone] to [noun / verb-ing]
entries.variants: used to — identical in meaning, far commoner, informal to neutral. Habituated to and inured to are the clinical and the grim versions; inured to implies the thing endured is unpleasant.
entries.contrast: Accustomed to + -ing versus the habitual past used to + bare verb is the pair to keep straight: I'm accustomed to driving (I find it normal) is not I used to drive (I no longer do). An older accustomed to do survives in nineteenth-century prose and in a few frozen legal phrases, but in modern American English it reads as a mistake — write the gerund. Note also that the adjective describes a settled state while get accustomed to describes the process of arriving at it.
entries.see also: used to, familiar with, comfortable with, look forward to, to

entries.meaning: Introduced to someone, or informed enough about a subject to find your way around it.
examples: I'm only slightly acquainted with her husband.
Anyone acquainted with the case knows the timeline doesn't work.
It took the new hire a week to get acquainted with the filing system.
The judge is thoroughly acquainted with the record and won't need the summary.
We became acquainted with the neighbors over a fence repair neither of us wanted.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /əˈkweɪntəd wəθ/, the final consonant often voiced to /wəð/ before a vowel
entries.русский: знакомый с — с человеком или с предметом, темой
entries.register: formal-leaning; in speech Americans say know or familiar with and save acquainted with for introductions and legal statements
entries.complement: a noun phrase or pronoun naming a person, a subject, a document, or a place. A gerund is grammatical but rare and stiff (acquainted with running a floor crew), and a to-infinitive is impossible — ✗ acquainted with to run the crew. The noun test settles it: acquainted with the crew ✓, so with is doing ordinary prepositional work.
entries.pattern: be acquainted with [person / subject] · get / become acquainted with · acquaint [someone] with [noun] · be well / slightly / only vaguely acquainted with · make the acquaintance of — the noun frame, with of
entries.variants: familiar with is the neutral everyday synonym; conversant with is the formal one for a body of knowledge; know is the plain verb and takes a direct object with no preposition at all.
entries.contrast: Against familiar with, which reports how much you know, acquainted with keeps a trace of the introduction — you become acquainted with a person by meeting them, and the phrase is faintly cool about how well you know them. ✗ acquainted to is an error in every frame, including the causative: you acquaint someone with the rules, never ✗ to the rules. Note that the related noun changes the preposition twice over: an acquaintance with the material, but an acquaintance of mine.
entries.see also: familiar with, conversant with, cognizant of, aware of, with

entries.meaning: Unable to stop taking or doing something, whether that is meant literally or as a joke about a habit.
examples: He was addicted to prescription painkillers for two years.
Half the office is addicted to that cold brew from downstairs.
Kids who get addicted to scrolling sleep about an hour less.
She's addicted to buying supplies she already owns.
The clinic treats patients addicted to opioids and alcohol alike.
entries.русский: зависимый от, подсевший на — о наркотике или, шутливо, о привычке
entries.register: neutral in the clinical sense; casually hyperbolic in the other (addicted to that show)
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (addicted to checking her phone) — never a to-infinitive (✗ addicted to check) and never a clause.
entries.pattern: be / become / get addicted to [noun / verb-ing] · addict [someone] to [noun] · addicted to [substance]
entries.variants: hooked on is the informal equivalent and takes on, not to. Dependent on is the medical term for the physical half of addiction.
entries.contrast: ✗ addicted with and ✗ addicted of are errors. Against hooked on, which is slang and almost always light-hearted, addicted to carries the clinical sense unless the context is plainly joking. Note that the noun keeps the preposition — an addiction to painkillers — while the everyday alternative changes it: a dependence on painkillers.
entries.see also: hooked on, dependent on, obsessed with, crazy about, to

entries.meaning: Sharing a border or a wall with something — touching it, or as near as makes no difference.
examples: The lot adjacent to the school was rezoned for townhouses.
Park in the garage adjacent to the courthouse, not the lot across the street.
The mass is adjacent to the artery, which is why they won't operate.
Two rooms adjacent to the kitchen were knocked together into an office.
In the figure, the shaded square is adjacent to the right angle.
entries.русский: прилегающий к, соседний с — граничащий вплотную
entries.register: formal to technical — zoning ordinances, real-estate listings, radiology reports, geometry; conversation says next to
entries.type: adjective + preposition, working as a complex preposition of place
entries.complement: a noun phrase or pronoun naming a place or a physical thing — never a gerund (✗ adjacent to parking) and never a clause. Used attributively with no complement at all (the adjacent room), it is a plain adjective and not a preposition; that use is outside this entry.
entries.pattern: be adjacent to [place] · [noun] adjacent to [noun] · immediately / directly / physically adjacent to · the adjacent [noun] — attributive, no preposition
entries.variants: next to is the everyday equivalent; abutting and contiguous with are the surveyor's and the statute's words; bordering on adds a shared edge and carries a figurative use (bordering on rude) that adjacent to does not have.
entries.contrast: Adjacent to claims a shared boundary; close to claims only nearness. Two lots adjacent to each other touch; two lots close to each other need not. In American zoning and title work that difference decides cases, which is why the formal word survives. ✗ adjacent with and ✗ adjacent of are errors. The purely spatial prepositions this competes with — next to, beside, by — are catalogued in place and position.
entries.see also: close to, parallel to, perpendicular to, proximal to, distal to, to

entries.meaning: Running against someone's interest — of a ruling, a fact, a condition, or an opposing party.
examples: Counsel disclosed a client whose interests are adverse to the estate's.
The ruling was adverse to every party except the insurer.
Testimony adverse to the defense came from its own expert.
A finding adverse to the agency would cost it the contract.
Anything adverse to the bondholders has to appear in the filing.
entries.русский: противоречащий интересам, неблагоприятный для — юр./книжн.
entries.register: formal; an American meets it in legal filings (a position adverse to the trustee), in medical reporting (adverse event), and in finance, essentially never in conversation
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming an interest, a party, or a position — never a gerund (✗ adverse to signing) and never a to-infinitive. The word is also common attributively with no complement (adverse weather, an adverse ruling, adverse possession), which is the adjective alone.
entries.pattern: [noun] adverse to [interest / party] · take a position adverse to [noun] · adverse [noun] — attributive · adversely affect [noun] — the adverb, with no preposition
entries.variants: contrary to and opposed to cover the general sense in plain English; hostile to covers the personal one; unfavorable to is the neutral choice for rulings and conditions.
entries.contrast: Adverse is not averse, and this is the single commonest educated mix-up in American English. Averse to means personally disinclined and is what you want after I'm not: ✓ I'm not averse to a second cup, ✗ I'm not adverse to a second cup. Adverse to means working against someone's interest, and its subject is a condition, a ruling, or a party — not a feeling. Note also the frozen legal compounds, where no to follows at all: adverse party, adverse witness, adverse possession.
entries.see also: opposed to, prejudicial to, detrimental to, repugnant to, to

entries.meaning: Frightened of something, or unwilling to do something because of what might follow.
examples: She's been afraid of dogs since she was bitten at six.
He was afraid of saying the wrong thing in front of the whole department.
I'm not afraid of hard work — I'm afraid of pointless work.
They were afraid for their parents, who lived two blocks from the fire.
Don't be afraid of asking; the worst they can say is no.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /əˈfreɪd əv/, and before a consonant often /əˈfreɪd ə/
entries.русский: боящийся чего-л. — в русском «бояться» + родительный падеж
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (afraid of falling) — never a to-infinitive after of. The adjective also takes a bare to-infinitive with no preposition (afraid to ask) and a that-clause (afraid that we're too late), but those are different frames, not alternatives inside this one.
entries.pattern: be afraid of [noun / verb-ing] · be afraid to [verb] · be afraid (that) [clause] · be afraid for [someone] · afraid of [someone] -ing (afraid of the roof collapsing)
entries.variants: scared of is the everyday synonym, frightened of the slightly more formal one, terrified of the intensified one — all three take of.
entries.contrast: Afraid of doing versus afraid to do is a real difference. Afraid of falling names a fear of something that might happen to you; afraid to jump names a reluctance to act. I was afraid of waking her is about the risk; I was afraid to wake her is about hesitating. And afraid for changes the target entirely — afraid for the children means you fear on their behalf, not that you fear them. ✗ afraid from is an error.
entries.see also: scared of, frightened of, nervous about, worried about, of

entries.respell: uh-MEE-nuh-bul too; the older uh-MEN-uh-bul survives in law
entries.meaning: Willing to go along with something, when the subject is a person; open to being treated, analyzed, or sued, when it is a thing.
examples: The seller turned out to be amenable to closing two weeks early.
Nobody on the committee is amenable to another round of edits.
The infection proved amenable to a two-week course of antibiotics.
That question isn't amenable to a yes-or-no answer.
A foreign parent may still be amenable to suit in the state where it sells.
entries.русский: готовый согласиться на; о вещи — поддающийся (лечению, анализу); книжн.
entries.register: formal to neutral; the "willing" sense is ordinary business English, the "yields to" sense belongs to science, medicine, and law
entries.complement: a noun phrase or a gerund — amenable to moving the date ✓ — and never a to-infinitive: ✗ amenable to move the date. The noun test proves the point: amenable to the change ✓, so the to here is a preposition and the -ing form is obligatory.
entries.pattern: be amenable to [proposal / verb-ing] · be amenable to [treatment / analysis / suit] · find [someone] amenable to [noun] · perfectly / entirely / not especially amenable to
entries.variants: open to and receptive to are the everyday equivalents in the willingness sense; susceptible to and susceptible of cover the "yields to" sense; tractable covers it with no preposition at all.
entries.contrast: The subject decides the sense. With a person, amenable to means willing to go along: she's amenable to a later start. With a thing, it means it yields to some treatment or procedure: amenable to surgery, amenable to statistical analysis, and in law amenable to suit — subject to a court's power. Against opposed to, which is a settled position, amenable to reports a door left open. ✗ amenable with is an error.
entries.see also: susceptible to, susceptible of, conducive to, opposed to, subject to, to

entries.meaning: Corresponding in function or in structure of relations, so that reasoning about the one carries over to the other.
examples: The heart is analogous to a pump, though the metaphor gives out quickly.
Her situation is closely analogous to the one the court decided in 2019.
A bird's wing is analogous to an insect's wing but not homologous with it.
Billing by the hour here is analogous to metering electricity.
The claim is roughly analogous to arguing that umbrellas cause rain.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /əˈnæləɡəs tə/. The g is hard /ɡ/, unlike the /dʒ/ of the noun analogy — ✗ "uh-NAL-uh-jus" is a common misreading
entries.русский: аналогичный чему-л. — сходный по функции или по структуре отношений
entries.register: formal and scholarly — scientific writing, legal reasoning from precedent, academic prose; conversation says like
entries.complement: a noun phrase or a gerund (analogous to running the trial twice) — never a to-infinitive (✗ analogous to run the trial twice) and never a that-clause. A wh-clause is fine: analogous to what happens in the second reactor.
entries.pattern: be analogous to [noun / verb-ing] · a case analogous to [noun] · closely / roughly / only loosely analogous to · by analogy to [noun] — the noun frame
entries.variants: analogous with turns up but is not the standard American choice; comparable to and parallel to are the neutral alternatives; the noun goes both ways — an analogy to or an analogy with, catalogued in noun patterns.
entries.contrast: Analogous to claims that two things stand in the same relation, not that they look alike — a heart is analogous to a pump because of what it does, not what it resembles, while similar to claims plain likeness. In biology the word is a term of art opposed to homologous: a bird's wing and an insect's wing are analogous (same function, separate origins) and not homologous (same origin). ✗ analogous of and ✗ analogous from are errors.
entries.see also: similar to, equivalent to, parallel to, isomorphic to, to

entries.meaning: Supporting the main thing rather than being it — a service, a document, or a proceeding that exists to make the principal one work.
examples: Imaging and lab work are billed as services ancillary to the procedure.
The confidentiality letter is ancillary to the purchase agreement and expires with it.
Storage is ancillary to the shipping business, not a line of its own.
The court kept the counterclaim as a matter ancillary to the main action.
Everything else in the budget is ancillary to payroll.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˈænsəˌlɛri tə/. British English stresses the second syllable, an-SIL-uh-ree; American English does not
entries.русский: вспомогательный по отношению к, служебный при чём-л. — книжн./юр.
entries.register: formal — hospital billing (ancillary services), contracts (ancillary agreement), and federal courts (ancillary jurisdiction); it is an office and a filing word, not a spoken one
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the main thing supported. A gerund is possible in careful writing (ancillary to running the main plant) but rare, and a to-infinitive is impossible: ✗ ancillary to run the plant.
entries.pattern: be ancillary to [main activity] · [service / agreement] ancillary to [noun] · ancillary [noun] — attributive · merely / purely ancillary to
entries.variants: incidental to and collateral to are the near twins in legal drafting; subordinate to and secondary to are the plainer versions; auxiliary to is the older and slightly more mechanical one.
entries.contrast: Ancillary to says a thing exists to support the main thing; incidental to says it merely comes along with it. A hospital's lab is ancillary to patient care because it serves it; the parking fee is incidental to the visit because it just happens alongside. Against subordinate to, which ranks two things, ancillary to describes a supporting function and implies no chain of command. ✗ ancillary of and ✗ ancillary with are errors.
entries.see also: incidental to, incident to, subordinate to, appurtenant to, to

entries.meaning: Feeling strong displeasure — with a person, at a thing, or about a state of affairs.
examples: She was angry with her brother for weeks after the funeral.
Don't get angry at the referee; get better at defense.
Everyone in the room was angry about how the vote had been scheduled.
He's still angry with himself for not asking more questions.
I was angry that nobody had bothered to call.
entries.русский: сердитый на — with на человека, at на вещь, about из-за положения дел
entries.register: neutral; mad at is the American conversational default
entries.complement: noun phrase or pronoun after with and at; noun phrase or gerund after about (angry about being passed over) — never a to-infinitive after any of the three. A that-clause attaches to the bare adjective: angry that no one told her.
entries.pattern: be angry with [person] · be angry at [person or thing] · be angry about [situation] · be angry (that) [clause] · get angry with [person] about [thing]
entries.variants: angry at and angry with are both standard American English before a person; older handbooks insist on with for people and at for things, and that distribution still reads as slightly more careful, but angry at her is unremarkable in American print.
entries.contrast: The three prepositions split by target. With (and, in American usage, at) takes the person; about takes the situation; at alone is what you use for an inanimate cause (angry at the delay). You can be angry with your brother about the money — both slots filled at once — but ✗ angry with the money is wrong. Compare annoyed with, which follows the same split at lower intensity, and furious with, at higher.
entries.see also: mad at, annoyed with, furious with, upset about, with

entries.meaning: Mildly angry — the low end of the same scale that runs up through angry to furious.
examples: I'm annoyed with my landlord for ignoring three emails.
She looked annoyed at the interruption but waved him in.
Passengers were annoyed by the constant announcements.
He's annoyed about having to redo the entire form.
Try not to get annoyed with her; she's had a week of this.
entries.русский: раздражённый, недовольный кем-л. — слабее, чем angry
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or pronoun after with and at; noun phrase or gerund after about and by (annoyed by having to ask twice) — never a to-infinitive. A that-clause attaches to the bare adjective: annoyed that it took three calls.
entries.pattern: be annoyed with [person] · be annoyed at / about [thing or situation] · be annoyed by [the thing doing the annoying] · be annoyed (that) [clause] · annoyed with [person] for [verb-ing]
entries.variants: irritated with/by, irked by, and put out with all sit in the same range; bugged by is the casual American version.
entries.contrast: Three prepositions, three roles. With takes the person you are annoyed at; about or at takes the situation; by takes the cause acting on you and is the passive-flavored one — annoyed by the noise treats the noise as the agent, while annoyed about the noise treats it as the topic of your complaint. Use for + -ing to name what the person did: annoyed with him for forgetting. ✗ annoyed of is an error.
entries.see also: angry with, upset about, fed up with, patient with, by

entries.meaning: Obliged to give an account of yourself to someone, or for something.
examples: The inspector general is answerable to Congress, not to the agency she audits.
Elected officials are answerable to the people who put them there.
He behaved as if he were answerable to nobody at all.
The contractor is answerable for every subcontractor on the site.
She is answerable to the trustees for how the endowment is invested.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˈænsərəbəl tə/ — and note the silent w, as in the verb
entries.русский: подотчётный кому-л., обязанный отчитываться за что-л.
entries.register: formal, with a British tilt; American English usually reaches for accountable to or the plain reports to, and keeps answerable for rhetorical weight (answerable to no one)
entries.complement: after to, a noun or pronoun naming the person or body owed the explanation — never a gerund; after for, a noun phrase or a gerund (answerable for having signed it), never a to-infinitive.
entries.pattern: be answerable to [person / body] · be answerable for [thing / verb-ing] · answerable to [person] for [thing] · answerable to no one — the fixed rhetorical frame
entries.variants: accountable to / accountable for is the ordinary American equivalent and splits identically. Responsible to / responsible for is the everyday pair. The verb answer itself takes the same two prepositions in the same two senses, with no adjective in between.
entries.contrast: The split matches accountable to, accountable for exactly: to takes the one who may demand an answer, for takes the matter. What separates the two adjectives is tone — answerable is the older and more moralized word, at home in answerable to history and answerable to the voters, while accountable is the neutral organizational term. Note the trap of the other answerable, meaning "able to be answered" (an answerable charge), which takes no preposition at all. See also the zero-preposition verb entry at answer: you answer to a supervisor but answer a question, with nothing in between.
entries.see also: accountable to, accountable for, responsible for, liable for, liable to, answer, to

entries.meaning: Coming before something else, either in time or in the order of reasoning.
examples: Every condition antecedent to closing had been satisfied by Friday.
The right of way was antecedent to the subdivision and survived it.
Hume's question is whether any idea is antecedent to experience.
Facts antecedent to the merger are outside the scope of the audit.
A duty of care antecedent to the contract may still be owed.
entries.русский: предшествующий чему-л. — во времени или в порядке рассуждения; книжн.
entries.register: formal and dated — nineteenth-century prose, older judicial opinions, philosophy; an American meets it in quoted authority, not in speech, where the words are before and prior to
entries.type: adjective + preposition, often working as a complex preposition
entries.complement: a noun phrase, or a gerund in careful writing (antecedent to filing suit) — never a to-infinitive (✗ antecedent to file suit) and never a clause.
entries.pattern: [noun] antecedent to [event] · be antecedent to [noun] · logically / temporally antecedent to · the antecedent — the noun, in grammar the word a pronoun points back to
entries.variants: prior to is the living formal equivalent, previous to the slightly stiffer one, anterior to the exact synonym in the same dated register, and before the plain word that beats all of them.
entries.contrast: Antecedent to covers both coming earlier in time and coming first in logic, and the second is what keeps it alive in philosophical writing: a duty antecedent to any promise is not merely earlier, it is more basic. Against previous to and prior to, which are purely temporal, that logical use is the only reason to prefer it. Do not confuse the adjective with the grammatical noun antecedent, which takes of (the antecedent of "which"). For the plain time prepositions see time.
entries.see also: anterior to, posterior to, previous to, preparatory to, subject to, to

entries.meaning: Situated toward the front of the body, or toward the back of it, relative to some other structure.
examples: The sternum is anterior to the heart.
The kidneys lie posterior to the intestines, against the back wall.
The lesion sits just anterior to the ear canal.
The esophagus runs posterior to the trachea.
In the older reports, any conveyance anterior to the mortgage took priority — the archaic temporal use.
entries.русский: расположенный спереди / сзади от — анат., относительно другой структуры
entries.register: technical — anatomy, radiology, and dentistry, where they are the everyday professional words; plus an archaic formal use for time, found in old legal and scholarly prose and nowhere else
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a body structure, or, in the dated temporal use, a date or an event — never a gerund and never a clause. Both words also stand attributively with no complement (the anterior wall, the posterior fossa), which is the plain adjective.
entries.pattern: [structure] anterior to [structure] · [structure] posterior to [structure] · just / immediately anterior to · anteroposterior — the compound, as in an AP film
entries.variants: in front of and behind are the plain equivalents; ventral to and dorsal to are the comparative-anatomy pair, which for a four-legged animal is not the same axis; prior to and subsequent to replace the dated temporal use.
entries.contrast: In American clinical use these are strictly spatial, and the temporal sense is dead outside quotation. Write the incision is anterior to the ear, but not ✗ anterior to the surgery for "before it" unless you are imitating older prose. The pair is also relative, not absolute: a structure is anterior to something, so the object is obligatory — the anterior surface alone is the attributive adjective, not this pattern. In dentistry the plural nouns anteriors and posteriors name the front and back teeth and take no preposition.
entries.see also: antecedent to, proximal to, distal to, adjacent to, previous to, to

entries.meaning: Uneasy about something ahead — and, in the infinitive frame, keen for it to happen.
examples: He's anxious about the biopsy results.
She was anxious about moving so far from her sister.
Parents are anxious about the new attendance policy.
I'm anxious to get started before the weather turns.
Everyone in the waiting room was anxious for news.
entries.русский: тревожащийся о чём-л.; с инфинитивом (anxious to) — страстно желающий
entries.register: neutral; slightly more formal than nervous about
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after about (anxious about flying) — never a to-infinitive after about. The adjective separately takes a bare to-infinitive (anxious to help), for + noun (anxious for news), and a that-clause (anxious that nothing goes wrong, with an optional subjunctive in formal writing).
entries.pattern: be anxious about [noun / verb-ing] · be anxious to [verb] · be anxious for [noun] · be anxious (that) [clause]
entries.variants: nervous about and worried about are the everyday equivalents; apprehensive about is the formal one.
entries.contrast: Anxious about is worry; anxious to is eagerness. Anxious about starting means dreading it; anxious to start means impatient to begin — the same adjective, opposite emotional loads, decided entirely by the preposition versus the infinitive. Purists once objected to the eager sense altogether, but it is standard American English now. Anxious for splits the difference: anxious for the results is wanting them badly, usually with an edge of worry.
entries.see also: nervous about, worried about, eager for, afraid of, about

entries.meaning: Informed of something by someone whose job it was to tell you.
examples: Keep me apprised of any change in her condition.
The board was never apprised of the second offer.
Counsel will keep the court apprised of the settlement talks.
Residents were apprised of the shutoff two days in advance.
He claims he was not apprised of being named in the complaint.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /əˈpraɪzd əv/, and before a consonant often /əˈpraɪzd ə/
entries.русский: поставленный в известность о — офиц.
entries.register: formal — police reports, corporate memoranda, and court filings, where keep the court apprised is a fixed phrase; conversation says told or kept posted
entries.complement: a noun phrase or a gerund (apprised of being under investigation) — never a to-infinitive (✗ apprised of to change the date). A that-clause attaches to the verb, not to this frame: the clerk apprised him that the hearing had moved, but ✗ apprised of that the hearing had moved.
entries.pattern: be apprised of [noun / verb-ing] · keep [someone] apprised of [noun] · apprise [someone] of [noun] — the active verb · fully / duly / promptly apprised of
entries.variants: informed of and notified of are the plain equivalents and take the same of; advised of is the police and banking version; made aware of is the everyday paraphrase.
entries.contrast: Apprised is not appraised. To apprise is to inform; to appraise is to value or assess, and it takes a direct object with no preposition: ✓ the jeweler appraised the ring, ✗ I was appraised of the situation. This misspelling is common enough in American business writing to be worth a deliberate check. Against aware of, which reports a state of knowledge however acquired, apprised of reports that somebody actively told you.
entries.see also: aware of, cognizant of, conscious of, mindful of, of

entries.meaning: Attached by law to a piece of land, so that whoever takes the land takes the right along with it.
examples: The driveway easement is appurtenant to the back parcel and passes with the deed.
Parking space 14 is appurtenant to the unit, not separately salable.
Water rights appurtenant to the ranch were valued separately in the estate.
The declaration lists every right appurtenant to ownership of a unit.
A dock permit appurtenant to the lot cannot be transferred to a neighbor.
entries.русский: принадлежащий земельному участку — юр., переходит вместе с землёй
entries.register: legal, and narrowly so — real-property law, deeds, title reports, and condominium declarations; outside a closing binder an American will never meet it
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming land, an estate, or a right attached to land — never a gerund, never a clause. The word is also used attributively in the frozen term an easement appurtenant, where the noun comes first and no complement follows.
entries.pattern: an easement appurtenant to [parcel] · [right] appurtenant to [estate] · rights and privileges appurtenant to [noun] · the appurtenances — the noun, in the deed formula together with all appurtenances
entries.variants: incident to is the broader legal synonym; attached to and belonging to are the plain-English versions; pertaining to covers the looser sense of "having to do with."
entries.contrast: The point of the word is that the right travels with the land. An easement appurtenant to a parcel passes automatically to the next owner; an easement in gross belongs to a person and does not. Against incident to, which is general, appurtenant to is specific to real property. Do not confuse it with pertinent to, which means relevant: ✗ the question is appurtenant to the issue is not English. ✗ appurtenant of and ✗ appurtenant with are errors.
entries.see also: incident to, ancillary to, incidental to, pertinent to, to

entries.meaning: Feeling guilt or dishonor about something you have done, or about someone connected to you.
examples: She was ashamed of the way she'd spoken to the clerk.
Nobody should be ashamed of needing help.
He was ashamed of himself before the front door closed.
I'm ashamed to say I never opened the envelope.
They were ashamed of their father for the first time in their lives.
entries.русский: стыдящийся чего-л. — «мне стыдно за»
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (ashamed of lying) — never a to-infinitive after of. The adjective also takes a bare to-infinitive (ashamed to admit it) and a that-clause (ashamed that he'd said nothing).
entries.pattern: be ashamed of [noun / verb-ing] · be ashamed of [someone] for [verb-ing] · be ashamed to [verb] · be ashamed (that) [clause] · ashamed of oneself
entries.variants: embarrassed about / by covers the mild social version; ashamed is the moral one. Mortified by is the intensified form.
entries.contrast: Ashamed of doing versus ashamed to do — the first looks back at something already done, the second hesitates before doing it. I'm ashamed of asking means the asking happened and I regret it; I'm ashamed to ask means I have not asked and would rather not. ✗ ashamed about is not idiomatic for the moral sense — that is embarrassed about's territory — and ✗ ashamed for works only when someone else's conduct is meant (I'm ashamed for you, feeling shame on your behalf).
entries.see also: guilty of, sorry for, proud of, of

entries.meaning: Struck by something so unexpected that it briefly stops you.
examples: I was astonished at how quickly the line moved.
She was astonished at the size of the bill.
Visitors are always astonished by the acoustics in that room.
He was astonished to find his name on the list.
They were astonished at finding the cabin exactly as they'd left it.
entries.русский: поражённый, изумлённый чем-л.
entries.register: neutral to literary; stronger and rarer than surprised
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after at and by (astonished at finding the door open) — never a to-infinitive after either. A bare to-infinitive attaches to the adjective directly (astonished to learn), as does a that-clause (astonished that anyone showed up).
entries.pattern: be astonished at [noun / verb-ing] · be astonished by [noun] · be astonished to [verb] · be astonished (that) [clause]
entries.variants: astonished at and astonished by are both standard; at leans toward the reaction, by toward the cause. Amazed at/by, astounded by, and stunned by are the near-neighbors.
entries.contrast: Same split as surprised and shocked: at frames the thing as what you are reacting to; by frames it as what acted on you — astonished at the price is your reaction to a number, astonished by the news is the news doing something to you. With a verb, the two available frames mean different things: astonished at hearing it reports the moment of hearing, astonished to hear it reports the reaction on hearing. ✗ astonished of and ✗ astonished from are errors.
entries.see also: surprised at, shocked at, impressed with, at

entries.meaning: Able to be had, used, reached, or spoken to.
examples: Transcripts are available to any student who requests one.
The gym is available for private events on Sundays.
Dr. Alvarez is available to meet on Thursday morning.
That grant is only available to first-time applicants.
Two of the three units are still available for rent.
entries.русский: доступный кому-л. — который можно получить, использовать или к кому можно обратиться
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or pronoun naming a person or group after to; noun phrase or gerund after for (available for hire, available for booking) — never a gerund after to. The adjective also takes a bare to-infinitive meaning "free to" (available to talk at four), which is a different frame from available to + person.
entries.pattern: be available to [person] · be available for [purpose / verb-ing] · be available to [verb] · make [something] available to [person] · available from [source] · available at [place]
entries.variants: open to covers the "not restricted" sense; accessible to the "reachable" one.
entries.contrast: Available to names who can get it; available for names what it is for. The report is available to members (who may have it) versus The room is available for meetings (what it may be used for). The infinitive frame is a third thing entirely: She's available to answer questions is about her free time, not about who has access to her. ✗ available with is an error, though available in is correct for formats and sizes (available in blue).
entries.see also: useful for, prepared for, suitable for, to, for

entries.meaning: Knowing that something exists or is the case.
examples: Were you aware of the change in the return policy?
She's aware of how it looks and doesn't care.
He became aware of someone standing behind him.
The board was fully aware that the numbers wouldn't hold.
I'm painfully aware of having missed the obvious answer.
entries.русский: осознающий что-л., знающий о — «в курсе»
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, gerund (aware of being watched), or a wh-clause (aware of what it would cost) — never a to-infinitive. A that-clause attaches to the bare adjective with no of: aware that the deadline had moved, and ✗ aware of that the deadline had moved is an error.
entries.pattern: be aware of [noun / verb-ing / wh-clause] · be aware (that) [clause] · become / make [someone] aware of [noun] · acutely / dimly / painfully aware of [noun]
entries.variants: conscious of is the close synonym and behaves identically; cognizant of is the bureaucratic version.
entries.contrast: The of drops before a that-clause. This is the single error worth watching: ✓ aware of the problem, ✓ aware that there's a problem, ✗ aware of that there's a problem. Against conscious of, which leans toward felt, bodily awareness (conscious of a draft), aware of leans toward knowledge. And note aware has no comparative with more aware of as a fixed pattern — it takes degree adverbs instead: fully, keenly, vaguely aware of.
entries.see also: conscious of, familiar with, sensitive to, of

entries.meaning: Not good at something, or harmful to something — the split depends entirely on the preposition.
examples: I'm hopelessly bad at spelling anyone's name right the first time.
Standing all day is bad for your back.
He's bad with directions and always has been.
She's bad about answering email between semesters.
Our whole family is bad at small talk.
entries.русский: неумелый в чём-л. — bad at неумелый, bad for вредный, bad with не умеющий обращаться с
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after at (bad at remembering names) — never a to-infinitive. ✗ bad at remember names and ✗ bad at to remember are both wrong. After for the complement is a person or thing affected, and a gerund is possible (bad for keeping food fresh is odd; bad for your teeth is the norm).
entries.pattern: be bad at [noun / verb-ing] · be bad for [person / thing] · be bad with [category of thing one handles badly] · be bad about [verb-ing] (habitually negligent)
entries.variants: poor at is the formal version, terrible at and awful at the emphatic ones, hopeless at and useless at the self-deprecating ones, slow at the specific one. All take at.
entries.contrast: Three prepositions, three meanings, and they are not interchangeable. Bad at math = unskilled. Bad for you = harmful. Bad with money = unable to handle a whole category well — with is the one used for people, animals, money, and tools (bad with kids, bad with numbers). A fourth frame, bad about + -ing, means chronically failing to do something: I'm bad about returning calls. ✗ bad in math is an error in American English, though bad in bed and bad in a crisis are fixed idioms where in names a situation.
entries.see also: good at, poor at, terrible at, hopeless at, harmful to, at

entries.meaning: Built or derived from a source, a set of facts, or a principle.
examples: The screenplay is based on a magazine article from 1974.
Rates are based on your driving record, not your zip code.
She made the call based on twenty years of doing this.
The whole argument is based on assuming that nobody moves.
Their pricing is based upon volume, tier by tier.
entries.русский: основанный на — на источнике, фактах или принципе
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (based on assuming the worst) — never a to-infinitive and never a that-clause. ✗ based on that the market recovers must be based on the assumption that the market recovers.
entries.pattern: be based on [noun / verb-ing] · [noun] based on [noun] · base [something] on [something] · based on [noun], [clause] — the dangling sentence-adverbial use
entries.variants: based upon is the formal equivalent, common in contracts and older prose. Based in is a different word combination meaning headquartered, not derived: a firm based in Denver.
entries.contrast: Based on versus based in is the trap: The movie is based on a true story (derived from) versus The company is based in Seattle (located at). ✗ based off of is widespread in American speech and still nonstandard in writing; editors change it to based on. The floating sentence-opener Based on the survey, we cut the budget is criticized as a dangling participle — the budget is not based on the survey, the decision is — and careful writing prefers On the basis of or Judging by. See on the basis of.
entries.see also: dependent on, related to, subject to, on

entries.meaning: Under an obligation to someone who did you a favor, and constrained by it.
examples: He ran without taking corporate money so he'd be beholden to nobody.
The board is beholden to two donors who between them fund the building.
I don't want to be beholden to my brother-in-law for a job.
Editors who are beholden to advertisers stop printing certain stories.
She remained beholden to the professor who had vouched for her.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /bəˈhoʊldən tə/ — the d is usually swallowed into the n, giving "bih-HOHL-un-tuh"
entries.русский: обязанный кому-л. за услугу и связанный этим — книжн.
entries.register: formal to literary, and a standing word in American political journalism (beholden to donors); it survives almost nowhere else
entries.complement: a noun or pronoun naming the person, group, or interest you owe — never a gerund (✗ beholden to giving) and never an infinitive. A second slot with for names the debt: beholden to her for the introduction.
entries.pattern: be beholden to [person / group] · beholden to [person] for [favor] · beholden to no one — by far the commonest frame · feel / remain beholden to
entries.variants: indebted to is the neutral equivalent and takes for the same way; obligated to covers the duty; in someone's debt is the everyday paraphrase; under obligation to is the formal noun frame.
entries.contrast: Beholden to is about owing a favor that constrains you, which is why it is nearly always negative in American use: to say a senator is beholden to an industry is to say the industry owns the vote. Against obligated to, obliged to, which names a duty that may be perfectly honorable, beholden to names a dependence somebody would rather not admit. Note that the word is archaic outside this frame — beholden is not a participle of behold in modern English, whatever it looks like. ✗ beholden of and ✗ beholden by are errors.
entries.see also: obligated to, obliged to, grateful to, answerable to, dependent on, to

entries.meaning: Having legal force against someone, so that they cannot walk away from it.
examples: The settlement is binding on both parties and their successors.
A ruling from the Ninth Circuit is binding on district courts in that circuit.
The letter of intent is binding upon the seller only as to confidentiality.
Arbitration under this section is final and binding on the employer.
Nothing said in mediation is binding on anyone unless it is written down.
entries.русский: обязательный для кого-л. — юр., имеющий обязательную силу
entries.register: legal and formal; the natural home is a contract, an arbitration clause, or an appellate opinion, and binding upon is the drafter's variant of the same phrase
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the person or entity bound — a party, a successor, an agency, a court — and never a gerund (✗ binding on signing) and never a clause. What the obligation is does not go in this slot; that goes in the sentence around it.
entries.pattern: be binding on [party] · binding upon [party] and [party's successors] — the standard drafting formula · legally / contractually binding on · a binding agreement — attributive, no complement
entries.variants: binding upon is stylistically identical and commoner in drafted documents; enforceable against is the sharper term for the same idea; bind as a verb takes a direct object with no preposition (the agreement binds the parties).
entries.contrast: Binding on takes the person bound, while bound by takes the thing that binds — the same fact from the two ends: the arbitration clause is binding on the parties = the parties are bound by the arbitration clause. Do not confuse either with the temporal upon: binding upon execution means "binding as soon as it is signed," and there the upon is a time preposition with a different job. ✗ binding to and ✗ binding for are errors in this sense.
entries.see also: bound by, enforceable against, subject to, incumbent on, incumbent upon, on

entries.meaning: Tired of something because it holds no interest.
examples: The kids got bored with the museum after twenty minutes.
She's bored with explaining the same policy every August.
I was bored by the first hour and asleep by the second.
He gets bored with any project once the hard part is over.
Nobody is bored with the paycheck, just with the work.
entries.русский: которому скучно от чего-л., наскучивший
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (bored with waiting) — never a to-infinitive. Bored to exists only in the fixed hyperboles bored to death and bored to tears, which are not this pattern.
entries.pattern: be bored with [noun / verb-ing] · be bored by [the thing that bores you] · get bored with [noun / verb-ing] · bored out of one's mind
entries.variants: bored with and bored by are both standard American English. Bored of is now extremely common in speech on both sides of the Atlantic and still marked in careful American writing — it began as a British colloquialism, modeled on tired of, and editors change it to with. If you want a safe choice, use with.
entries.contrast: With takes the thing you have had enough of; by takes the thing actively boring you — bored with the job is your state, bored by his lecture points at the cause, exactly as annoyed with / annoyed by divides. Against tired of, which can mean either weary or fed up, bored with is specifically about lack of interest, and against fed up with, which carries irritation, bored with carries only flatness.
entries.see also: tired of, fed up with, sick of, interested in, with

entries.meaning: Legally or morally tied to a rule, a promise, or a document, and unable to disregard it.
examples: Everyone who signs is bound by the confidentiality clause for five years.
The court is bound by precedent it may privately dislike.
I'm bound by what I told them last week, whether or not it was smart.
Employees are bound by the handbook only where it tracks the contract.
She didn't feel bound by an agreement she'd never seen.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /baʊnd bə/, and the d usually drops before a consonant: "BOWN-buh"
entries.русский: связанный чем-л. — правилом, обещанием, документом
entries.register: neutral to formal; ordinary in contracts, oaths, and journalism, and common in everyday speech about rules
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the rule, promise, or document that constrains — never a gerund (✗ bound by keeping quiet) and never a to-infinitive. The other bound patterns take entirely different complements and are listed under Contrast.
entries.pattern: be bound by [contract / rule / oath] · feel bound by [noun] · legally / morally / contractually bound by · bound by law to [verb] — the two frames stacked
entries.variants: subject to covers the same ground more loosely; governed by is the neutral drafting word; tied to is the informal one; bound to + noun survives in bound to secrecy and bound to an apprenticeship.
entries.contrast: Three different bounds live behind this word, and only one of them is this entry. Bound by + noun means constrained by a rule (bound by the NDA). Bound to + bare verb means certain to happen and has nothing to do with obligation (it's bound to rain) — the to there is an infinitive marker, not a preposition. Bound for + place names a destination (bound for Denver), a use catalogued in participial prepositions. Keeping the three apart is worth the trouble, because ✗ bound by to rain and ✗ bound to the NDA are both wrong.
entries.see also: binding on, binding upon, subject to, obligated to, obliged to, committed to, by

entries.meaning: Occupied by something that is taking up your time.
examples: She's busy with the year-end close until the fifteenth.
He was busy with getting the storm windows up before the rain.
The whole crew is busy with a rush order and nobody can take the call.
Don't bother him — he's busy fixing the dishwasher.
I'm too busy this week to take on anything else.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˈbɪzi wəθ/ — note the spelling trap: busy is pronounced with /ɪ/, not the /u/ the u suggests
entries.русский: занятый чем-л.
entries.register: neutral and everyday
entries.complement: a noun phrase or a gerund (busy with getting the truck loaded) — never a to-infinitive after with: ✗ busy with to load the truck. The adjective's other frame takes a bare -ing with no preposition at all (busy loading the truck), which is the commoner construction in speech.
entries.pattern: be busy with [noun / verb-ing] · be busy [verb-ing] — no preposition · keep [someone] busy with [noun] · too busy for [noun] · too busy to [verb] — infinitive after too
entries.variants: occupied with and tied up with are the near equivalents; swamped with and buried in are the informal intensifiers; engaged in is the formal one.
entries.contrast: Busy with + noun, busy + -ing with nothing between, and too busy to + infinitive are three separate frames, and mixing them produces the standard errors: ✗ busy with cook dinner, ✗ busy to cook dinner. Note also the difference between busy with the kids (they are what occupies you) and busy for the kids (which is not English) — the "on behalf of" idea needs a rewrite. ✗ busy in cooking is an Indian-English pattern that American readers hear as foreign, though it is centuries old.
entries.see also: involved in, engaged to, committed to, content with, with

entries.meaning: Having the power, skill, or disposition to do something.
examples: She's capable of running the department without any help.
The engine is capable of two hundred thousand miles with care.
I didn't think he was capable of that kind of patience.
Anyone is capable of making that mistake at four in the morning.
The new scanner is capable of reading damaged plates.
entries.русский: способный на что-л., умеющий — после of герундий
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (capable of running the whole shift alone) — never a to-infinitive. ✗ capable to do it is one of the most common errors in this file; the correct forms are capable of doing it or able to do it, and the two adjectives are not interchangeable in structure.
entries.pattern: be capable of [noun / verb-ing] · more than capable of [verb-ing] · capable of [noun] (capable of great cruelty)
entries.variants: able to + infinitive is the everyday equivalent with the opposite structure. Up to + -ing is the informal one (up to running it alone).
entries.contrast: Capable of + -ing versus able to + verb is the pair to memorize, because they mean nearly the same thing and take opposite complements: ✓ capable of finishing, ✓ able to finish, ✗ capable to finish, ✗ able of finishing. Note also the flavor difference: capable of often implies latent capacity — including the capacity to do harm (capable of murder) — while able to reports plain ability in a situation. Incapable of is the negative and behaves identically.
entries.see also: incapable of, expert at, skilled at, good at, of

entries.meaning: Taking pains — with a thing, about a decision, of a danger, or to do something right.
examples: Be careful with that box; the bottom is soft.
She's careful about who she lends money to.
Careful of the loose railing on the second landing.
He was careful to copy the whole team on the reply.
You have to be careful with dogs you don't know.
entries.русский: осторожный с — with с вещью, about в решении, of остерегаться, to не забыть сделать
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase after with and of; noun phrase or gerund after about (careful about choosing a contractor) — never a to-infinitive after any preposition, though the adjective takes a bare infinitive directly (careful to lock up), which is a separate frame and a very common one.
entries.pattern: be careful with [thing handled] · be careful about [matter / verb-ing] · be careful of [hazard] · be careful to [verb] · be careful (that) [clause] · Careful! (imperative alone)
entries.variants: cautious about, wary of, and particular about cover neighboring ground; watch out for is the informal equivalent of careful of.
entries.contrast: Four frames, four jobs. Careful with the glasses = handle the thing gently. Careful about what you promise = exercise judgment in a matter. Careful of the step = watch out for a hazard, slightly formal in American English, where watch out for or mind is commoner. Careful to sign both copies = don't forget to do it. The infinitive frame is the one that means "make sure you do"; ✗ careful of signing would not carry that meaning at all.
entries.see also: suspicious of, sensitive to, serious about, with

entries.meaning: Free of doubt — or, in the infinitive frame, guaranteed to happen.
examples: I'm certain of the date because it was my mother's birthday.
She wasn't certain about signing a two-year lease.
Make certain of the spelling before it goes to print.
Rain is certain to ruin the Saturday game.
Nobody was certain that the vote would even be held.
entries.русский: уверенный в чём-л.; с инфинитивом — непременно случится
entries.register: neutral to formal; sure is the everyday word
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, gerund (certain of winning), or a wh-clause (certain about what she saw) — never a to-infinitive after the preposition. A that-clause attaches to the bare adjective (certain that he'd locked it), and a bare to-infinitive attaches directly with a different meaning (certain to happen = bound to happen).
entries.pattern: be certain of [noun / verb-ing] · be certain about [matter] · be certain (that) [clause] · be certain to [verb] · make certain of [noun] · for certain
entries.variants: sure of / sure about is the everyday twin and follows every one of these frames. Positive about is the emphatic conversational version.
entries.contrast: Certain of versus certain to is a genuine ambiguity trap: He's certain of promotion means he feels sure; He's certain to be promoted means it is bound to happen and says nothing about his feelings. Of leans toward a fact you are confident in (certain of the date); about leans toward a matter you have considered (certain about the decision), and about is the one that takes a wh-clause comfortably. ✗ certain for is an error.
entries.see also: sure of, confident of, confused about, aware of, of

entries.meaning: Belonging to the recognizable pattern of a person, group, style, or period.
examples: The long opening sentence is characteristic of her later essays.
Fog like this is characteristic of the coast in June.
Restraint was characteristic of the whole administration.
That kind of joinery is characteristic of Shaker furniture.
It's characteristic of him to send a note the next morning.
entries.русский: характерный для, свойственный кому-л. или чему-л.
entries.register: formal to neutral; common in academic and critical writing
entries.complement: noun phrase or pronoun, and a gerund where the thing described is an action (characteristic of dismissing critics out of hand is possible but heavy) — never a to-infinitive and never a clause.
entries.pattern: be characteristic of [person / group / period] · [noun] characteristic of [noun] · it is characteristic of [someone] to [verb]
entries.variants: typical of is the everyday equivalent and can be mildly disapproving; distinctive of stresses what sets something apart; peculiar to means found in that one place only.
entries.contrast: Characteristic of is neutral; typical of often is not. That's typical of him usually means he has disappointed you again, while That's characteristic of him is a description. Note the frame It's characteristic of her to volunteer first, where the infinitive belongs to the it-construction and not to the preposition. ✗ characteristic for and ✗ characteristic to are errors, though peculiar to and unique to correctly take to.
entries.see also: typical of, similar to, known for, of

entries.meaning: Near — in space, in relationship, in quantity, or in time.
examples: Their new place is close to the water treatment plant, unfortunately.
She's very close to her older sister.
Repairs came close to four thousand dollars.
He was close to walking out in the middle of the meeting.
We're close to having enough signatures.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /kloʊs tə/ — note the adjective is /kloʊs/ with an s, not the verb /kloʊz/
entries.русский: близкий к — в пространстве, в отношениях, по количеству или во времени
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (close to giving up) — never a to-infinitive. ✗ close to give up is the error the noun test catches: close to the end ✓, so the to is a preposition.
entries.pattern: be close to [place / person / amount / verb-ing] · come close to [verb-ing] · close to [number] · nowhere close to [noun / verb-ing]
entries.variants: near to is possible but near alone is the American default before a place (near the airport). On the verge of + -ing is the formal equivalent of the "about to" sense.
entries.contrast: Three senses, one preposition. Physical (close to the station), emotional (close to her grandmother), and quantitative or imminent (close to sixty, close to quitting). The last of these competes with about to, which takes a bare infinitive: ✓ close to quitting, ✓ about to quit, ✗ close to quit. Note that close in the "nearly" sense also works adverbially with no to at all (close on a hundred people), and that the neighboring spatial preposition near is treated in its own right.
entries.see also: related to, similar to, ready for, near, to

entries.meaning: Covering exactly the same range or scope as something else, with no part of either falling outside the other.
examples: The insurer's duty to defend is not coextensive with its duty to indemnify.
The statute's reach is coextensive with the commerce power, and no wider.
The city's water district is roughly coextensive with the county line.
The class of people harmed is not coextensive with the class who filed.
He argued that the moral rule is coextensive with the legal one here.
entries.русский: совпадающий по объёму с — книжн./юр., покрывающий ровно ту же область
entries.register: formal and technical — legal opinions, philosophy, and logic, where it is a precise word for "covering exactly the same ground"; never conversational
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the other extent, scope, or set — never a gerund and never a clause. The two things compared must be of the same kind: a duty with a duty, a set with a set, a term with a term.
entries.pattern: be coextensive with [scope / term / set] · exactly / not quite / roughly coextensive with · coextensive in scope with [noun]
entries.variants: coterminous with is the near twin and is commoner for periods of time and for boundaries; congruent with and identical to are the plainer words; conterminous with is the geographer's spelling for shared borders.
entries.contrast: Coextensive with says two things cover the same range; coterminous with says they begin and end together. A duty coextensive with a risk is exactly as broad as the risk; a lease coterminous with the loan expires the day the loan does. Against equivalent to, which claims equal value, coextensive with claims equal extent and nothing more. ✗ coextensive to is an error.
entries.see also: coterminous with, concurrent with, congruent to, congruent with, equivalent to, with

entries.meaning: Aware of something, and aware of it in a way you are prepared to be held to.
examples: The committee was fully cognizant of the risk when it approved the loan.
Officers must be cognizant of the policy before they use the device.
She was cognizant of being the only person in the room who had read it.
The opinion is cognizant of the burden this puts on small filers.
We are cognizant of the deadline and are working through the weekend.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˈkɑɡnəzənt əv/; the older KON-uh-zunt, with a silent g, still turns up in law
entries.русский: осведомлённый о — книжн./юр.
entries.register: formal — memos, opinions, and official statements; in speech it sounds like a person reaching for a bigger word than aware
entries.complement: a noun phrase or a gerund (cognizant of being the only one there) — never a to-infinitive (✗ cognizant of to be there). A that-clause attaches to the bare adjective with no preposition: cognizant that the deadline had passed ✓, but ✗ cognizant of that the deadline had passed.
entries.pattern: be cognizant of [noun / verb-ing] · be cognizant (that) [clause] · fully / well / painfully cognizant of · take cognizance of [noun] — the noun frame, standard in law
entries.variants: aware of is the neutral everyday word; conscious of stresses the noticing; mindful of adds that you are letting the fact guide you; apprised of means somebody told you.
entries.contrast: Against aware of, which is the plain word, cognizant of is a register choice and nothing more — it means the same thing at a higher altitude, and American editors often cut it back. The legal noun phrase take cognizance of is different in kind: a court that takes cognizance of a matter assumes jurisdiction over it. ✗ cognizant about, ✗ cognizant to, and ✗ cognizant with are errors.
entries.see also: aware of, conscious of, mindful of, apprised of, of

entries.meaning: At ease with a thing, an arrangement, or a course of action — willing to accept it.
examples: Are you comfortable with the numbers as they stand?
She's not comfortable with speaking in front of the board.
I'd be more comfortable with a written agreement.
He's comfortable with silence in a way most people aren't.
Nobody was comfortable with how fast the vote was scheduled.
entries.русский: спокойно относящийся к чему-л., которого что-л. устраивает
entries.register: neutral; heavily used in American workplace English
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (comfortable with saying no) — never a to-infinitive after with. The adjective separately takes a bare to-infinitive (comfortable to sit in, describing the chair, not the sitter), which is a different construction.
entries.pattern: be comfortable with [noun / verb-ing] · be comfortable (that) [clause] · feel comfortable with [noun] · comfortable in [a role or setting]
entries.variants: at ease with is the formal version; okay with and fine with are the conversational ones and take the same complements.
entries.contrast: Comfortable with is about the person's ease; comfortable to + infinitive is about the object's comfort. I'm comfortable with the chair means I accept it; The chair is comfortable to sit in means it feels good. Against used to, which reports habituation, comfortable with reports acceptance — you can be used to something without being comfortable with it, which is exactly why both phrases exist. ✗ comfortable of is an error.
entries.see also: used to, accustomed to, content with, familiar with, with

entries.meaning: Bound by conviction or promise to a cause, a course of action, or a relationship.
examples: The district is committed to keeping class sizes under twenty-five.
She's committed to the neighborhood in a way newcomers rarely are.
We are fully committed to finishing before the frost.
He wasn't ready to be committed to anyone.
Both parties say they're committed to reopening the talks.
entries.русский: приверженный чему-л., связавший себя обязательством — после to герундий
entries.register: neutral; institutional in tone when used of organizations
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (committed to reducing emissions) — never a to-infinitive. ✗ committed to reduce emissions is among the most frequent errors in corporate and academic English. The noun test settles it: committed to the reduction ✓, so to is a preposition.
entries.pattern: be committed to [noun / verb-ing] · commit [oneself] to [noun / verb-ing] · deeply / firmly / fully committed to [noun]
entries.variants: dedicated to and devoted to are the close synonyms, both with the same gerund requirement. Pledged to takes an infinitive instead (pledged to cut rates), which is why the two get confused.
entries.contrast: Committed to + -ing versus pledged to / vowed to + infinitive. Same meaning, opposite structures: ✓ committed to cutting rates, ✓ pledged to cut rates, ✗ committed to cut rates. Note the unrelated sense of the verb commit with no preposition (commit a crime) and the passive committed to meaning institutionalized (committed to a state hospital), which uses the same string for something else entirely.
entries.see also: devoted to, dedicated to, opposed to, intent on, to

entries.meaning: Shared by two or more things, so that each of them has it.
examples: A dislike of paperwork is common to every trade I've worked in.
The bug is common to both the desktop and the phone builds.
Sickle cell trait is common to populations where malaria was endemic.
What's common to all four accounts is the missing half hour.
Roof access is common to the units and maintained by the association.
entries.русский: общий для — присущий каждому из названных
entries.register: neutral to formal; ordinary in scientific and analytical writing (a feature common to both groups)
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming two or more things, or a plural or collective noun — common to both drafts, common to mammals, common to the whole family. A gerund is impossible here (✗ common to running), and so is a clause. The complement must be plural or collective in sense, because the word means "shared by."
entries.pattern: [feature] common to [group] · common to both / all / every [noun] · have [something] in common with [noun] — the noun frame, which switches to with
entries.variants: shared by is the plain equivalent; universal to and characteristic of cover neighboring ideas; in common with is the phrase you need when the subject is one of the sharers.
entries.contrast: Common to takes the sharers; in common with takes the other party. A trait common to both species is shared by them; in common with most birds, it molts in fall puts the subject alongside the group. Against characteristic of, which says a trait is typical of one thing, common to says a trait is present in several. Watch the everyday sense of common meaning "frequent," which takes no preposition (a common mistake) and, in the phrase common in, takes a place or population: the fungus is common in the Southeast — frequent there, not shared by it.
entries.see also: characteristic of, peculiar to, typical of, specific to, to

entries.meaning: Able to exist or work together without conflict.
examples: The new cable isn't compatible with anything we already own.
That schedule isn't compatible with having a family.
Their goals turned out to be compatible with ours after all.
The format is compatible with every reader we tested.
His account is not compatible with the timeline in the report.
entries.русский: совместимый с
entries.register: neutral; technical in computing, formal in argument
entries.complement: noun phrase or pronoun, and a gerund where an activity is meant (compatible with running two shifts) — never a to-infinitive and never a clause.
entries.pattern: be compatible with [noun / verb-ing] · [noun] compatible with [noun] · not compatible with [noun] · backward compatible with [noun]
entries.variants: consistent with is the argument-and-evidence version; suited to the person-and-role version. Incompatible with is the direct negative.
entries.contrast: Compatible with asks whether two things can coexist; consistent with asks whether they contradict each other. A finding is consistent with a theory (it does not disprove it); a printer is compatible with a laptop (they work together). ✗ compatible to is an error, which is worth flagging because similar to, identical to, and equal to all take to and pull compatible toward it. See consistent with.
entries.see also: consistent with, suitable for, similar to, with

entries.meaning: Worried about something, dealing with something, or anxious on someone's behalf.
examples: Residents are concerned about the noise from the new terminal.
The second half of the book is concerned with labor law.
She was concerned for her father, alone in the house all winter.
I'm concerned about signing anything before the audit closes.
As far as the bank is concerned, the loan is already closed.
entries.русский: обеспокоенный чем-л.; concerned with — занимающийся чем-л., касающийся чего-л.
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after about, with, and for (concerned about losing the contract) — never a to-infinitive after any of them. A that-clause attaches to the bare adjective: concerned that the numbers were revised twice.
entries.pattern: be concerned about [noun / verb-ing] · be concerned with [subject matter] · be concerned for [someone's welfare] · be concerned (that) [clause] · as far as [X] is concerned
entries.variants: worried about is the everyday equivalent of the about sense only. Deal with and be about replace the with sense in plainer prose.
entries.contrast: This is one of the sharpest three-way splits in the file. Concerned about = worried. Concerned with = having to do with, dealing with — no worry at all: Chapter 4 is concerned with tax policy means it is about tax policy. Concerned for = anxious on someone's behalf: concerned for her safety. Substituting one for another changes the sentence completely: a report concerned with air quality studies it, while a report concerned about air quality is alarmed by it. The frozen as far as I'm concerned uses yet another sense — "in my judgment."
entries.see also: worried about, anxious about, involved in, about

entries.meaning: Occurring alongside something else, as part of the same situation.
examples: Fatigue is concomitant with nearly every drug in this class.
The layoffs were concomitant with a slump nobody had forecast.
Rising rents, concomitant with flat wages, pushed the vacancy rate down.
List any medication concomitant with the study drug on page two.
The risks concomitant with early release were argued at length.
entries.русский: сопутствующий чему-л. — книжн.
entries.register: formal and technical — clinical writing above all (concomitant medications on any American intake form), plus economics and academic prose
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming what accompanies — never a gerund in normal use and never a clause. The word is also common attributively with no complement at all: concomitant therapy, the concomitant rise in costs.
entries.pattern: [thing] concomitant with [thing] · concomitant [noun] — attributive · with the concomitant [noun] — the fixed prepositional phrase · concomitantly with — the adverb
entries.variants: accompanying and attendant on are the near synonyms; coincident with stresses the timing; along with is the plain preposition; simultaneous with is the neutral technical word.
entries.contrast: Concomitant with claims that two things go together, not that one causes the other — which is exactly why medical and economic writing likes it: a concomitant rise in costs accompanies the change without being blamed on it. Against concurrent with, which is strictly about running at the same time, concomitant with implies the two belong to one picture. In clinical use the attributive form has nearly swallowed the prepositional one: a chart lists concomitant medications, not drugs concomitant with the trial drug. ✗ concomitant to is occasionally seen and is not the standard choice.
entries.see also: concurrent with, contemporaneous with, coextensive with, incidental to, with

entries.meaning: Running at the same time as something else.
examples: The two sentences run concurrent with each other, so he serves eight years.
Demolition is concurrent with the utility work, which is why the street is closed.
Her fellowship was concurrent with the last year of the grant.
State and federal courts have jurisdiction concurrent with one another here.
The audit was concurrent with the transition to the new system.
entries.русский: одновременный с, идущий параллельно по времени
entries.register: formal — sentencing orders, project schedules, and academic calendars; the adverb concurrently is the commoner form in speech
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the other event, term, or period — never a gerund (✗ concurrent with filing, where careful writing puts a noun: concurrent with the filing) and never a clause.
entries.pattern: [term / event] concurrent with [term / event] · run concurrent with [noun] · concurrently with — the adverb, which is what most writers actually use · concurrent jurisdiction / a concurring opinion — attributive relatives
entries.variants: simultaneous with is the neutral equivalent; contemporaneous with is the historian's and the lawyer's word for documents made at the same time; coincident with stresses that the overlap may be accidental; at the same time as is the plain phrase.
entries.contrast: Concurrent with means running at the same time; contemporaneous with means made or existing at the same time. Sentences run concurrent with one another; a memo is contemporaneous with the meeting it records. Against coterminous with, which requires the same beginning and end, concurrent with only requires overlap. In American sentencing the pair to know is concurrent versus consecutive: concurrent sentences are served together, consecutive ones back to back. ✗ concurrent to is an error.
entries.see also: contemporaneous with, coterminous with, concomitant with, coextensive with, with

entries.meaning: Holding only if something else happens or turns out to be true.
examples: The offer is conditional on a clean background check.
Admission is conditional upon finishing the two prerequisites this summer.
Funding for the second year is conditional on hitting the enrollment target.
Everything in the estimate is conditional on the permit coming through.
The forecast is conditional on the reservoir staying above sixty percent.
entries.русский: обусловленный чем-л. — действует, только если
entries.register: formal to neutral; ordinary in offers, admissions letters, statistics, and contracts, with upon the drafter's variant
entries.complement: a noun phrase or a gerund (conditional on passing the physical) — never a to-infinitive: ✗ conditional on pass the physical, ✗ conditional on to pass. A that-clause is possible only through a dummy noun: conditional on the understanding that you resign.
