entries.pattern: be conditional on [noun / verb-ing] · conditional upon [noun] — same phrase, formal spelling · make [something] conditional on [noun] · a conditional offer — attributive · conditional on [noun] in statistics: the probability conditional on X
entries.variants: contingent on and contingent upon are the exact equivalents and are commoner in American contracts; dependent on covers the same ground in plain English; subject to is the loosest of the family.
entries.contrast: Conditional on and contingent on, contingent upon are interchangeable in ordinary use; where they part is flavor — conditional points at a stated condition somebody wrote down, contingent at an uncertain future event. In statistics conditional on is a term of art with no substitute: the distribution of Y conditional on X is the distribution once X is known. Against dependent on, which can describe an ongoing reliance, conditional on describes a gate that has to be passed. ✗ conditional to is an error.
entries.see also: contingent on, contingent upon, dependent on, subject to, reliant on, on

entries.meaning: Tending to bring something about, by making the conditions right for it.
examples: Fluorescent lighting and a broken chair are not conducive to concentration.
The new schedule is more conducive to getting the trucks out on time.
Warm, wet weather is conducive to mold in these crawlspaces.
Nothing about that meeting was conducive to an honest answer.
A short walk after dinner is conducive to sleeping through the night.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /kənˈdusəv tə/; the British kun-DYOO-siv is not used in America
entries.русский: способствующий чему-л. — создающий подходящие условия
entries.register: formal to neutral; common in writing about conditions and environments (conducive to learning, conducive to sleep)
entries.complement: a noun phrase or a gerund — conducive to learning, conducive to getting anything done — and never a to-infinitive: ✗ conducive to learn, ✗ conducive to get anything done. The noun test settles it instantly: conducive to sleep ✓, so the to is a preposition. Because so many of its complements are -ing nouns already, the error hides easily.
entries.pattern: be conducive to [noun / verb-ing] · hardly / not exactly / far from conducive to · conditions conducive to [noun] · conduce to [noun] — the rare formal verb
entries.variants: favorable to is the neutral equivalent; good for is the plain one; helpful to and supportive of cover parts of the range; propitious for is the literary version.
entries.contrast: Conducive to names conditions that make something more likely, not something that causes it — a quiet room is conducive to studying, it does not produce studying. The subject is nearly always a setting, a policy, or a state of affairs rather than a person: ✗ she is conducive to the project is not English. Against amenable to, which is about willingness, conducive to is about circumstances. ✗ conducive for is a frequent error in American student writing, and ✗ conducive with is worse.
entries.see also: amenable to, detrimental to, harmful to, useful for, to

entries.meaning: Feeling sure — of an outcome, about a matter, or in someone's ability.
examples: The coach is confident of a win on Saturday.
She's confident about going back to school at forty.
I'm confident in the crew; I'm less confident in the forecast.
He's confident of finishing the draft before the holidays.
Investors were confident that rates had peaked.
entries.русский: уверенный в исходе; about в вопросе, in в чьих-л. способностях
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after of and about (confident of winning, confident about starting over) — never a to-infinitive. A that-clause attaches to the bare adjective (confident that the funding will come through), and confident in takes the thing or person trusted, not the outcome.
entries.pattern: be confident of [outcome / verb-ing] · be confident about [matter] · be confident in [person / method / oneself] · be confident (that) [clause]
entries.variants: sure of and certain of cover the same ground more plainly; optimistic about is the hedged version.
entries.contrast: Confident of the result is about the outcome; confident in the team is about the thing you trust. You can be confident in a surgeon without being confident of a cure. About is the loose everyday option and takes a general matter (confident about the move). ✗ confident on is an error, and ✗ confident to do it should be confident enough to do it or confident about doing it.
entries.see also: certain of, sure of, proud of, of

entries.meaning: Unable to understand something, or mixed up about it.
examples: Half the class was confused about which chapters were on the exam.
I'm confused about what the second charge is for.
Voters were confused by the new ballot layout.
She got confused about the time zones and called at four a.m.
Don't confuse the deadline with the postmark date.
entries.русский: не понимающий чего-л., запутавшийся в
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (confused about being billed twice), or a wh-clause (confused about what to do next) after about; noun phrase or gerund after by — never a to-infinitive after either.
entries.pattern: be confused about [matter / wh-clause] · be confused by [the thing causing confusion] · get confused about [noun] · confuse [X] with [Y]
entries.variants: unclear about and fuzzy on are the neighbors; puzzled by and baffled by are the intensified versions and prefer by.
entries.contrast: About names the topic of your confusion; by names its cause — confused about the schedule (I don't understand it) versus confused by the schedule (it confuses me). Keep both apart from confuse X with Y, the verb pattern meaning to mistake one for the other: I always confuse him with his brother, where ✗ confuse him to his brother is wrong. ✗ confused of and ✗ confused on are errors, though fuzzy on the details is idiomatic.
entries.see also: aware of, certain of, familiar with, about

entries.meaning: Matching another thing exactly — in shape and size, in the mathematical use; in substance, in the figurative one.
examples: The two triangles are congruent to each other by side-angle-side.
Seventeen is congruent to two modulo five.
Her testimony is not congruent with what she wrote in the log.
We hire people whose habits are congruent with how the shop actually runs.
The budget has to be congruent with the plan the board approved in March.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˈkɑŋɡruənt tə/ and /ˈkɑŋɡruənt wəθ/; the stress-shifted kun-GROO-unt is also heard
entries.русский: конгруэнтный (мат.); согласующийся с чем-л. (перен.)
entries.register: technical in the to frame (geometry, number theory), formal-neutral in the with frame (psychology, management, and ordinary argument)
entries.complement: a noun phrase — a figure, a number, a set of values, a description. A gerund is possible but rare in the with frame (congruent with saying one thing and doing another), and a to-infinitive is impossible in either.
entries.pattern: [figure] is congruent to [figure] — geometry · a ≡ b congruent to [modulus] — number theory, read "congruent to b modulo n" · be congruent with [values / account] · not entirely congruent with [noun]
entries.variants: congruent with is the everyday choice outside mathematics and is what most American writers use for beliefs, values, and accounts. Consistent with is the plain equivalent; consonant with the formal one; in keeping with the idiomatic one.
entries.contrast: The preposition tracks the field. Geometry says triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DEF, and a math teacher will mark congruent with wrong there; outside mathematics, congruent with is standard and congruent to sounds like a misapplied classroom habit. Against equivalent to, which claims equal value, congruence claims that two things match point for point. Against consonant with, which is nearly a synonym in the figurative use, congruent with is the commoner word in American management and therapy talk.
entries.see also: equivalent to, consonant with, isomorphic to, compatible with, with

entries.meaning: Noticing something, or keeping it in mind.
examples: He was conscious of every squeak the floor made.
She's conscious of how much the delay is costing them.
I became conscious of someone watching from the porch.
The design is conscious of the building's original proportions.
She's self-conscious about her accent on the phone.
entries.русский: осознающий, замечающий что-л. и держащий это в уме
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (conscious of being stared at) — never a to-infinitive. A that-clause attaches to the bare adjective (conscious that the room had gone quiet), and ✗ conscious of that is an error.
entries.pattern: be conscious of [noun / verb-ing] · be conscious (that) [clause] · become conscious of [noun] · acutely conscious of [noun] · [noun]-conscious as a suffix: health-conscious, cost-conscious
entries.variants: aware of is the everyday twin and follows the same frames. Mindful of adds a note of deliberate attention.
entries.contrast: Conscious of leans toward felt, immediate awareness; aware of leans toward knowledge. You are conscious of a draft on your neck and aware of a change in the law; either word will pass in most sentences, but the drift is real. The suffixed compounds are a separate and very productive pattern — safety-conscious, brand-conscious — where no preposition appears at all. ✗ conscious about is an error in this sense, though self-conscious about is correct and means embarrassed.
entries.see also: aware of, sensitive to, careful with, of

entries.meaning: In agreement with a principle, a practice, or a body of values.
examples: The ruling is consonant with forty years of the court's own precedent.
Their treatment of the tenants was hardly consonant with the mission statement.
Nothing in the proposal is consonant with what the charter says about notice.
The restoration is consonant with the building's original 1911 plans.
He wanted a career consonant with the way he'd been raised.
entries.русский: согласующийся с принципом, ценностями — книжн.
entries.register: formal and somewhat literary — judicial opinions, policy writing, and criticism; in speech an American says in line with or consistent with
entries.complement: a noun phrase, or a gerund in careful writing (consonant with treating everyone alike) — never a to-infinitive (✗ consonant with treat everyone alike) and never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: be consonant with [principle / practice] · wholly / entirely / not consonant with · consonance with — the noun frame, also with with
entries.variants: consistent with is the neutral American equivalent and is what most editors will substitute; in keeping with is the idiomatic one; congruent with and in harmony with cover the same ground; compatible with is the everyday word.
entries.contrast: The word carries its musical metaphor: things consonant with each other sound well together, so it fits principles, traditions, and values better than facts. For a factual match, compatible with or consistent with is the better word — the injuries are consistent with a fall, not ✗ consonant with a fall, which a doctor would never write. Do not confuse the adjective with the noun consonant (the speech sound), which takes no preposition. ✗ consonant to is an error.
entries.see also: compatible with, congruent to, congruent with, germane to, repugnant to, with

entries.meaning: Made or happening at the same time as something else, and valuable precisely for that.
examples: Her notes are contemporaneous with the call and were never edited.
The eruption was contemporaneous with the collapse of the settlement.
The email is contemporaneous with the meeting, so it carries weight.
Those deposits are roughly contemporaneous with the lower layer at the dig.
A memo written a year later is not contemporaneous with anything.
entries.русский: одновременный с, относящийся к тому же времени — книжн./юр.
entries.register: formal and technical — evidence law (contemporaneous notes), history, and geology; the everyday word is at the same time as
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the other event, document, or period — never a gerund (careful writing nominalizes: contemporaneous with the signing, not ✗ contemporaneous with signing) and never a clause.
entries.pattern: [document / event] contemporaneous with [event] · roughly / nearly / exactly contemporaneous with · a contemporaneous record — attributive · contemporaneously with — the adverb
entries.variants: concurrent with is the word for things running at the same time; simultaneous with is the neutral technical choice; coeval with is the literary and geological one; of the same period as is the plain paraphrase.
entries.contrast: Contemporaneous is not contemporary. Contemporary means either "of the present day" (contemporary art) or "of the same era as," and takes with only in the second sense; contemporaneous with always means "made or occurring at the same time as" and is the word American lawyers use for notes written while events happened — the whole evidentiary point being that they were not written later. Against concurrent with, which is about duration overlapping, contemporaneous with is about the moment of origin. ✗ contemporaneous to is an error.
entries.see also: concurrent with, concomitant with, coterminous with, antecedent to, with

entries.meaning: Satisfied with what there is, and not pushing for more.
examples: She's content with a small garden and no lawn at all.
He was content to let his brother do the talking.
They had to content themselves with second place.
I'm perfectly content with the arrangement as written.
Nobody here is content with running the same numbers twice.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /kənˈtɛnt wəθ/ — the adjective stresses the second syllable, unlike the noun content /ˈkɑntɛnt/
entries.русский: довольный тем, что есть, не требующий большего
entries.register: neutral to slightly literary
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after with (content with staying home) — never a to-infinitive after with. The adjective also takes a bare to-infinitive directly (content to wait), which is the commoner frame of the two.
entries.pattern: be content with [noun / verb-ing] · be content to [verb] · content oneself with [noun / verb-ing] · perfectly / quite content with [noun]
entries.variants: satisfied with is the plainer synonym; happy with is the everyday one. Contented with is the same word in its fuller adjectival form and sounds more settled.
entries.contrast: Content with + -ing and content to + verb both exist and mean nearly the same thing — content with waiting and content to wait — which makes this one of the few adjectives here where the infinitive is not an error. The difference is slight: with frames the situation as something accepted, to frames it as something willingly done. Content oneself with is the reflexive frame meaning to settle for less than you wanted. ✗ content of is an error.
entries.see also: satisfied with, happy about, pleased with, with

entries.meaning: Happening only if some uncertain thing happens first.
examples: The offer is contingent on financing and on a satisfactory inspection.
Her bonus is contingent upon the division clearing its target.
Everything after phase two is contingent on the grant being renewed.
The permit is contingent on the traffic study, which nobody has scheduled.
Whether we drive is contingent on what the pass looks like Saturday.
entries.русский: зависящий от — состоится, только если случится нечто неопределённое
entries.register: formal to neutral; the standard word in American real-estate contracts (contingent on financing), employment offers, and grant agreements, with upon the drafter's variant
entries.complement: a noun phrase or a gerund — contingent on selling the house ✓ — and never a to-infinitive: ✗ contingent on sell the house, ✗ contingent to sell the house. A clause needs a dummy noun: contingent on the condition that the appraisal clears.
entries.pattern: be contingent on [noun / verb-ing] · contingent upon [noun] · make [something] contingent on [noun] · a contingency / contingent fee / contingent liability — attributive relatives, no preposition
entries.variants: conditional on and conditional upon are the exact equivalents; dependent on is the plain-English version; subject to is looser and covers a wider range; hinges on is the informal verb.
entries.contrast: Contingent on points at an uncertain future event; conditional on points at a stated condition. In practice American contracts use them interchangeably, and contingent on dominates in real estate: an offer contingent on inspection dies if the inspection fails. Against dependent on, which describes standing reliance (dependent on the grant for salary), contingent on describes a single gate. Note the noun contingency, which takes no preposition in its ordinary use, and the fee arrangement on contingency, where no of or to is possible.
entries.see also: conditional on, conditional upon, dependent on, subject to, reliant on, on

entries.meaning: Knowing a subject or a system well enough to work in it without help.
examples: Applicants must be conversant with federal procurement rules.
She's conversant with every payroll system this company has ever run.
The witness was not conversant with the actual conditions on the floor.
He's conversant in Portuguese and can handle the Lisbon calls.
Get conversant with the new codes before the inspection.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /kənˈvɜrsənt wəθ/; the older KON-vur-sunt is chiefly British
entries.русский: хорошо разбирающийся в — книжн.
entries.register: formal — résumés, expert declarations, and job descriptions; a spoken American says knows his way around
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a subject, a body of rules, or a tool — never a to-infinitive (✗ conversant with to use the software). A gerund is grammatical but stiff (conversant with running a mill); careful writers use a noun instead.
entries.pattern: be conversant with [subject / system] · be conversant in [language / field] · thoroughly / fully / not especially conversant with · make oneself conversant with [noun]
entries.variants: conversant in is standard for languages and disciplines — conversant in Spanish, conversant in tax law — while conversant with suits documents, systems, and practices. Familiar with is the neutral everyday equivalent; versed in and well versed in are the formal ones; fluent in belongs to languages only.
entries.contrast: With for a thing you have worked with, in for a field you have studied. Both are correct English, and the choice is idiomatic rather than logical: ✓ conversant with the filing system, ✓ conversant in French. Against acquainted with, which reports an introduction, conversant with claims working knowledge — enough to hold up your end of a conversation, which is where the word comes from. Note that conversant has nothing to do with the verb converse in modern use. ✗ conversant about and ✗ conversant to are errors.
entries.see also: familiar with, acquainted with, expert at, skilled at, with

entries.meaning: Ending at the same point as something else — in time, or along a shared border.
examples: We made the sublease coterminous with the master lease so both end in June.
The school district is coterminous with the township, which simplifies the tax roll.
His term as trustee is coterminous with the mayor's.
The park's north edge is coterminous with the county line.
The warranty is coterminous with the financing, not with the roof's life.
entries.русский: совпадающий по границам или по срокам с — книжн./юр.
entries.register: formal — leases and loan documents (a term coterminous with the note), municipal law, and political geography; never conversational
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the other term, boundary, or period — never a gerund and never a clause.
entries.pattern: [term / district] be coterminous with [term / district] · make the lease coterminous with [noun] · exactly / not quite coterminous with
entries.variants: conterminous with is the same word in the spelling geographers prefer for shared borders — and the conterminous United States is the fixed term for the lower forty-eight. Coextensive with is the near twin for scope rather than time; concurrent with for events running together.
entries.contrast: Coterminous with means beginning and ending together, or sharing a boundary; coextensive with means covering the same ground. A sublease coterminous with the master lease expires on the same day; a duty coextensive with a risk is the same size as the risk. Against concurrent with, which needs only overlap, coterminous with demands the same endpoints. ✗ coterminous to is an error.
entries.see also: coextensive with, concurrent with, contemporaneous with, equivalent to, with

entries.meaning: Enthusiastic about something or someone, to a degree the speaker admits is unreasonable.
examples: He's been crazy about trains since he was four.
I'm not crazy about driving that stretch after dark.
She's crazy about the new place, cracked driveway and all.
The kids are crazy about their swim coach.
Everyone's crazy about that bakery on Third.
entries.русский: без ума от — разг.
entries.register: informal; conversational American English
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (crazy about camping) — never a to-infinitive. ✗ crazy about to camp is not English.
entries.pattern: be crazy about [noun / verb-ing] · not crazy about [noun / verb-ing] · go crazy over [noun] · drive [someone] crazy (no preposition on the object)
entries.variants: wild about and nuts about are the same register; mad about is the British equivalent and is not the American default. Crazy for survives mostly in song titles and in crazy for you.
entries.contrast: The negative is the commonest use and it is understatement, not neutrality: I'm not crazy about the color means you dislike it. Keep crazy about (fond of) apart from crazy with (overwhelmed by an emotion — crazy with worry) and from drive someone crazy, which takes a direct object and no preposition at all. In American English mad about means angry about, so mad about her and crazy about her are not synonyms here even though they are in London.
entries.see also: mad at, keen on, fond of, obsessed with, about

entries.meaning: Finding fault with something — or, with to and for, indispensable to it.
examples: The auditor was critical of how the invoices were logged.
She's critical of everything except her own department.
Several members were openly critical of holding the vote in August.
Timing is critical to the whole operation.
Reviewers were critical of the ending but praised everything before it.
entries.русский: критикующий что-л., недовольный чем-л.; critical to/for — жизненно важный для
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (critical of spending that much) — never a to-infinitive and never a clause.
entries.pattern: be critical of [noun / verb-ing] · highly / sharply / openly critical of [noun] · critical to [something] — a different sense entirely · critical for [purpose]
entries.variants: disapproving of and disparaging about are the near-synonyms; hard on is the informal one.
entries.contrast: Critical of means finding fault; critical to and critical for mean essential. This is one word doing two unrelated jobs, and the preposition is the only signal: critical of the plan opposes it, critical to the plan is indispensable to it. A third sense, in critical condition, takes no preposition at all. ✗ critical about is an error for the fault-finding sense; use of.
entries.see also: suspicious of, essential to, impressed with, of

entries.meaning: Containing more people or things than there is comfortable room for.
examples: The platform was crowded with commuters by six-fifteen.
Her desk is crowded with photographs and unopened mail.
The calendar is crowded with meetings that could have been emails.
Every bar downtown was crowded with people watching the game.
The little museum is crowded with objects nobody has cataloged.
entries.русский: переполненный чем-л., набитый
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase, usually plural or mass (crowded with tourists, crowded with furniture) — never a gerund, never a to-infinitive, and never a clause.
entries.pattern: be crowded with [plural / mass noun] · [place] crowded with [noun] · crowd into [place] — the verb, with a different preposition
entries.variants: packed with, jammed with, thick with, and filled with all take with in the same frame; full of takes of and is the commonest of the family.
entries.contrast: Crowded with takes with; full of takes of. They mean nearly the same thing and their prepositions do not swap: ✗ crowded of people, ✗ full with people. Note that the verb goes elsewhere again — people crowded into the lobby, crowd around the stage — and that crowded alone, with no preposition, is the ordinary way to say a place has too many people in it.
entries.see also: full of, rich in, short of, with

entries.meaning: Deliberately causing pain or suffering to someone.
examples: He was cruel to the dog when he thought nobody was watching.
Middle school is cruel to anyone who stands out.
It was cruel of her to bring it up at the table.
The schedule is cruel to anyone with a long commute.
Time has been cruel to that building.
entries.русский: жестокий к кому-л.
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or pronoun naming the person or animal treated badly — never a gerund after to and never a clause. The adjective also takes the it-frame with an infinitive: It was cruel to say that, where the infinitive belongs to it, not to cruel.
entries.pattern: be cruel to [person / animal] · it is cruel to [verb] · it was cruel of [someone] to [verb] · cruel to be kind
entries.variants: mean to, harsh with, hard on, and unkind to cover the range from playground to courtroom; all the "behavior toward a person" adjectives in this family take to.
entries.contrast: Every adjective of how you treat someone takes to: cruel to, kind to, nice to, polite to, rude to, mean to, good to. The pattern is reliable enough to guess with. What breaks it is gentle with, patient with, and honest with, which take with because they describe the manner of the handling rather than the direction of the treatment. The double frame It was cruel of him to say that uses of for the doer and to for the deed — ✗ It was cruel from him is an error.
entries.see also: kind to, rude to, nice to, gentle with, to

entries.meaning: Wanting to know about something.
examples: She's curious about how the machine actually works.
I was curious about the cost before I mentioned it to anyone.
Neighbors were curious about the trucks parked all week.
He was curious to hear what she'd say next.
Nobody seemed curious about where the money had gone.
entries.русский: любопытствующий, желающий узнать о
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (curious about trying it), or a wh-clause (curious about how they did it) after about — never a to-infinitive after about. The adjective takes a bare to-infinitive directly (curious to see what happens), which is a separate and very common frame.
entries.pattern: be curious about [noun / verb-ing / wh-clause] · be curious to [verb] · curious as to [wh-clause] · make [someone] curious about [noun]
entries.variants: interested in is the neutral equivalent; nosy about is the disapproving one. Curious as to whether is the formal register.
entries.contrast: Curious about names the topic; curious to names what you want to do about it. Curious about the results is wondering; curious to see the results is wanting to look. This adjective is one of the small set — with anxious, eager, interested, and keen — where the bare infinitive is standard alongside the preposition. ✗ curious of and ✗ curious for are errors.
entries.see also: interested in, eager for, enthusiastic about, about

entries.meaning: Giving one's whole effort to something — or, of a thing, set aside for a single purpose.
examples: The foundation is dedicated to keeping small-town newspapers alive.
She's dedicated to her patients in a way the schedule never rewards.
Two rooms upstairs are dedicated to files nobody has opened since 2009.
He dedicated the book to the teacher who failed him twice.
The office is dedicated to answering every complaint within a week.
entries.русский: посвятивший себя чему-л.; о вещи — предназначенный только для этого
entries.register: neutral; warm about a person, institutional about an organization
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (dedicated to keeping the archive open) — never a to-infinitive. ✗ dedicated to keep the archive open is the error, and the noun test settles it: dedicated to the archive ✓, so the to is a preposition. A that-clause is impossible.
entries.pattern: be dedicated to [cause / person / verb-ing] · dedicate [a book / a bench / one's life] to [someone] · [portion] dedicated to [noun] · a dedicated [noun] — attributive, meaning reserved for one use: a dedicated line
entries.variants: devoted to and committed to are the near-twins and take the same gerund. Dedicated to sits between them — warmer than committed, more disciplined than devoted. Pledged to and vowed to mean the same thing and take an infinitive instead.
entries.contrast: Dedicated to + -ing versus pledged to / vowed to + verb. Same meaning, opposite structures: ✓ dedicated to reducing waste, ✓ pledged to reduce waste, ✗ dedicated to reduce waste — an error that turns up constantly in mission statements. Two other senses share the string and are not this pattern: the commemorative one (a bench dedicated to her mother) and the attributive one meaning single-purpose (a dedicated server), which takes no preposition at all. ✗ dedicated for and ✗ dedicated with are errors.
entries.see also: devoted to, committed to, opposed to, accustomed to, to

entries.meaning: Very pleased — a step warmer than pleased, a step cooler than thrilled.
examples: The client was delighted with the first round of drawings.
She was delighted by how many people showed up.
He was delighted at the news that the school had reopened.
We'd be delighted to have you both for dinner.
Everyone was delighted with the way the porch turned out.
entries.русский: очень довольный, в восторге от
entries.register: neutral, warm; commoner in writing than in casual American speech
entries.complement: noun phrase after with, by, and at; a gerund is possible after at (delighted at finding it still open) — never a to-infinitive after a preposition. The adjective takes a bare to-infinitive directly (delighted to help), which is by far its commonest frame, and a that-clause (delighted that you could come).
entries.pattern: be delighted with [thing received or achieved] · be delighted by [the cause] · be delighted at [news / turn of events] · be delighted to [verb] · be delighted (that) [clause]
entries.variants: pleased with is the same shape at lower temperature; thrilled with / by is the same shape at higher.
entries.contrast: With takes the thing you got; by takes the thing that acted on you; at takes the news or the turn of events. Delighted with the results is your verdict on them; delighted by her reply points at what caused the delight; delighted at the news reports a reaction to information. The infinitive frame is the polite formula of American correspondence — I'd be delighted to — and it never takes a preposition. ✗ delighted for is an error except in delighted for you, meaning happy on your behalf.
entries.see also: pleased with, happy about, satisfied with, impressed with, with

entries.meaning: Needing someone or something in order to survive or continue — or determined by it.
examples: The town is almost entirely dependent on the mill.
Whether we open Monday is dependent on the inspection.
She has two children dependent on her.
Funding is dependent upon a match from the county.
The whole schedule is dependent on getting the parts by Friday.
entries.русский: зависящий от — нуждающийся в чём-л. или определяемый чем-л.
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (dependent on getting the permit) — never a to-infinitive and never a that-clause. A wh-clause is possible in the "determined by" sense: dependent on how the vote goes.
entries.pattern: be dependent on [noun / verb-ing] · heavily / entirely / largely dependent on [noun] · dependent on [someone] for [something] · make [X] dependent on [Y]
entries.variants: dependent upon is the formal equivalent, standard in contracts and academic writing. Reliant on is the close synonym; contingent on is the conditional one.
entries.contrast: ✗ dependent of and ✗ dependent from are errors — the preposition is fixed. Two spelling notes matter in American English: the adjective is dependent with -ent in every case, and the noun for a person you support is also dependent in American usage (claim two dependents), where British English spells the noun dependant. Note the two senses that share the pattern: dependent on her mother (needing support) versus dependent on the weather (determined by), which is why The picnic is dependent on the weather has nothing to do with trust. The opposite is independent of, with of, not from.
entries.see also: reliant on, independent of, based on, subject to, on

entries.meaning: Having its origin or its substance in something earlier — a source material, a text, or a calculation.
examples: The dye is derived from a root that only grows in two counties.
Nearly half the town's revenue is derived from the port.
The word is derived from an Old Norse verb meaning to scrape.
These figures are derived from the same survey the state uses.
Most of her income is derived from renting out the two back units.
entries.русский: происходящий от, выведенный из — из источника, текста или расчёта
entries.register: neutral to formal; standard in science, etymology, finance, and cooking labels
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the source, or a gerund naming the activity a thing comes out of (income derived from renting the top floor) — never a to-infinitive: ✗ derived from rent the top floor. A clause is impossible.
entries.pattern: be derived from [source] · [noun] derived from [noun] — the reduced relative, which is where the phrase does most of its work · derive [something] from [source] — the active verb · derived from [language] — in etymology
entries.variants: comes from is the everyday equivalent; obtained from and extracted from are the physical ones; based on covers a looser relationship; stems from and springs from are the metaphorical verbs.
entries.contrast: Derived from names an origin the thing was actually made out of or worked out from, which is more than based on claims: a screenplay is based on a novel, but morphine is derived from opium. In finance the word is exact — a derivative derived from an underlying asset takes its value from it. Note that the source, not the product, follows from: ✓ aspirin is derived from willow bark, ✗ willow bark is derived from aspirin. ✗ derived of is an error, and derived by names the person or method, not the source: derived by Gauss, derived by regression.
entries.see also: based on, grounded in, founded on, founded upon, independent of, from

entries.meaning: Having earned something by conduct or merit, and so entitled to it.
examples: The proposal is deserving of a serious hearing, whatever its flaws.
Nobody on that crew was less deserving of the blame.
Her thirty years there are deserving of more than a sheet cake.
The complaint is deserving of being investigated, not filed away.
He behaved as if he were deserving of an exception to every rule.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /dəˈzɜrvɪŋ əv/, and before a consonant often /dəˈzɜrvɪŋ ə/
entries.русский: заслуживающий чего-л. по делам или по достоинствам
entries.register: formal; in speech Americans use the plain verb (she deserves a raise) and keep deserving of for writing and for emphasis
entries.complement: a noun phrase, usually abstract — deserving of praise, deserving of a second look — or a gerund (deserving of being taken seriously). Never a to-infinitive after of: ✗ deserving of to win. The bare adjective takes no preposition at all in the deserving poor.
entries.pattern: be deserving of [noun / verb-ing] · hardly / richly / wholly deserving of · deserve [noun] — the verb, with a direct object and no preposition · deserve to [verb] — the verb with an infinitive
entries.variants: worthy of is the close twin and is commoner; meriting is the participial version; the plain verb deserve replaces the whole phrase in ordinary speech.
entries.contrast: The adjective takes of; the verb takes nothing. ✓ She deserves an answer. ✓ She is deserving of an answer. ✗ She deserves of an answer. That is the whole trap, and it is the same trap as worthy of. Against worthy of, which can weigh a thing's quality (a film worthy of the original), deserving of is about what someone has earned by conduct. Note the fixed phrase the deserving poor, an old piece of charity vocabulary that now reads as loaded.
entries.see also: worthy of, entitled to, eligible for, guilty of, of

entries.meaning: Wanting something — in a formal, and now largely ceremonial, register.
examples: The parties, being desirous of settling all claims, agree as follows.
The company is desirous of acquiring the adjoining parcel.
Any member desirous of speaking must be recognized by the chair.
He was desirous of an appointment but too proud to ask for one.
Both governments are desirous of avoiding further escalation.
entries.русский: желающий чего-л. — устар./офиц., торжественный регистр
entries.register: formal and dated — contract recitals (the parties being desirous of settling all claims), diplomatic notes, and nineteenth-century prose; in any other setting it sounds pompous, and modern American drafting guides tell you to write want
entries.complement: a noun phrase or a gerund (desirous of obtaining a license) — the gerund is by far the commoner of the two in the surviving legal formula. An older to-infinitive (desirous to please) is genuine but archaic and should not be imitated. No that-clause.
entries.pattern: be desirous of [noun / verb-ing] · the parties, being desirous of [verb-ing], agree as follows — the recital formula · desirous of [noun] in official correspondence
entries.variants: desiring to + infinitive and wishing to + infinitive are the living formal equivalents; anxious to and eager for cover the everyday range; want is the word to use in any modern document.
entries.contrast: This is a survival, not a live pattern. Where desirous of still appears, it is nearly always inside a whereas clause in a contract, and the modern replacement is a plain verb: The parties want to settle all claims. Against eager for and anxious about, which describe feelings, desirous of in legal use describes an intention formally recorded. Do not confuse desirous (wanting something) with desirable (wanted by others) — ✗ a desirous location is a common slip for desirable.
entries.see also: eager for, intent on, content with, worthy of, of

entries.meaning: Causing harm or loss to somebody or something.
examples: Long shifts without a break are detrimental to accuracy on the line.
Any delay now would be detrimental to the whole schedule.
The report says the runoff is detrimental to the fishery downstream.
Posting about the case was detrimental to her own claim.
Nothing here is detrimental to the tenants; the change is administrative.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˌdɛtrəˈmɛntəl tə/, with the medial t flapped: "det-ruh-MEN-nul-tuh"
entries.русский: вредный для, наносящий ущерб — книжн.
entries.register: formal to neutral; standard in public-health writing, HR documents, and legal filings, where the plain word would be bad for
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming what suffers, or a gerund with the same role — never a to-infinitive: ✗ detrimental to sleep well. Note that the complement is the victim, not the cause: detrimental to your health, never ✗ detrimental to smoking.
entries.pattern: be detrimental to [person / interest / health] · seriously / materially detrimental to · to the detriment of [noun] — the noun frame · detrimental reliance — the legal term, no preposition
entries.variants: harmful to and damaging to are the neutral equivalents; bad for is the plain one; prejudicial to is the legal one and adds unfairness; deleterious to is the clinical one.
entries.contrast: Against harmful to, which is the ordinary word for injury, detrimental to is the institutional register and is often used of interests, reputations, and finances rather than bodies. Against prejudicial to, which in law means unfairly damaging to a party's case, detrimental to is neutral about fairness. Watch the direction of the preposition: the thing after to is the one being hurt. ✗ detrimental for and ✗ detrimental of are errors.
entries.see also: harmful to, prejudicial to, conducive to, adverse to, to

entries.meaning: Giving loyalty, love, or resources entirely to someone or something.
examples: She was devoted to her students for thirty-one years.
Half the budget is devoted to maintaining the trails.
He's devoted to getting the archive digitized before he retires.
The last chapter is devoted to the 1919 strike.
They're a devoted pair, devoted to each other and to nobody else.
entries.русский: преданный кому-л., целиком отдающий себя чему-л.
entries.register: neutral to warm
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (devoted to restoring the building) — never a to-infinitive. ✗ devoted to restore the building is the error; the noun test settles it (devoted to the restoration ✓).
entries.pattern: be devoted to [person / cause / verb-ing] · devote [time / a chapter] to [noun / verb-ing] · [portion] devoted to [noun]
entries.variants: dedicated to and committed to are near-identical and take the same gerund. Given over to is the version used of space and time.
entries.contrast: Devoted to is warmer than dedicated to and warmer still than committed to — devotion suggests love, dedication suggests discipline, commitment suggests obligation. All three take the gerund, and this is the single most useful thing to know about the trio. A second, purely spatial sense assigns a portion of something: two pages devoted to footnotes, where no feeling is involved. ✗ devoted for and ✗ devoted with are errors.
entries.see also: committed to, dedicated to, intent on, married to, to

entries.meaning: Not the same as something else — the central comparison adjective of English, and the one usage question in this file that is still live.
examples: Her second album is completely different from the first.
City driving is different from anything he'd done upstate.
The final bill was different than we'd been told it would be.
This is no different from what happened in 2011.
Winters here are different from winters anywhere else I've lived.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˈdɪfrənt frəm/; the careful three-syllable /ˈdɪfərənt/ is also standard
entries.русский: отличающийся от, не такой, как — from стандартная американская форма
entries.register: neutral; different from is the standard American form in every register
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, gerund (different from working alone), or a free relative (different from what I expected) after from — never a to-infinitive. Different than additionally takes a finite clause (different than I expected), which is exactly the environment that makes it useful.
entries.pattern: [X] is different from [Y] · no different from [noun] · very / quite / entirely different from [noun] · different than [clause] · differ from [noun] — the verb, from only
entries.variants: different than is common, respectable American English, strongest before a clause; different to is British and is not used in the United States. Differing from and distinct from are the formal equivalents.
entries.contrast: The honest American position has three parts. From is standard and never wrong: use it before a noun or pronoun. Than is the better choice before a clause, where from forces the clumsy from what: The job turned out different than I expected reads better than different from what I expected, and no American editor will stop you. Before a bare noun (different than his) some editors still object, so from is safer there. To is British — correct in London, foreign in Chicago. Note that the verb differ takes only from: ✗ differs than, ✗ differs to. See also different from, where the word is treated as a comparison preposition in its own right.
entries.see also: similar to, identical to, equal to, different from, than, from

entries.meaning: Let down because something or someone did not measure up.
examples: Fans were disappointed with the ending.
Her father said he was disappointed in her, which was worse than shouting.
We were disappointed by how little the report actually said.
He's disappointed about missing the trip a second year running.
I was disappointed to find the office already closed.
entries.русский: разочарованный в ком-л. или чём-л., обманувшийся в ожиданиях
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase after with, in, and by; a gerund after about (disappointed about missing it) — never a to-infinitive after a preposition. The adjective takes a bare to-infinitive directly (disappointed to learn) and a that-clause (disappointed that no one called).
entries.pattern: be disappointed with [thing] · be disappointed in [person] · be disappointed by [the cause] · be disappointed about [situation / verb-ing] · be disappointed to [verb] · be disappointed (that) [clause]
entries.variants: let down by is the informal equivalent; dissatisfied with is the formal one and takes only with.
entries.contrast: Disappointed in is personal and moral; disappointed with is an assessment. I'm disappointed in you is a rebuke about character; I'm disappointed with the room is a review. Use in for people whose conduct fell short, with for things and outcomes, by when you want to point at the cause as an agent, and about for a situation. American speech leans on in for people far more than British English does. ✗ disappointed of and ✗ disappointed from are errors.
entries.see also: satisfied with, pleased with, upset about, sad about, with

entries.meaning: Settling a question outright, so that nothing further needs deciding.
examples: The waiver, if valid, is dispositive of the entire claim.
That one email is not dispositive of intent, whatever the plaintiff says.
The court found the timing dispositive of the jurisdictional question.
Neither affidavit is dispositive of who was driving.
Counsel conceded the point was dispositive of the appeal.
entries.русский: разрешающий вопрос окончательно — юр.
entries.register: legal, narrowly — briefs, opinions, and motions; an American meets it in a court document and essentially nowhere else
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the question, issue, or case that the thing settles — never a gerund, never a clause. What follows of is the matter decided, not the deciding fact.
entries.pattern: be dispositive of [issue / case] · not dispositive of [noun] — the commonest use, since the word usually appears in a denial · a dispositive motion — attributive, meaning one that can end the case
entries.variants: decisive of is the near equivalent; determinative of is the drier one; conclusive as to takes a different preposition; in plain English, settles the question.
entries.contrast: Dispositive of means it ends the inquiry, not merely that it matters — which is why the word so often appears negated: the affidavit is relevant but not dispositive of the issue. Against material to, which means capable of affecting the outcome, and probative of, which means tending to prove a fact, dispositive of is the strongest of the three: material evidence bears on the question, probative evidence supports a finding, dispositive evidence closes it. Note the separate legal sense of dispositive meaning "relating to the disposition of property" (the dispositive provisions of the will), where no of follows. ✗ dispositive to is an error.
entries.see also: material to, probative of, indicative of, pertinent to, of

entries.meaning: Impatiently wanting something to arrive or to happen.
examples: The whole town was eager for a decision either way.
She's eager to get back on the water.
Investors are eager for any sign that hiring has picked up.
He was eager for his daughter to see the place before it sold.
New hires are always eager for feedback in the first month.
entries.русский: жаждущий чего-л., нетерпеливо ожидающий
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase after for (eager for news) — a gerund after for is possible but stilted, and the natural way to put a verb after this adjective is the bare to-infinitive (eager to start), which is the commonest frame by a wide margin. A that-clause is possible in formal writing (eager that the record show).
entries.pattern: be eager for [noun] · be eager to [verb] · be eager for [someone] to [verb] · eager beaver (fixed compound)
entries.variants: keen on + -ing and keen to + verb are the British-flavored equivalents; anxious to and impatient for / to are the everyday American ones.
entries.contrast: Eager for takes a thing; eager to takes an action. Eager for the results versus eager to see the results — and the second is what to write when a verb is involved, because eager for seeing the results is not idiomatic. Note the sharp difference from anxious about, which is dread: eager for Monday and anxious about Monday are opposite emotions with the same referent. ✗ eager of and ✗ eager at are errors.
entries.see also: anxious about, keen on, enthusiastic about, ready for, for

entries.meaning: Meeting the conditions that let you apply for something or take part in it.
examples: You're eligible for the credit if your income was under the cap last year.
He becomes eligible for parole in November.
Part-time staff are eligible for dental coverage after ninety days.
She's eligible to vote in the primary but not in the special election.
The building is eligible for listing on the state register.
entries.русский: имеющий право на, подходящий по условиям для
entries.register: neutral; the standard word of American benefits, insurance, financial aid, and sports rosters
entries.complement: after for, a noun phrase naming the benefit, program, or status (eligible for parole, eligible for the tax credit) — and a gerund where the benefit is an activity (eligible for reinstatement, more naturally a noun). After bare to, a to-infinitive: eligible to vote, eligible to apply. The two frames do not mix: ✗ eligible for apply, ✗ eligible to a refund.
entries.pattern: be eligible for [benefit / program] · be eligible to [verb] · eligible for [noun] after [period] · deem / declare [someone] eligible for [noun] · eligibility for [noun] — the noun frame keeps for
entries.variants: entitled to is the stronger word — eligibility lets you apply, entitlement means it is owed to you. Qualified for stresses ability rather than status; in line for is informal and predictive.
entries.contrast: Eligible for + noun, eligible to + verb. This is the single thing to get right, and the mixed forms are the standard errors on American applications: ✓ eligible for benefits, ✓ eligible to receive benefits, ✗ eligible for receive benefits. Against entitled to, the difference is legal and real: an eligible applicant may still be denied, an entitled one may not. ✗ eligible of and ✗ eligible in are errors.
entries.see also: entitled to, suitable for, ready for, exempt from, for

entries.meaning: Weighed down by something you have to carry — a debt or lien on property, or a load of any kind.
examples: The parcel is encumbered by a mortgage and two utility easements.
She arrived encumbered with a cooler, a folding chair, and a dog.
The agency is encumbered by rules written for a different century.
A title encumbered by an old judgment can't be insured until it clears.
He offers opinions unencumbered by any acquaintance with the file.
entries.русский: обременённый чем-л. — юр. залогом на имуществе; вообще — нагруженный ношей
entries.register: formal; a legal term of art about property, and a literary word about burdens generally
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the burden — a lien, a mortgage, a debt, a load, a set of duties. A gerund is not used here (✗ encumbered with paying), and no clause follows.
entries.pattern: be encumbered by [burden] · be encumbered with [burden] · encumbered by debt / by regulation / with baggage · unencumbered by [noun] — the negative, which is commoner in journalism · an encumbrance on [property] — the noun frame, with on
entries.variants: burdened with and saddled with are the plainer versions; weighed down by is the physical one; subject to is the neutral legal term for property carrying a lien.
entries.contrast: The two prepositions are close, and the split is one of feel rather than rule: encumbered by points at the agent doing the burdening (encumbered by debt, encumbered by the rules), while encumbered with points at the load itself (encumbered with three suitcases, encumbered with obligations). In property law both appear, and encumbered by a mortgage is the commoner phrasing. Note the frequent literary use of the negative, unencumbered by, which usually carries a sneer: unencumbered by any knowledge of the subject. The related noun takes on: an encumbrance on the title.
entries.see also: fraught with, replete with, subject to, appurtenant to, with

entries.meaning: Found only in a particular place or population, and permanently present there.
examples: The tortoise is endemic to a single island in the chain.
Cholera remains endemic to several delta regions.
Delays of this kind seem endemic to the permitting office.
Half the plants in the preserve are endemic to this valley.
The parasite is endemic to herds in the northern counties.
entries.русский: эндемичный для — встречающийся только здесь и постоянно
entries.register: technical — ecology, epidemiology, and public health; used loosely in journalism for a problem that will not go away
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a place or a population — endemic to New Zealand, endemic to the region, endemic to that industry. Never a gerund (✗ endemic to logging trees) and never a clause. If what follows is not a place or a group, the word is being misused.
entries.pattern: [species / disease] be endemic to [place] · endemic in [population] — the epidemiologist's variant · endemic [noun] — attributive (endemic corruption, endemic species)
entries.variants: native to is the neutral word for where a species originated; indigenous to is its formal twin for peoples and species; confined to and restricted to say the same thing about distribution without the biology.
entries.contrast: Endemic to means found only there; epidemic and pandemic are about rate, not place. A disease endemic to a region is permanently present at a baseline level; an epidemic is a surge above it. Against native to, which says a species originated somewhere, endemic to says it is found nowhere else — every endemic species is native, but not every native one is endemic. The loose journalistic use (corruption endemic to the department) is now standard but keeps the "built into this place" idea. ✗ endemic of is an error; endemic in is fine before a population.
entries.see also: native to, peculiar to, specific to, common to, to

entries.meaning: Given some quality, power, or fund of money by someone or something else.
examples: The charter leaves the commission endowed with real subpoena power.
She was endowed with a memory for names that made the job easy.
The chair is endowed with a gift from a class that graduated in 1948.
The soil here is endowed with nothing but rocks and good drainage.
Human beings, the text says, are endowed with reason and conscience.
entries.русский: наделённый чем-л. — качеством, полномочием или средствами
entries.register: formal to literary; an American knows it from the Declaration of Independence — endowed by their Creator with certain unalienable Rights — and from institutional writing about gifts
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the quality, power, or funds bestowed — never a gerund (✗ endowed with running fast) and never a clause. The giver, when named, goes in a by-phrase before the with-phrase.
entries.pattern: be endowed with [quality / power] · endowed by [giver] with [gift] · richly / generously / amply endowed with · endow [an institution] with [funds] · an endowed chair — attributive
entries.variants: blessed with is the warm everyday version; gifted with the slightly precious one; possessed of the formal one for qualities already held; furnished with and equipped with the practical ones.
entries.contrast: Against possessed of, which reports what somebody has, endowed with implies the quality was given — by nature, by a creator, or by a donor — which is why it fits rights, talents, and funds and not, say, debts. Note the two live senses: the abstract one (endowed with patience) and the financial one (an endowed professorship), where the verb takes money as its second object. A jocular use about physique exists and is worth knowing so as not to trip over it. ✗ endowed by + quality reverses the roles: endowed by nature names the giver, not the gift.
entries.see also: possessed of, vested with, replete with, full of, with

entries.meaning: Capable of being made binding on a particular person by a court.
examples: The guaranty is enforceable against the parent company, not just the subsidiary.
An oral promise like that is rarely enforceable against anyone.
Counsel opined that the note is valid and enforceable against the borrower.
The covenant runs with the land and is enforceable against later owners.
A settlement signed by one heir is not enforceable against the others.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ənˈfɔrsəbəl əˈɡɛnst/, the final t usually dropped before a consonant: "uh-GENS"
entries.русский: принудительно исполнимый в отношении кого-л. — юр.
entries.register: legal; the natural home is the enforceability opinion in a loan closing (a valid obligation enforceable against the borrower in accordance with its terms)
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the party against whom the obligation can be enforced — never a gerund and never a clause. Related slots take other prepositions: enforceable by [the party who may enforce], enforceable in [a court], enforceable under [a body of law].
entries.pattern: [obligation] be enforceable against [party] · valid, binding, and enforceable against [party] — the closing-opinion formula · enforceable by [party] against [party] · not enforceable against [third party]
entries.variants: binding on is the everyday equivalent from the other direction; actionable against is narrower and concerns suits; good against is the older property phrase (good against the world).
entries.three prepositions divide the roles clea: enforceable against the one who must perform, enforceable by the one who may sue, enforceable in the forum. A clause may be enforceable by the employer against the employee in state court — all three at once. Against binding on, binding upon, which states the same fact in the ordinary drafting idiom, enforceable against is the term used when the question is whether a court would actually make somebody perform. ✗ enforceable to and ✗ enforceable on are errors.
entries.see also: binding on, binding upon, bound by, liable for, liable to, immune from, immune to, against

entries.meaning: Promised in marriage, or occupied in an activity, depending on the preposition.
examples: She got engaged to her college roommate's brother.
The two firms are engaged in a dispute over the patent.
He's been engaged to the same woman for six years.
The department is engaged in rewriting the entire handbook.
Students who are engaged with the material don't need to be told twice.
entries.русский: помолвленный с; engaged in — занятый чем-л., engaged with — вовлечённый во что-л.
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: a person after to — never a gerund (✗ engaged to marrying). After in, a noun phrase or gerund (engaged in negotiating the lease) — never a to-infinitive after either. The single exception is the frozen engaged to be married, where to is an infinitive marker inside a set phrase and no person follows it; that phrase is not a model for anything else the adjective does.
entries.pattern: be engaged to [person] · get engaged to [person] · be engaged in [activity / verb-ing] · be engaged with [an issue or a community] · engaged to be married
entries.variants: betrothed to is the archaic form; promised to survives in period fiction. For the activity sense, involved in and occupied with are the everyday equivalents.
entries.contrast: Engaged to is about marriage; engaged in is about activity; engaged with is about sustained attention. She's engaged to a lawyer (they will marry), She's engaged in litigation (that is what she is doing), She's engaged with the community (she participates seriously). Swapping them produces nonsense or comedy. ✗ engaged with a lawyer does not mean betrothed. Note also engaged meaning occupied — the line is engaged — which is British; American English says busy.
entries.see also: married to, involved in, committed to, to, in

entries.meaning: Showing eager approval of something.
examples: The staff was enthusiastic about moving to a four-day week.
He's enthusiastic about anything with a two-stroke engine.
The board was less than enthusiastic about the price tag.
She's enthusiastic about teaching the intro section again.
Reviewers were enthusiastic about the first season and cooler about the second.
entries.русский: восторженно относящийся к, горячо поддерживающий
entries.register: neutral to formal; the everyday words are excited about and into
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (enthusiastic about trying again) — never a to-infinitive. ✗ enthusiastic to start is not idiomatic; write eager to start.
entries.pattern: be enthusiastic about [noun / verb-ing] · less than enthusiastic about [noun] · enthusiastic supporter of [noun] — the noun form takes of
entries.variants: excited about is the everyday twin; keen on the British one; into the casual American one (she's really into pottery).
entries.contrast: Enthusiastic about takes a gerund; eager to takes an infinitive — this pair is worth memorizing together, because they mean nearly the same thing and cannot borrow each other's structure: ✓ enthusiastic about starting, ✓ eager to start, ✗ enthusiastic to start. The litotes less than enthusiastic about is the standard American way of saying someone hated it. ✗ enthusiastic for and ✗ enthusiastic of are errors, though the noun enthusiasm takes for: enthusiasm for the project.
entries.see also: excited about, eager for, keen on, interested in, about

entries.meaning: Having a right to something, whether by law, by contract, or by plain desert.
examples: Every employee is entitled to an itemized pay stub.
You're entitled to know what the charge was before you sign.
She's entitled to three weeks off and hasn't taken a day.
Riders are entitled to a refund if the delay runs over an hour.
He isn't entitled to a hearing until the appeal is docketed.
entries.русский: имеющий право на — по закону, договору или по заслугам
entries.register: neutral to formal; the standard word in American benefits law, contracts, and everyday argument about rights
entries.complement: two frames, and both are correct. With a noun phrase, the to is a preposition: entitled to a refund, entitled to back pay. With a bare verb, the to is an infinitive marker: entitled to know, entitled to vote. What is not available is the gerund: ✗ entitled to knowing, ✗ entitled to receiving a refund. This is the one entry in the file where the noun test comes out positive (entitled to a refund ✓) and the infinitive is still legal, so the test has to be used in the other direction — the -ing form is the form to avoid.
entries.pattern: be entitled to [noun] · be entitled to [verb] · entitle [someone] to [noun] · an entitlement to [noun] — the noun frame · entitled [title] — the unrelated sense, "given the title," as in a book entitled ...
entries.variants: eligible for is the weaker word (you may apply); have a right to is the plain paraphrase and behaves the same way; due takes no preposition (the refund due her).
entries.contrast: Entitled to means it is owed you; eligible for means you may apply for it. An eligible applicant can be turned down; an entitled claimant can sue. Note the second, unrelated entitled meaning "titled" — a memo entitled "Weekend Coverage" — which takes no preposition and no complement of this kind; some American editors prefer plain titled there to keep the two apart. And note the modern pejorative entitled used alone (an entitled kid), which takes no complement at all. ✗ entitled for and ✗ entitled of are errors.
entries.see also: eligible for, deserving of, worthy of, liable for, liable to, to

entries.meaning: Wanting what someone else has.
examples: I'm envious of anyone who can sleep on a plane.
She was envious of the extra week they got in August.
He's envious of his brother's easy way with strangers.
Colleagues were quietly envious of the corner office.
Nobody is envious of the job once they've seen the hours.
entries.русский: завидующий кому-л.
entries.register: neutral to formal; jealous of is the everyday word
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (envious of having the whole summer free) — never a to-infinitive and never a clause.
entries.pattern: be envious of [person / thing] · envious of [someone's] [possession] · make [someone] envious
entries.variants: jealous of covers the same ground in speech; covetous of is the biblical register.
entries.contrast: Envious of wants what someone else has; jealous of also guards what it already has. Envious of her promotion is straightforward; jealous of her promotion means the same thing in ordinary speech, but jealous of his time means protective of it, a sense envious cannot carry. Careful writers keep envy for wanting and jealousy for guarding, though the distinction is widely ignored. ✗ envious about and ✗ envious at are errors.
entries.see also: jealous of, proud of, suspicious of, of

entries.meaning: The same in amount, value, or capability — or, idiomatically, up to what a job demands.
examples: One tablespoon is equal to three teaspoons.
The settlement was equal to four months' pay.
She proved equal to the task within a week.
Nothing on the menu is equal to what they served here in 2003.
Their offer is equal to ours in everything but timing.
entries.русский: равный чему-л.; идиом. — способный справиться с задачей
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (equal to running the whole thing alone) — never a to-infinitive. ✗ equal to run it is an error, though the idiom equal to the task is a fixed noun frame that hides the same structure.
entries.pattern: [X] is equal to [Y] · equal to the task / equal to the occasion · equal in [respect] to [noun] · equal parts [X] and [Y] · all things being equal
entries.variants: equivalent to is the technical version; the same as is the everyday one; on a par with is the idiom of comparison.
entries.contrast: Equal to takes to, never than. ✗ equal than is a persistent error made by speakers whose first language uses a comparative there; the same warning applies to superior to, inferior to, senior to, and preferable to, which all reject than. The idiomatic sense — equal to the task, meaning up to it — is not about quantity at all, and equal to + -ing belongs with it. See equal to for the word as a comparison preposition.
entries.see also: identical to, similar to, superior to, inferior to, equal to

entries.meaning: Equal in value, effect, or function to something else, without necessarily being the same thing.
examples: The stipend is equivalent to about nineteen dollars an hour.
A year of the certificate program is equivalent to two semesters of credit.
Saying nothing here is equivalent to agreeing with them.
The generic is chemically equivalent to the brand and costs a fifth as much.
That degree is equivalent to an American master's for licensing purposes.
entries.русский: равнозначный, эквивалентный чему-л. — равный по действию, но не тождественный
entries.register: neutral to technical; standard in science, finance, and translation, and common in ordinary argument
entries.complement: a noun phrase or a gerund (equivalent to admitting the whole thing) — never a to-infinitive: ✗ equivalent to admit the whole thing. A wh-clause is fine: equivalent to what the state pays.
entries.pattern: be equivalent to [noun / verb-ing] · roughly / functionally / morally equivalent to · the equivalent of [noun] — the noun frame, which switches to of · equivalent in [respect] to [noun]
entries.variants: tantamount to is the near twin, restricted to the "amounts to the same thing" sense and nearly always about something bad; identical to claims sameness rather than equal value; the same as is the plain phrase; comparable to claims only that a comparison is fair.
entries.contrast: Equivalent to claims equal value or effect; identical to claims the things are the same. A metric wrench may be equivalent to an inch wrench for the job without being identical to it. Note the switch of preposition between adjective and noun: equivalent to a month's rent, but the equivalent of a month's rent. Against tantamount to, which is judgmental, equivalent to is neutral and quantitative. ✗ equivalent with is an error, and ✗ equivalent as is worse.
entries.see also: identical to, tantamount to, equal to, synonymous with, to

entries.meaning: Absolutely necessary — the thing without which the rest fails.
examples: Trust is essential to any working partnership.
Water at the right temperature is essential for getting the dough to rise.
Timing was essential to the whole rescue.
It is essential to read the second page before signing.
Redundancy is essential to a system that can't be allowed to fail.
entries.русский: необходимый для — то, без чего всё рушится
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after to and for (essential to keeping the doors open) — never a to-infinitive after the preposition. The it-frame takes an infinitive with no preposition: It is essential to arrive early, and formal writing uses a subjunctive that-clause: essential that he be present.
entries.pattern: [X] is essential to [Y] · [X] is essential for [purpose / verb-ing] · it is essential to [verb] · it is essential that [subjunctive clause] · absolutely essential
entries.variants: vital to, crucial to, critical to, indispensable to, and integral to all pattern the same way and all take to by default and for before a purpose.
entries.contrast: To names what the thing is essential to; for names what it is essential for. Essential to the plan (the plan needs it) versus essential for germination (it makes germination happen) — the drift is real but the two overlap widely and neither is wrong in most sentences. Watch the subjunctive: formal American writing keeps It is essential that she be notified, not is notified. ✗ essential of is an error.
entries.see also: critical of, relevant to, useful for, suitable for, to

entries.meaning: Eagerly looking forward to something, or stirred up by it.
examples: The kids are excited about the trip to the coast.
We're excited to announce the new fall schedule.
She's excited about moving closer to her sister.
He was genuinely excited for her when the offer came through.
Everybody got excited about the renovation until they saw the estimate.
entries.русский: радостно предвкушающий что-л., воодушевлённый
entries.register: neutral; extremely common in American speech and business writing
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after about and by (excited about starting) — never a to-infinitive after a preposition. The adjective takes a bare to-infinitive directly (excited to announce), and that frame is standard American English, not an error.
entries.pattern: be excited about [noun / verb-ing] · be excited by [the cause] · be excited for [an event, or a person on their behalf] · be excited to [verb] · get excited about [noun]
entries.variants: thrilled about / to, psyched about (informal), and pumped about (informal) all follow the same frames.
entries.contrast: This adjective is unusual in taking both the gerund and the infinitive naturally, with a small difference: excited about starting is about the whole prospect, excited to start is about the act itself and is the standard frame in announcements (we're excited to share). Excited by points at the cause as agent (excited by the possibility). Excited for has two uses that are worth separating: excited for the game (looking forward to an event, once informal and now general American) and excited for you (happy on your behalf). ✗ excited of is an error.
entries.see also: enthusiastic about, eager for, happy about, about

entries.meaning: Released by a rule from something that would otherwise apply to you.
examples: Nonprofits are exempt from the local business tax.
She's exempt from the language requirement because of the test score.
Nobody in this building is exempt from the fire drill.
Farm vehicles are exempt from the weight limit on that stretch.
Salaried supervisors are exempt from overtime under the state rule.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /əɡˈzɛmp frəm/ — the pt cluster simplifies to /p/ before a consonant, so exempt from is normally "ig-ZEM-frum"
entries.русский: освобождённый от — от правила, налога, обязанности
entries.register: neutral to formal; the standard word of American tax, wage-and-hour law, and school and military rules
entries.complement: a noun phrase or a gerund — exempt from paying sales tax ✓ — and never a to-infinitive: ✗ exempt from pay sales tax. The noun test is decisive: exempt from the tax ✓. No clause follows.
entries.pattern: be exempt from [rule / tax / requirement] · exempt [someone] from [obligation] — the verb · exempt from [noun] under [statute] · tax-exempt / an exempt employee — attributive, no preposition
entries.variants: excused from is the everyday version for duties and classes; immune from is the legal one for liability and process; free of and free from cover the general sense; not subject to is the drafter's paraphrase.
entries.contrast: Exempt from releases you from a rule that would otherwise apply to you — which is the exact opposite of subject to, and the two often appear in the same sentence. Against immune from, immune to, the difference is what is escaped: an exemption is granted by a rule, an immunity is a shield against liability or process. In American employment law the word is a noun as well: an exempt employee is one exempt from overtime, and nonexempt is the pay-by-the-hour category. ✗ exempt of and ✗ exempt to are errors.
entries.see also: immune from, immune to, free of, subject to, eligible for, from

entries.meaning: Highly skilled — at a practice, in a field, or, as a noun, on a subject.
examples: He's expert at talking people down from a bad decision.
She's expert in the kind of soil chemistry nobody else here understands.
The witness is an expert on structural failures in older bridges.
They're expert at finding parking downtown, which is its own talent.
We need someone expert in export controls before we bid.
entries.русский: искусный в чём-л. — прилагательное берёт at/in, а существительное an expert on
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after at (expert at getting people to talk) and after in (expert in tax law) — never a to-infinitive. ✗ expert to do it is not English.
entries.pattern: be expert at [skill / verb-ing] · be expert in [field] · an expert on [subject] — the noun takes on · an expert in [field] · expert witness (no preposition)
entries.variants: skilled at / in, proficient in, adept at, and a whiz at cover the range from formal to slangy.
entries.contrast: The adjective and the noun take different prepositions, and this is the trap. ✓ She is expert at reading X-rays (adjective, at + skill) and ✓ She is an expert on medieval coins (noun, on + subject). In works for both when a field rather than a skill or a topic is meant: expert in immunology. ✗ expert of is an error in every frame. Note that American English uses the adjective expert far less than the noun; she's an expert at is commoner than she's expert at.
entries.see also: skilled at, good at, capable of, at

entries.meaning: Knowing something well enough to work with it — or, from the other side, being recognizable to someone.
examples: Are you familiar with the county's permitting process?
Her face was familiar to everyone in the courtroom.
It takes a week to get familiar with the layout.
He's familiar with running a kitchen twice this size.
The tune was familiar to me but I couldn't place it.
entries.русский: хорошо знакомый с чем-л.; familiar to — знакомый кому-л., с другой стороны
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (familiar with running a crew) — never a to-infinitive. A wh-clause is possible in the loose sense (familiar with how it works), and a that-clause is not: ✗ familiar that.
entries.pattern: be familiar with [thing known] · be familiar to [person who knows it] · become / get familiar with [noun] · be too familiar with [person] — the disapproving sense
entries.variants: acquainted with is the formal equivalent; up on is the casual one (up on the new rules).
entries.contrast: The subject flips between the two prepositions, and this is the classic error. I'm familiar with the software — the knower is the subject. The software is familiar to me — the thing known is the subject. ✗ The software is familiar with me and ✗ I'm familiar to the software are both wrong. A third sense of the bare adjective means presumptuous intimacy (don't be familiar), which is why too familiar with the customers can be a complaint rather than a compliment.
entries.see also: accustomed to, aware of, used to, known for, with, to

entries.meaning: Widely known — for something done, or as something one is.
examples: The town is famous for a pie nobody there actually eats.
She's famous for never missing a deadline.
He was famous as a defense attorney long before the trial.
That stretch of coast is famous for fog in July.
The diner is famous for staying open through three hurricanes.
entries.русский: знаменитый чем-л.; famous as — знаменитый в качестве кого-л.
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (famous for turning down the part) after for — never a to-infinitive. After as, a noun phrase naming a role (famous as a trial lawyer).
entries.pattern: be famous for [noun / verb-ing] · be famous as [role] · famous for being [adjective] · world-famous for [noun] · famous throughout [place]
entries.variants: known for is the neutral everyday version; renowned for and celebrated for are the formal ones; notorious for is the negative one.
entries.contrast: For names what you did; as names what you are. Famous for her Fourth Symphony versus famous as a conductor.
