Against notorious for, which is always negative, famous for is neutral to positive — so famous for cutting corners is a joke that works because it borrows the wrong word on purpose. ✗ famous of and ✗ famous by are errors.
entries.see also: known for, notorious for, popular with, for

entries.meaning: Out of patience with something that has gone on too long.
examples: She's fed up with being the only one who answers the phone.
Residents are fed up with the potholes on Elm.
I got fed up with the whole process and hired someone.
He's fed up with excuses about the delivery date.
By March everyone is fed up with winter.
entries.русский: сытый по горло чем-л. — разг.
entries.register: informal to neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (fed up with waiting) — never a to-infinitive and never a clause.
entries.pattern: be fed up with [noun / verb-ing] · get fed up with [noun] · fed up (alone, with no complement) · thoroughly / completely fed up with [noun]
entries.variants: sick of, tired of, sick and tired of, and done with are the American equivalents. Fed up of is British colloquial and is an error in American English.
entries.contrast: Fed up takes with; sick and tired take of. ✗ fed up of the noise and ✗ sick with the noise both go wrong by borrowing the other pattern. Against bored with, which reports flatness, fed up with reports irritation that has been building — it is the end of a person's patience, not the end of their interest. The three-word intensifier sick and tired of is fixed and cannot be rebuilt as ✗ sick and fed up of.
entries.see also: sick of, tired of, bored with, annoyed with, with

entries.meaning: Having affection or a liking for something — often an established, habitual one.
examples: She's fond of her students in a way that shows up in the details.
He's fond of saying the roof will last another winter.
I've grown fond of the noise from the rail yard.
They're not overly fond of surprises at that office.
My grandmother was fond of anything with cardamom in it.
entries.русский: любящий что-л., питающий давнюю склонность к
entries.register: neutral, slightly old-fashioned and warm
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (fond of telling that story) — never a to-infinitive. ✗ fond to tell is not English.
entries.pattern: be fond of [noun / verb-ing] · grow / become fond of [noun] · fond of saying [quotation] · not overly fond of [noun]
entries.variants: keen on is British; partial to is the same shade with a hint of indulgence; like is the plain verb.
entries.contrast: Fond of + -ing often carries a note of habit rather than pleasure: He's fond of reminding us that he warned them is a criticism, not a compliment. The bare adjective before a noun means affectionate (a fond farewell, fond memories) and is a different use with no preposition. ✗ fond about and ✗ fond for are errors, though the noun takes for: a fondness for old maps.
entries.see also: crazy about, keen on, proud of, of

entries.meaning: Built on something as its base — a principle, a body of evidence, or an assumption.
examples: The whole complaint is founded on a misreading of one paragraph.
Their objection is founded upon forty years of practice in the district.
A partnership founded on a handshake is hard to unwind.
The estimate was founded on prices from before the tariffs.
Her confidence is founded on having done the job twice before.
entries.русский: основанный на — на принципе, доказательствах или допущении
entries.register: formal; the natural home is writing about principles, claims, and institutions, and upon is the rhetorical variant
entries.complement: a noun phrase or a gerund (founded on keeping everyone in the dark) — never a to-infinitive: ✗ founded on keep everyone in the dark. Also founded in before an abstract quality (founded in fact, founded in law), where in is idiomatic.
entries.pattern: be founded on [principle / evidence] · founded upon [noun] — the formal variant · well founded / ill founded — as one word in unfounded · found [an institution] on [principle] — the active verb
entries.variants: based on is the ordinary everyday equivalent; grounded in is the near twin and prefers in; predicated on is the drier formal one; resting on is the metaphor made visible.
entries.contrast: Against based on, which is neutral and common, founded on carries the architectural metaphor and suits institutions, doctrines, and claims — a republic founded on a written constitution, a suspicion founded on nothing. Against grounded in, note the preposition split: things are founded on a foundation but grounded in a medium. The negative has fused into a single word: an unfounded rumor, never ✗ a not founded rumor. ✗ founded in is fine before fact, law, and truth, but ✗ founded of and ✗ founded to are errors.
entries.see also: based on, grounded in, derived from, dependent on, on

entries.meaning: Loaded with something bad — risk, difficulty, tension, or error.
examples: The handoff between the two systems is fraught with opportunities for error.
Any conversation about the will is fraught with forty years of grievance.
The route is fraught with switchbacks and no place to turn around.
Early estimates were fraught with assumptions nobody wrote down.
Their first season back was fraught with injuries.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /frɔt wəθ/, the t often lost before the w: "FRAW-with"
entries.русский: чреватый чем-л. — риском, трудностями, напряжением; книжн.
entries.register: formal to journalistic; the phrase fraught with peril and fraught with risk are near-clichés of American editorial writing
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming something bad and abundant — danger, difficulty, risk, error, tension. Never a gerund (✗ fraught with delaying) and never a clause. The complement is essentially always negative: ✗ fraught with opportunity reads as a mistake, though the word once meant simply "laden."
entries.pattern: be fraught with [danger / difficulty] · a process fraught with [noun] · fraught — used alone as a modern adjective meaning tense (a fraught conversation), with no complement
entries.variants: riddled with is the near twin for flaws and errors; rife with is the journalist's word for something bad and widespread; replete with is the neutral-to-positive counterpart; laden with keeps the original cargo metaphor.
entries.contrast: Against replete with, which is neutral or admiring and means "abundantly supplied," fraught with is always negative — the two words are the same idea with opposite polarity. Note the recent and now fully standard bare use of fraught: the whole meeting was fraught takes no complement at all and means tense rather than dangerous, and it is an adjective, not this preposition pattern. ✗ fraught of and ✗ fraught by are errors.
entries.see also: replete with, encumbered by, encumbered with, full of, crowded with, with

entries.meaning: Without something unwanted, or released from it.
examples: The house came back from inspection free of any structural issues.
She's been free of the debt for two years.
The area is now free from the flooding that plagued it for a decade.
You're free to leave whenever you like.
Their new formula is free of dyes and preservatives.
entries.русский: свободный от, лишённый чего-л. нежелательного
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase after of and from (free of debt, free from interference) — a gerund is possible but rare (free from having to explain herself). The adjective takes a bare to-infinitive directly (free to leave), which is a different frame meaning permitted, not lacking.
entries.pattern: be free of [unwanted thing] · be free from [an imposed condition] · be free to [verb] · [noun]-free as a suffix: tax-free, gluten-free, scot-free
entries.variants: free of and free from overlap almost completely; from is slightly more formal and is preferred where the thing removed was imposed by someone (free from persecution). Rid of and devoid of are the neighbors, both with of.
entries.contrast: Free of / from means lacking; free to means allowed. Free of charge costs nothing; free to go may leave. The suffix -free has become the productive American way to say the same thing in a single word (fee-free, fragrance-free) and takes no preposition at all. ✗ free with means something different again — generous, and often too generous: free with other people's money.
entries.see also: safe from, absent from, independent of, short of, of

entries.meaning: On good terms with someone, or pleasant in manner toward them.
examples: He's been friendly with the family since before the kids were born.
The staff is friendly to anyone who walks in, regulars or not.
She got friendly with the contractor and now gets the good slots.
Their policy is friendly toward small vendors.
It's a friendly town, friendly to newcomers in a way that surprised us.
entries.русский: в дружеских отношениях с; friendly to — приветливый, доброжелательный к
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: a person or group after with and to; a noun after toward — never a gerund and never a to-infinitive after any of them.
entries.pattern: be friendly with [person] · be friendly to / toward [person] · get friendly with [person] · [noun]-friendly as a suffix: kid-friendly, pet-friendly, user-friendly
entries.variants: toward is the American spelling; towards is the British one, and both are read as ordinary in the United States. On good terms with is the formal equivalent of friendly with.
entries.contrast: Friendly with means you have a relationship; friendly to means you behave pleasantly. She's friendly with the mayor implies they know each other; She's friendly to everyone who comes in describes her manner and implies nothing about acquaintance. That difference matters — the first can insinuate favoritism, which is exactly why reporters choose it. The productive suffix -friendly means accommodating to and takes no preposition: a dog-friendly patio. ✗ friendly of is an error, though That was friendly of you is a different, correct frame.
entries.see also: kind to, nice to, polite to, popular with, with

entries.meaning: Feeling fear — of something in general, or by something in particular.
examples: He's been frightened of elevators since the outage.
The horse was frightened by the truck backfiring.
She was too frightened to say anything at the time.
Small children are often frightened of men with beards.
They were frightened for their neighbors, whose lights had been off for days.
entries.русский: напуганный чем-л., боящийся
entries.register: neutral; slightly more formal than scared of
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (frightened of falling) after of; noun phrase after by — never a to-infinitive after a preposition. The adjective takes a bare to-infinitive directly (frightened to move), a separate frame.
entries.pattern: be frightened of [noun / verb-ing] · be frightened by [the event that caused it] · be frightened to [verb] · be frightened for [someone] · frighten [someone] (no preposition on the object)
entries.variants: afraid of and scared of are the everyday twins; terrified of and petrified of are the intensified ones.
entries.contrast: Frightened of is a standing fear; frightened by is a single event. She's frightened of dogs describes a phobia; She was frightened by the dog describes one afternoon. This of / by split is the same one that runs through annoyed, bored, confused, and shocked, and it is the most transferable pattern in this file: of or with for the standing state, by for the agent that produced it. And as with afraid, frightened to move means too scared to act, not scared of the movement.
entries.see also: afraid of, scared of, nervous about, shocked at, of

entries.meaning: Containing as much as it can hold, or containing a great deal of something.
examples: The trunk was full of road salt and jumper cables.
Her first draft is full of good sentences in the wrong order.
The lot was full of cars with out-of-state plates.
He's full of plans and short on follow-through.
The room was full of people who had never met the deceased.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /fʊl əv/, and in fast speech /ˈfʊlə/ — the fulla of fulla nonsense
entries.русский: полный чего-л.
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase, usually without an article for mass and plural nouns (full of sand, full of tourists) — a gerund is not used, and never a to-infinitive.
entries.pattern: be full of [noun] · full of [abstract quality]: full of ideas, full of himself · fill [something] with [something] — the verb takes with · filled with [noun]
entries.variants: filled with, packed with, and loaded with take with; replete with is the formal one; chock-full of is the emphatic American one.
entries.contrast: Full takes of; fill and filled take with. ✗ full with water and ✗ filled of water are the two errors, and they are mirror images. The idiomatic full of himself means conceited; full of it is a polite American way to say someone is lying. Note that full also works with no complement (I'm full), where it means having eaten enough.
entries.see also: crowded with, rich in, short of, of

entries.meaning: Extremely angry.
examples: She was furious with the contractor for starting without a permit.
Parents were furious about the way the closure was announced.
He's furious at himself for not reading the fine print.
The whole shop was furious with management by Thursday.
They were furious that nobody had thought to call the family first.
entries.русский: в ярости на кого-л.
entries.register: neutral; the strongest ordinary word for anger
entries.complement: a person after with; a noun phrase or gerund after about and at (furious about being kept waiting) — never a to-infinitive. A that-clause attaches to the bare adjective: furious that no one had called.
entries.pattern: be furious with [person] · be furious about / at / over [situation] · be furious (that) [clause] · furious with [person] for [verb-ing]
entries.variants: livid, irate, and incensed are the same intensity; incensed prefers at or by, irate prefers about or at.
entries.contrast: Same split as angry: with for the person, about or over for the situation, at for either. Furious with her lawyer about the delay fills both slots at once. Note that furious also means very fast (a furious pace), a sense with no preposition at all and no anger in it. ✗ furious on is an error.
entries.see also: angry with, mad at, annoyed with, upset about, with

entries.meaning: Giving freely — of a resource, or to a person.
examples: She's generous with her time in a way that costs her weekends.
The company has been generous to families of the crew.
He's generous with praise and stingy with raises.
It was generous of you to cover the difference.
Be generous with the butter or the whole thing sticks.
entries.русский: щедрый на что-л.; generous to — щедрый к кому-л.
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: a noun naming what is given after with (generous with her time); a person after to and toward — never a gerund after either, and never a to-infinitive, though the it-frame takes one: It was generous of you to offer.
entries.pattern: be generous with [resource] · be generous to / toward [person] · it is generous of [someone] to [verb] · generous in [respect]
entries.variants: liberal with is the older, less loaded version; free with is the version that implies excess (free with his opinions).
entries.contrast: With takes what you give; to takes who you give it to. Generous with his time and generous to his employees both work, and generous to his time does not. The of-frame is a third pattern common to all judgment adjectives — kind of you, rude of him, generous of them — where of names the doer and an infinitive names the deed. ✗ generous for is an error.
entries.see also: kind to, gentle with, patient with, with

entries.meaning: Handling someone or something carefully, without force.
examples: Be gentle with the latch; it's original to the house.
She's remarkably gentle with frightened animals.
The nurse was gentle with him during the whole exam.
Go easy — be gentle with yourself about the first draft.
The formula is gentle on skin and still gets the grease off.
entries.русский: бережно, мягко обращающийся с кем-л. или чем-л.
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: a noun naming what is handled after with — a person, an animal, or an object. Never a gerund, never a to-infinitive, and never a clause. The it-frame takes an infinitive: It was gentle of him to say it that way is possible but rare.
entries.pattern: be gentle with [person / animal / object] · go gentle on [someone] — informal · gentle on [something], of products: gentle on skin
entries.variants: easy on is the informal equivalent (go easy on him); tender with is the warmer one; careful with overlaps almost entirely.
entries.contrast: Gentle takes with, not to, which breaks the pattern that governs most of the behavior adjectives — kind to, cruel to, rude to, but gentle with and patient with. The reason is that gentle and patient describe the manner of handling rather than the direction of treatment, and with is the preposition of manner. Product English uses a fourth frame, gentle on: gentle on sensitive skin. ✗ gentle to is not idiomatic in American English.
entries.see also: careful with, patient with, kind to, with

entries.meaning: Belonging to the very subject under discussion, not merely touching on it.
examples: The chair ruled that the amendment was not germane to the bill.
Whatever happened in 2011 is not germane to this year's audit.
Only questions germane to the witness's direct testimony are allowed.
Keep the comments germane to the item on the agenda.
That objection is germane to the schedule but not to the design.
entries.русский: имеющий прямое отношение к обсуждаемому предмету — книжн.
entries.register: formal; an American meets it in parliamentary procedure (the amendment is not germane to the bill), in court, and in academic argument
entries.complement: a noun phrase or a gerund (germane to deciding the motion) — never a to-infinitive: ✗ germane to decide the motion. A wh-clause is fine: germane to what the committee is considering.
entries.pattern: be germane to [question / matter] · not germane to [noun] — the commonest frame, since the word is usually used to rule something out · strictly / directly germane to
entries.variants: relevant to is the neutral everyday equivalent; pertinent to is its formal twin; material to is the legal one and is stronger; apposite to is the literary one; on point is the American lawyer's idiom.
entries.contrast: Germane to is the word for topical fit, and its home is the rules of debate — in the House and in most American legislatures an amendment must be germane to the bill, meaning it must address the same subject. Against relevant to, which is the general word, germane to claims a closer relation: relevant evidence bears on the case, a germane amendment belongs to the very question at hand. Against material to, which asks whether something could change the outcome, germane to asks only whether it belongs to the subject. ✗ germane with and ✗ germane for are errors.
entries.see also: relevant to, pertinent to, material to, specific to, to

entries.meaning: Pleased that something is the case.
examples: I'm glad about the way the whole thing worked out.
She's glad about not having to make the drive twice.
He was glad of the company on such a long stretch.
We'd be glad to look at the drawings tomorrow.
I'm just glad that somebody said it out loud.
entries.русский: радующийся тому, что что-л. так
entries.register: neutral, slightly old-fashioned in the about frame
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after about (glad about not having to drive) — never a to-infinitive after about. The adjective takes a bare to-infinitive directly (glad to help) and a that-clause (glad that you called), and those two frames are far commoner than the prepositional one.
entries.pattern: be glad about [noun / verb-ing] · be glad of [something one is grateful for] · be glad to [verb] · be glad (that) [clause] · be glad for [someone]
entries.variants: happy about is the everyday equivalent and covers all the same frames; pleased about is the slightly more formal one.
entries.contrast: Glad to + verb is the workhorse and means willing (glad to help); glad about + noun reports a feeling about a state of affairs. Glad of is an older frame that survives in glad of the company and glad of the chance and reads as literary in American English. Glad for you means pleased on your behalf, exactly parallel to happy for you and excited for you. ✗ glad with is an error.
entries.see also: happy about, pleased with, grateful to, about

entries.meaning: Skilled, beneficial, capable with something, or kind — the preposition decides which.
examples: She's good at explaining the same thing four different ways.
Walking is good for your back and your temper.
He's good with horses and hopeless with paperwork.
That neighbor was good to us when my father was sick.
They're good about letting you know before the water goes off.
entries.русский: умелый в чём-л. — at умение, for полезный, with умеющий обращаться с, to добрый к
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after at (good at listening) — never a to-infinitive. ✗ good at listen and ✗ good to listening are the two ways this goes wrong. After for, a person or purpose; after with, a category of thing handled.
entries.pattern: be good at [skill / verb-ing] · be good for [person / purpose] · be good with [people / money / one's hands] · be good to [person] · be good about [verb-ing] · no good at [noun]
entries.variants: skilled at, strong at, and a natural at are the formal, the sporting, and the admiring versions.
entries.contrast: This is the four-way split that every learner of English eventually has to memorize. Good at = skilled: good at chemistry. Good for = beneficial: good for your knees; and, in a second sense, good for one more season = lasting. Good with = able to handle a category: good with kids, good with numbers, good with her hands. Good to = kind: She was good to me. A fifth, good about + -ing, means reliably doing something: good about calling ahead. ✗ good in math is an error in American English, though good in a crisis is fixed and correct.
entries.see also: bad at, skilled at, expert at, useful for, kind to, at

entries.meaning: Feeling thanks — to whoever gave it, for whatever was given.
examples: We're grateful to the crew that stayed through the night.
She's grateful for every extra week the treatment bought.
I'm grateful to my sister for not saying I told you so.
He'd be grateful to have the report by Friday.
They were grateful that the storm turned before it reached the harbor.
entries.русский: благодарный кому-л. (to) за что-л. (for)
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: a person or institution after to; a noun phrase or gerund after for (grateful for being given a second chance) — never a to-infinitive after a preposition. The adjective takes a bare to-infinitive directly (grateful to have it) and a that-clause (grateful that no one was hurt).
entries.pattern: be grateful to [person] · be grateful for [thing] · be grateful to [person] for [thing / verb-ing] · be grateful to [verb] · be grateful (that) [clause] · I'd be grateful if you would [verb]
entries.variants: thankful for covers the for half only; indebted to and obliged to cover the to half and are formal.
entries.contrast: To takes the person, for takes the thing, and both slots can be filled at once: grateful to the neighbors for the ride. The trap is the double to: I'm grateful to have it uses an infinitive, not the person-slot, so ✗ I'm grateful to the chance is an error where for was needed. Thankful cannot take a person at all: ✗ thankful to the neighbors is odd, though thankful to God is a fixed exception.
entries.see also: thankful for, proud of, sorry for, to, for

entries.meaning: Resting on something solid — evidence, tradition, or practical experience.
examples: The recommendation is grounded in three years of intake data.
Her teaching is grounded in the years she spent on the floor of a plant.
An argument grounded in nothing but anecdote won't survive review.
The program is grounded in the same theory the state manual uses.
He wanted a plan grounded in what the crews could actually do.
entries.русский: опирающийся на — на доказательства, традицию или практический опыт
entries.register: neutral to formal; common in academic writing, policy prose, and criticism
entries.complement: a noun phrase — a body of evidence, a tradition, a discipline — or a gerund (grounded in doing the work yourself). Never a to-infinitive: ✗ grounded in do the work. No clause follows.
entries.pattern: be grounded in [evidence / tradition] · firmly / solidly / deeply grounded in · ground [a claim] in [evidence] — the verb · well grounded in [subject] — meaning well trained in it
entries.variants: rooted in is the organic metaphor and the commonest alternative; based on is the plain word; founded on takes on rather than in; anchored in is the nautical version.
entries.contrast: The preposition is in, not on, and the metaphor explains why: you are grounded in a medium that surrounds and holds you, but founded on a base you sit atop. ✗ grounded on turns up and reads as a slip. Note the two other groundeds an American hears daily: the punished teenager (grounded for a week), and the aircraft that cannot fly (the fleet was grounded) — neither takes in. And note well-grounded in, which is about a person's training rather than an argument's support.
entries.see also: based on, founded on, founded upon, derived from, implicit in, in

entries.meaning: Having committed an offense — or, with about, feeling bad over something minor.
examples: He was found guilty of two counts of mail fraud.
She pleaded guilty to the lesser charge, which is the one frame that uses to.
I'm guilty of forgetting names about four seconds after hearing them.
He feels guilty about not visiting more often.
The report found the agency guilty of nothing worse than sloppiness.
entries.русский: виновный в чём-л.; guilty about — испытывающий чувство вины из-за мелочи
entries.register: neutral; legal in the of frame
entries.complement: a noun naming an offense, or a gerund naming the act (guilty of falsifying the records) after of — never a to-infinitive. After about, a noun phrase or gerund naming what you feel bad over (guilty about leaving early).
entries.pattern: be / be found guilty of [offense / verb-ing] · plead guilty to [charge] — the one frame with to · feel guilty about [noun / verb-ing] · guilty as charged · guilty conscience (no preposition)
entries.variants: culpable of is the formal legal version; responsible for covers the non-criminal sense of having caused something.
entries.contrast: Guilty of is about what you did; guilty about is about how you feel. He's guilty of tax fraud is a verdict; He feels guilty about the tax return is a mood. The two do not swap: ✗ guilty about tax fraud would report only remorse, and ✗ feel guilty of leaving early is wrong. A third preposition belongs to one fixed frame: you plead guilty to a charge — ✓ pleaded guilty to two counts, ✗ pleaded guilty of two counts — while the verdict itself keeps of: found guilty of two counts. The opposite of the legal sense is innocent of, also with of. ✗ guilty for is an error, though guilty for having done it appears in speech.
entries.see also: innocent of, ashamed of, responsible for, sorry for, of

entries.meaning: Pleased — about a state of affairs, with a result, or for someone else.
examples: Nobody was happy about the schedule change, but nobody fought it.
Are you happy with how the floors turned out?
She's genuinely happy for him, which is harder than it sounds.
I'd be happy to send over what we have.
Management wasn't happy about finding out from the newspaper.
entries.русский: довольный чем-л.; happy with результатом, happy for за кого-л.
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after about and with (happy about being asked) — never a to-infinitive after a preposition. The adjective takes a bare to-infinitive directly (happy to help) and a that-clause (happy that it's settled).
entries.pattern: be happy about [situation / verb-ing] · be happy with [thing or result being judged] · be happy for [person] · be happy to [verb] · be happy (that) [clause] · not happy about [noun]
entries.variants: pleased about / with is the more formal twin; glad about the slightly old-fashioned one; thrilled about the intensified one.
entries.contrast: Three prepositions, three targets. About = the situation: happy about the move. With = your verdict on a thing you are assessing: happy with the contractor's work — this is the one used in reviews and evaluations. For = on someone else's behalf: happy for you, which says nothing about your own situation. The infinitive frame happy to is a politeness formula in American business writing and means willing. The litotes not happy about is standard understatement for angry. ✗ happy of is an error.
entries.see also: pleased with, glad about, satisfied with, excited about, about

entries.meaning: Causing damage or injury to something.
examples: Sustained noise at that level is harmful to hearing.
The runoff is harmful to everything downstream of the plant.
Rumors like that are harmful to morale long after they're disproved.
The additive was found to be harmful to pollinators.
Delay is harmful to the case in ways the client doesn't see yet.
entries.русский: вредный для, причиняющий вред
entries.register: neutral to formal; the everyday equivalent is bad for
entries.complement: noun phrase naming the thing damaged — a person, a body part, an environment, an interest. A gerund is possible where a practice is meant (harmful to letting the market clear is awkward; prefer a noun). Never a to-infinitive, never a clause.
entries.pattern: [X] is harmful to [Y] · potentially / directly harmful to [noun] · harmful effects on [noun] — the noun effect takes on, not to
entries.variants: damaging to, injurious to, and detrimental to are the formal equivalents, all with to. Bad for is the everyday one, with for.
entries.contrast: Harmful to takes to; bad for takes for. They mean the same thing and their prepositions do not trade: ✗ harmful for your lungs is a common slip. Watch the related nouns, which take a third preposition: harm to the reef but an effect on the reef and an impact on the reef. ✗ harmful with is an error.
entries.see also: bad at, safe from, vulnerable to, sensitive to, to

entries.meaning: Unable to leave something alone — usually said lightly.
examples: She got hooked on crossword puzzles during the shutdown.
One taste and the kids were hooked on the stuff.
He's been hooked on those late-night repair videos for a year.
Don't get hooked on checking the numbers every hour.
The patient was hooked to a monitor — a different hooked entirely.
entries.русский: подсевший на что-л., не могущий оторваться — разг., чаще шутливо
entries.register: informal
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (hooked on watching the whole series at once) — never a to-infinitive and never a clause.
entries.pattern: be / get hooked on [noun / verb-ing] · get [someone] hooked on [noun] · hooked (alone): one episode and I was hooked
entries.variants: addicted to is the neutral-to-clinical equivalent with a different preposition; into is the mild informal one (she's into birding).
entries.contrast: Hooked takes on; addicted takes to. ✗ hooked to and ✗ addicted on are the two mirror errors, and they are common. Register also separates them: hooked on is almost always light, so using it for a real dependency reads as either euphemism or bravado. Note the unrelated literal hooked to, meaning physically attached (hooked to a monitor), which is correct and is a different word combination entirely.
entries.see also: addicted to, obsessed with, crazy about, on

entries.meaning: Very bad at something — said about oneself far more often than about anyone else.
examples: I'm hopeless at keeping plants alive.
He's hopeless at saying no to a second helping.
She's hopeless with anything that requires a manual.
We're both hopeless at directions and we married each other anyway.
They're hopeless at scheduling and excellent at everything after that.
entries.русский: безнадёжно неспособный к чему-л. — разг., чаще о себе
entries.register: informal; usually self-deprecating
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after at (hopeless at remembering birthdays) — never a to-infinitive. After with, a category handled badly. There is no clause frame.
entries.pattern: be hopeless at [skill / verb-ing] · be hopeless with [category] · a hopeless case · hopeless alone, of a situation: the traffic is hopeless
entries.variants: terrible at, useless at, no good at, and bad at are the same idea at different volumes; hopeless is the most theatrical and the least literal.
entries.contrast: All the "not good at" adjectives take at for skills and with for categories — hopeless at chess, hopeless with computers — exactly parallel to good at / good with. ✗ hopeless in math is an error in American English. Do not confuse the skill sense with the situational one: the situation is hopeless means beyond saving and takes no preposition at all.
entries.see also: bad at, terrible at, poor at, good at, at

entries.meaning: Exactly the same as something else in every detail.
examples: The second invoice was identical to the first, down to the typo.
Her handwriting is nearly identical to her mother's.
The replacement part is identical to the one that failed.
Their proposal is identical with ours in every material respect.
The two buildings are identical to each other from the street.
entries.русский: идентичный, в точности такой же, как
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: noun phrase or pronoun — never a gerund, never a to-infinitive, and never a clause. A free relative works: identical to what we ordered.
entries.pattern: [X] is identical to [Y] · [X] is identical with [Y] · virtually / nearly / all but identical to [noun] · identical twins (no preposition)
entries.variants: identical with is the older form, still standard and preferred in logic and mathematics (A is identical with B), while identical to is the ordinary modern choice in American English and the safer default.
entries.contrast: Identical takes to or with, never than and never as. ✗ identical than the first and ✗ identical as the first are both wrong; the as error comes from the same as, which is the one member of this family that does take as. Note the strength ladder: similar to (alike), identical to (indistinguishable), the same as (one and the same, or indistinguishable). Purists once objected to nearly identical on the grounds that identity admits no degrees; it is universal and unremarkable now.
entries.see also: similar to, equal to, different from, the same as, to

entries.meaning: Serving as an example that makes something clear.
examples: The 2019 filing is illustrative of the problem, though it isn't the worst one.
His answer was illustrative of how little the training had covered.
These two cases are illustrative of a pattern the auditors flagged.
The exhibit is illustrative of the technique, not a finished piece.
The numbers are illustrative of a trend that started well before the merger.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /əˈlʌstrətəv əv/; the older IL-uh-stray-tiv is chiefly British
entries.русский: наглядно показывающий что-л., служащий тому примером
entries.register: formal — academic and analytical writing, exhibits in briefs, museum labels; conversation says a good example of
entries.complement: a noun phrase, often abstract — a tendency, a problem, a style — or a gerund (illustrative of how the office handles complaints is the commoner wh-form). Never a to-infinitive: ✗ illustrative of to handle complaints.
entries.pattern: be illustrative of [tendency / problem] · merely / particularly illustrative of · by way of illustration — the noun frame · illustrative purposes only — attributive, in the standard American disclaimer
entries.variants: indicative of points at evidence for a conclusion; representative of claims the example is typical; emblematic of and symptomatic of are the loaded versions; an example of is the plain noun phrase.
entries.contrast: Illustrative of says a case shows what something is like; indicative of says it is evidence that something is so. A photograph is illustrative of the damage; a rising fever is indicative of infection. Against representative of, which claims the example is typical of a whole, illustrative of claims only that it makes the point clear. Note the fixed American legal and marketing phrase for illustrative purposes only, which disclaims that the sample binds anyone. ✗ illustrative for and ✗ illustrative to are errors.
entries.see also: indicative of, representative of, symptomatic of, suggestive of, of

entries.meaning: Protected against something — by biology or by habit in the to frame, and by law in the from frame.
examples: Most of the crew is immune to the strain that went through in the spring.
The witness testified only after being made immune from prosecution.
He seems entirely immune to embarrassment.
State agencies are immune from suit in these circumstances.
Nobody in that market was immune to the rate increase.
entries.русский: невосприимчивый к (to, биол. или по привычке); юр. обладающий иммунитетом от (from)
entries.register: neutral in the medical sense, legal in the from sense (immune from suit, immune from prosecution)
entries.complement: after either preposition, a noun phrase or a gerund (immune to being embarrassed, immune from having to testify) — never a to-infinitive: ✗ immune to be embarrassed. No clause follows either form.
entries.pattern: be immune to [disease / influence] · be immune from [suit / prosecution / liability] · grant [someone] immunity from [noun] — the noun frame keeps from · immune system — attributive, no complement
entries.variants: resistant to is the weaker medical word (it slows the thing down rather than stopping it); exempt from is the administrative twin of immune from; impervious to is the figurative twin of immune to; insulated from is the neutral paraphrase.
entries.contrast: To for what cannot affect you; from for what cannot reach you. You are immune to measles and immune to flattery because they no longer work on you; you are immune from prosecution and immune from liability because the law puts them out of reach. The figurative uses divide the same way: immune to criticism means it bounces off, immune from criticism means nobody may deliver it. Both are standard American English, and the noun almost always takes from: immunity from prosecution. ✗ immune of and ✗ immune against are errors, though vaccinated against is correct with the other adjective.
entries.see also: impervious to, exempt from, vulnerable to, susceptible to, susceptible of, from

entries.meaning: Letting nothing through — water, in the literal sense; argument, criticism, or shame in the figurative one.
examples: The liner is impervious to everything the plant runs through it.
He is impervious to hints and always has been.
The finish is impervious to road salt for about four winters.
The committee proved impervious to every argument the neighbors made.
She's impervious to the cold in a way the rest of us envy.
entries.русский: непроницаемый для (воды); перен. — глухой к доводам, критике, стыду
entries.register: neutral to formal; literal in building and materials writing (impervious to water), figurative and slightly literary about people
entries.complement: a noun phrase or a gerund (impervious to being told twice) — never a to-infinitive: ✗ impervious to be told. No clause follows.
entries.pattern: be impervious to [substance / influence] · utterly / seemingly / cheerfully impervious to · an impervious surface — attributive, and a term of art in stormwater ordinances
entries.variants: immune to is the near twin in the figurative use; resistant to is the weaker one; proof against is the older phrase and lives on in compounds (waterproof, bulletproof, fireproof); insensible to is the literary version.
entries.contrast: Against immune to, which suggests a defense that was acquired, impervious to suggests a material that never let anything through in the first place — which is why it is the crueler word about people: impervious to argument says nothing gets in. Note the American municipal use, where impervious surface means pavement and roof area that sheds rainwater, and the stormwater fee is charged by the square foot of it. ✗ impervious of and ✗ impervious from are errors.
entries.see also: immune from, immune to, oblivious to, indifferent to, vulnerable to, to

entries.meaning: Contained in something without being said outright.
examples: Implicit in the offer is an assumption that the roof gets replaced.
A duty of good faith is implicit in every contract in this state.
The criticism was implicit in the way she read the numbers aloud.
There's a threat implicit in the last paragraph, whatever they claim.
Consent is implicit in using the parking lot, according to the sign.
entries.русский: подразумеваемый в чём-л. — присутствующий, но прямо не сказанный
entries.register: formal; the natural home is analysis — of texts, contracts, arguments, and policies
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the thing that contains the unstated element — a text, a claim, a bargain, a design. A gerund works where the container is an action (implicit in asking for a raise), and a to-infinitive is impossible: ✗ implicit in to ask.
entries.pattern: be implicit in [text / claim / arrangement] · implicit in [noun] is [the thing implied] — the inverted frame, which is how the phrase usually appears · implicit bias / implicit consent — attributive, no preposition
entries.variants: inherent in is the near neighbor and means built into the nature of the thing rather than left unsaid; tacit covers the same ground as an attributive adjective (a tacit agreement); understood and unspoken are the plain words.
entries.contrast: Implicit in means present but unstated; inherent in means part of the thing's nature. A promise of good faith is implicit in the contract because nobody wrote it down; risk is inherent in the business because you cannot have the one without the other. The direct opposite is explicit, which takes no preposition in this sense (the contract is explicit), and implicit also has an unrelated older sense of "unquestioning," as in implicit trust, where again no in follows. ✗ implicit to is an error, and ✗ implicit of is not English.
entries.see also: inherent in, intrinsic to, integral to, indicative of, in

entries.meaning: Admiring something because it was better than expected.
examples: The committee was impressed with the second candidate.
I was impressed by how fast the crew cleared the lot.
She wasn't impressed with the excuse and said so.
Everyone was impressed that he'd fixed it with a pocketknife.
We came away impressed with the whole operation.
entries.русский: впечатлённый чем-л., приятно удивлённый
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after with and by (impressed by how quickly they turned it around) — never a to-infinitive. A wh-clause is common (impressed with how she handled it), and a that-clause attaches to the bare adjective (impressed that anyone noticed).
entries.pattern: be impressed with [person / thing] · be impressed by [the thing that impressed you] · be impressed (that) [clause] · impress [something] on [someone] — a different verb frame · not impressed
entries.variants: impressed with and impressed by are interchangeable in almost every sentence; by is a shade more formal and points harder at the cause. Taken with is the warmer version; struck by the more sudden one.
entries.contrast: This is the one with / by pair in the file where the difference is nearly nil — unlike annoyed with / annoyed by or bored with / bored by, where the split is real, impressed with the design and impressed by the design mean the same thing. Keep both apart from impress on, the verb frame meaning to make someone understand: impress on them that the deadline is real. ✗ impressed of and ✗ impressed about are errors, and the British not impressed with is identical to the American use.
entries.see also: delighted with, satisfied with, astonished at, critical of, with

entries.meaning: Lacking the power, skill, or character to do something.
examples: He seems incapable of leaving a message under two minutes.
The old boiler is incapable of heating the third floor.
She's incapable of passing a bookstore without going in.
The court found him incapable of managing his own affairs.
They were incapable of agreeing on even the meeting time.
entries.русский: неспособный на что-л., не имеющий сил или характера сделать
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (incapable of sitting still) — never a to-infinitive. ✗ incapable to do it is the error, exactly parallel to ✗ capable to do it; the negatives of able to are unable to and not able to, both with the infinitive.
entries.pattern: be incapable of [noun / verb-ing] · seemingly / apparently incapable of [verb-ing] · incapable of [abstract noun]: incapable of malice
entries.variants: unable to + infinitive is the everyday negative with the opposite structure; not up to + -ing is the informal one.
entries.contrast: Incapable of + -ing versus unable to + verb. The two negatives of ability take opposite complements and cannot borrow: ✓ incapable of finishing, ✓ unable to finish, ✗ incapable to finish, ✗ unable of finishing. There is also a difference of scope: unable to finish usually means blocked in this instance, while incapable of finishing impugns the person's capacity in general — which is why the second one insults and the first does not.
entries.see also: capable of, bad at, hopeless at, of

entries.meaning: Arising as a normal legal consequence of something else, and belonging to it as of right.
examples: Officers may search the passenger compartment incident to a lawful arrest.
The powers incident to the office pass to whoever holds it next.
Costs incident to recording the deed are the buyer's.
Injuries incident to employment are covered without regard to fault.
Any right incident to the policy has to be listed on the schedule.
entries.русский: вытекающий из чего-л. как правовое следствие — юр.
entries.register: legal; the American reader meets it in one place above all — a search incident to arrest — and otherwise in deeds, employment agreements, and tax rules
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the principal thing — an arrest, an office, an ownership interest, a transaction. A gerund appears in drafting (expenses incident to closing the sale), and a to-infinitive is impossible: ✗ incident to close the sale.
entries.pattern: [thing] incident to [principal thing] · a search incident to [arrest] — the constitutional doctrine · rights and duties incident to [office / ownership] · incident to employment — the workers' compensation phrase
entries.variants: incidental to is the everyday twin and is the form to use for minor accompanying things; appurtenant to is the property-law word for rights attached to land; attendant on is the literary version.
entries.contrast: Incident to says a thing belongs to another as one of its normal legal consequences; incidental to says it merely happens alongside and is minor. Powers incident to the office of trustee come with the office as of right; the printing costs incidental to the filing are trivia. American lawyers keep the pair apart deliberately, and outside law the shorter form has almost entirely won. Do not read incident here as the noun meaning "an event" — different word, and it takes no preposition. ✗ incident of means something else again (an incident of ownership, in estate tax, is a right that comes with it).
entries.see also: incidental to, appurtenant to, ancillary to, concomitant with, to

entries.meaning: Happening alongside the main thing and of small importance next to it.
examples: The travel costs are incidental to the grant and capped at eight percent.
Whatever damage the tree did was incidental to the storm, not the crew.
Filing is incidental to her actual job, which is answering the phone.
The gift shop is incidental to the museum's mission, if lucrative.
Any benefit to the neighbors was incidental to a project built for the port.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˌɪnsəˈdɛntəl tə/, with a flapped t: "in-suh-DEN-nul-tuh"
entries.русский: побочный при чём-л. — сопутствующий главному и малозначительный рядом с ним
entries.register: neutral to formal; ordinary in expense reports (incidental expenses), contracts, and analytical prose
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the main thing, or a gerund (incidental to running the shop) — never a to-infinitive: ✗ incidental to run the shop.
entries.pattern: be incidental to [main activity] · [cost / effect] incidental to [noun] · merely / purely incidental to · incidentals — the noun, meaning small extra costs, with no preposition
entries.variants: ancillary to is the formal twin for supporting services; incident to is the legal form for consequences that come as of right; secondary to ranks the two things; peripheral to stresses the edge.
entries.contrast: Incidental to means minor and merely accompanying, and it is the word to reach for outside law. Against incident to, which claims a legal connection, incidental to claims no connection beyond happening alongside. Against ancillary to, which supports the main thing on purpose, incidental to implies nobody planned it. In per-diem rules the frozen American phrase is meals and incidental expenses — the noun incidentals is what a hotel bill calls the minibar. ✗ incidental of and ✗ incidental with are errors.
entries.see also: incident to, ancillary to, concomitant with, peculiar to, to

entries.meaning: Resting on someone as a duty — in a fixed frame with it and an infinitive.
examples: It is incumbent on the seller to disclose what she knows about the roof.
It is incumbent upon every member to read the minutes before the vote.
The duty incumbent on a trustee does not end when the money runs out.
It's incumbent on us to say plainly what the study did not find.
It was incumbent upon the agency to publish the rule before enforcing it.
entries.русский: лежащий на ком-л. как обязанность — книжн., в обороте it is incumbent on X to
entries.register: formal — editorials, opinions, and official correspondence; the whole phrase is a set piece and upon is at least as common as on
entries.complement: a noun phrase or pronoun naming the person under the duty — never the duty itself. The duty goes in a to-infinitive at the end of the sentence, which makes this a two-part frame: it is incumbent on the board to review the policy. ✗ incumbent on reviewing the policy is an error, and so is ✗ the board is incumbent on reviewing.
entries.pattern: it is incumbent on [person] to [verb] — nearly the only frame in live use · it is incumbent upon us to [verb] · the duty incumbent on [person]
entries.variants: the burden is on [someone] to [verb] is the plain equivalent; obligated to and required to say the same thing about a person directly; behooves is the archaic verb that fills the same slot (it behooves us to check).
entries.contrast: The frame is impersonal and the infinitive is obligatory, which is what makes this entry unusual in a file about gerunds: the on takes the person, and the duty must be an infinitive. Note that the unrelated noun incumbent — the officeholder currently in the job — takes no preposition and is far commoner in American political writing; the incumbent is running again has nothing to do with this pattern. ✗ incumbent to and ✗ incumbent for are errors.
entries.see also: obligated to, obliged to, binding on, binding upon, responsible for, answerable to, on

entries.meaning: Not controlled by, supported by, or determined by something else.
examples: The audit is independent of both the board and the union.
Two labs reached the same figure independently of each other.
She's been financially independent of her parents since twenty.
The result is independent of how the sample was ordered.
The territory became independent from the mainland administration in 1976.
entries.русский: независимый от — не подконтрольный, не содержащийся и не определяемый чем-л.
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: noun phrase or pronoun; a gerund is possible where an activity is meant (independent of needing outside funding) — never a to-infinitive and never a clause.
entries.pattern: be independent of [noun] · be independent from [a former parent body] · independently of [noun] — the adverb · financially independent
entries.variants: independent from is used, and it is idiomatic where separation from a former controller is meant (independent from Spain since 1821). For the ordinary "not determined by" sense, of is the standard American choice: independent of the outcome.
entries.contrast: Independent of is the default; independent from is for secession. A variable is independent of another; a colony becomes independent from an empire. The negative side of the same word takes on, not of: ✓ dependent on, ✗ dependent of — so the pair dependent on / independent of is one of the small number of places in English where a prefix changes the preposition. The adverb keeps the of: arrived at independently of one another.
entries.see also: dependent on, free of, reliant on, of

entries.meaning: Serving as a sign that something is the case.
examples: The wear pattern is indicative of a wheel that was never aligned.
Two late filings are not indicative of fraud by themselves.
Her tone was indicative of how the rest of the meeting would go.
Past performance is not indicative of future results.
Soil staining indicative of an old leak turned up under the slab.
entries.русский: свидетельствующий о, указывающий на
entries.register: formal; standard in clinical notes, audit findings, and analytical journalism, where the plain phrase would be a sign of
entries.complement: a noun phrase, or a gerund where the sign points to an activity (indicative of having been moved) — never a to-infinitive: ✗ indicative of to be moved. A wh-clause is common and correct: indicative of what the crew found.
entries.pattern: be indicative of [condition / conclusion] · not necessarily indicative of [noun] — the hedged frame, and a standing phrase in American investment disclaimers (past performance is not indicative of future results) · the indicative mood — the grammar term, unrelated
entries.variants: a sign of and evidence of are the plain noun phrases; suggestive of is weaker; symptomatic of is the medical one; diagnostic of is the strongest — it settles the question.
entries.a scale of strength runs through this fa: suggestive of hints, indicative of points, symptomatic of names a condition by its signs, and diagnostic of proves. Against illustrative of, which offers an example, indicative of offers evidence. Do not confuse the adjective with the grammatical indicative (the mood of ordinary statements), which never takes of. ✗ indicative to and ✗ indicative for are errors.
entries.see also: suggestive of, symptomatic of, illustrative of, predictive of, of

entries.meaning: Having no interest in something, and no feeling either way about it.
examples: He is genuinely indifferent to what anyone thinks of the house.
The cat was indifferent to the entire commotion.
Voters were indifferent to both candidates and stayed home.
She's indifferent to prizes, which is why she keeps winning them.
The market has been indifferent to the announcement all week.
entries.русский: равнодушный к, безразличный
entries.register: formal to neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or pronoun; a gerund where an activity is meant (indifferent to being noticed) — never a to-infinitive and never a clause.
entries.pattern: be indifferent to [noun / verb-ing] · seemingly / utterly indifferent to [noun] · a matter of indifference to [someone] — the noun keeps to
entries.variants: unmoved by, unconcerned about, and apathetic about / toward are the neighbors; couldn't care less about is the informal one.
entries.contrast: Indifferent to takes to, not about or by. ✗ indifferent about the outcome is a common slip; the word that takes about is unconcerned. Note the second, older sense of indifferent meaning mediocre (an indifferent meal), where no preposition appears at all — this sense is now chiefly literary but still turns up in reviews.
entries.see also: interested in, bored with, sensitive to, to

entries.meaning: Lower in quality, rank, or importance than something else.
examples: The replacement fabric is noticeably inferior to the original.
He never felt inferior to anyone in the room, which was half the problem.
The second edition is inferior to the first in every way but the index.
These parts are inferior in finish to what we ordered.
Nothing about the design is inferior to the competition; it's just late.
entries.русский: уступающий чему-л. — ниже по качеству, рангу или значимости
entries.register: formal to neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or pronoun — never a gerund, never a to-infinitive, and never a clause.
entries.pattern: [X] is inferior to [Y] · inferior in [respect] to [noun] · vastly / markedly inferior to [noun] · an inferior [noun] — attributive, no preposition
entries.variants: worse than is the everyday equivalent and takes than, which is exactly the confusion this entry exists to prevent. Not a patch on is the informal British one.
entries.contrast: Inferior takes to, never than. ✗ inferior than is one of the most persistent errors in academic English, because the adjective is comparative in meaning even though it is not comparative in form. The same rule governs superior to, senior to, junior to, prior to, preferable to, and anterior to — all Latin comparatives, all with to, all rejecting than. Note also that inferior cannot be intensified with more: ✗ more inferior to is redundant.
entries.see also: superior to, equal to, different from, than, to

entries.meaning: Belonging to the nature of a thing, so that it cannot be separated from it.
examples: There's a conflict inherent in letting the vendor audit its own invoices.
The risks inherent in the procedure were explained twice.
Delay is inherent in any process that needs three signatures.
Courts have powers inherent in the judicial function itself.
The instability is inherent in the design, not a manufacturing defect.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ənˈhɪrənt ən/; the variant in-HAIR-unt is equally American
entries.русский: присущий чему-л. по природе, неотделимый от
entries.register: formal to neutral; standard in law, risk writing, and philosophy
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the thing whose nature contains the quality — inherent in the design, inherent in any partnership. A gerund is available where the container is an activity (inherent in running a plant this old), and a to-infinitive is impossible: ✗ inherent in to run a plant.
entries.pattern: be inherent in [thing / activity] · risks inherent in [noun] — the commonest collocation by a wide margin · inherent [noun] — attributive (an inherent conflict, inherent powers) · inhere in [noun] — the rare verb
entries.variants: intrinsic to is the near twin and takes to; built into is the plain modern phrase; of the essence of is the philosopher's formula; native to covers the biological case.
entries.contrast: Inherent takes in; intrinsic to takes to, and this is the pair most often crossed. ✗ inherent to the design is now common in American technical writing and is still marked as an error by careful editors; write inherent in the design or intrinsic to the design. Against implicit in, which is about what was left unsaid, inherent in is about what could not be removed: the risk inherent in the work would exist even if everyone spelled it out. ✗ inherent of is not English.
entries.see also: intrinsic to, implicit in, integral to, endemic to, in

entries.meaning: Not guilty of an offense — or, playfully, entirely without some quality.
examples: He maintained he was innocent of every charge on the indictment.
She was innocent of any involvement in the second transfer.
The jury found him not guilty; the paper said innocent of all counts.
His memo was innocent of any acquaintance with the actual budget.
They were innocent of the whole scheme until the subpoena arrived.
entries.русский: невиновный в чём-л.; шутл. — начисто лишённый какого-л. качества
entries.register: formal in the legal sense; literary in the extended one
entries.complement: a noun naming an offense, or a gerund naming the act (innocent of having any part in it) — never a to-infinitive and never a clause.
entries.pattern: be innocent of [offense / verb-ing] · be found innocent of [charge] · innocent of [any knowledge / all irony] — the extended sense · presumed innocent (no preposition)
entries.variants: not guilty of is the everyday and, strictly, the legally accurate phrase; cleared of is what happens after a verdict; blameless in covers the non-criminal sense.
entries.contrast: Innocent of takes of, matching guilty of. The legal note is worth knowing: American juries return not guilty, not innocent, so found innocent of is journalism rather than law. The extended sense means entirely lacking something and is faintly ironic: a paragraph innocent of punctuation has none. ✗ innocent from and ✗ innocent about are errors.
entries.see also: guilty of, free of, responsible for, of

entries.meaning: Forming a necessary part of a larger whole rather than an addition to it.
examples: The loading dock is integral to how the store gets restocked.
Her role became integral to the project about a month in.
Testing is integral to the release process, not a step you can skip.
The porch is integral to the structure and can't simply be removed.
Volunteers are integral to keeping the clinic open on Saturdays.
entries.pronunciation note: IN-tuh-grul too; the stress-shifted in-TEG-rul is also standard American — weak /ˈɪntəɡrəl tə/
entries.русский: составляющий неотъемлемую часть чего-л., а не добавку к нему
entries.register: neutral to formal; ordinary in business and technical writing about how parts fit into wholes
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the whole, or a gerund naming the activity (integral to keeping the line running) — never a to-infinitive: ✗ integral to keep the line running.
entries.pattern: be integral to [whole / process] · absolutely / utterly integral to · an integral part of [noun] — the noun frame, which switches to of · integral [noun] — attributive, as in integral memory
entries.variants: essential to and central to are the everyday equivalents; crucial to and vital to raise the temperature; part and parcel of is the idiom; intrinsic to is about nature rather than function.
entries.contrast: Adjective to, noun of. ✓ integral to the process, ✓ an integral part of the process, ✗ an integral part to the process. Against essential to, which says the whole fails without it, integral to says the thing is a built-in part of the whole — the difference is between necessity and membership, though in practice the two are used interchangeably. Against intrinsic to, note that integral is about structure (it is one of the parts) and intrinsic about nature (it is of the essence). ✗ integral for and ✗ integral in are errors.
entries.see also: essential to, intrinsic to, inherent in, ancillary to, to

entries.meaning: Fixed on doing something, with attention that excludes everything else.
examples: She was intent on getting the whole roof done in one weekend.
He seemed intent on proving a point nobody had disputed.
The department is intent on keeping the case out of the papers.
They were intent upon the map and didn't hear the door.
He was charged with assault with intent to rob — the noun frame.
entries.русский: твёрдо намеренный сделать что-л., поглощённый этим — после on герундий
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (intent on finishing before dark) — never a to-infinitive. ✗ intent to finish is wrong as an adjective phrase, though the noun intent does take an infinitive: with intent to defraud, which is exactly where the confusion comes from.
entries.pattern: be intent on [noun / verb-ing] · be intent upon [noun / verb-ing] · seemingly intent on [verb-ing] · with intent to [verb] — the noun frame
entries.variants: intent upon is the formal equivalent. Bent on is the near-identical informal one and always implies a bad outcome; determined to takes an infinitive instead.
entries.contrast: Intent on + -ing versus determined to + verb. Same meaning, opposite structure: ✓ intent on winning, ✓ determined to win, ✗ intent to win as an adjective. Note the legal noun phrase with intent to kill, where intent is a noun and takes an infinitive correctly — the adjective and the noun are spelled the same and take different complements, which is why this pair produces so many mistakes. Bent on is the version reserved for destructive purposes: bent on revenge.
entries.see also: committed to, serious about, reluctant to, obsessed with, on

entries.meaning: Wanting to know about something, or wanting to have or do it.
examples: She's interested in nineteenth-century glass, the more chipped the better.
We'd be interested in buying the lot next door if it ever comes up.
He's not interested in arguing about it again.
I'd be interested to hear how the meeting went.
Anyone interested in volunteering should email the office.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˈɪntrəstɪd ən/; the careful four-syllable /ˈɪntərəstɪd/ also occurs
entries.русский: интересующийся чем-л., заинтересованный в
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (interested in buying) — never a to-infinitive after in. ✗ interested in to buy and ✗ interested to buy for this meaning are both errors. The adjective does take a bare to-infinitive in a different sense — interested to hear, interested to see — meaning curious to learn, and that frame works only with verbs of perceiving and learning.
entries.pattern: be interested in [noun / verb-ing] · be interested in [someone] -ing · be interested to [hear / know / see / learn] · take an interest in [noun] · an interest in [noun] — the noun keeps in
entries.variants: into is the casual American version (he's into woodworking); keen on the British one; curious about the neighboring one.
entries.contrast: The single highest-frequency error with this adjective is ✗ I am interested to buy your car. Write interested in buying. The infinitive frame is real but narrow: it takes verbs of finding out — I'd be interested to hear what she says — and it means "curious", not "wanting to acquire". Compare interested in (wanting, engaged with) against curious about (wondering) and concerned with (dealing with). ✗ interested about is an error, though interested in and interested by differ the usual way, by pointing at the cause.
entries.see also: curious about, keen on, enthusiastic about, involved in, in

entries.meaning: Belonging to the essential nature of something rather than coming from outside it.
examples: Curiosity is intrinsic to the job; the paperwork is not.
Some risk is intrinsic to lending, however good the underwriting.
The delay is intrinsic to the process, not a sign anybody is slacking.
Rewards intrinsic to the work keep people longer than bonuses do.
That quality is intrinsic to the material and survives any finish.
entries.русский: внутренне присущий чему-л., идущий от самой его сути
entries.register: formal — philosophy, biology, economics, and careful technical writing
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the thing whose nature includes the property, or a gerund (intrinsic to being a small landlord) — never a to-infinitive: ✗ intrinsic to be a landlord.
entries.pattern: be intrinsic to [thing / role] · intrinsic [noun] — attributive (intrinsic value, intrinsic motivation, intrinsic muscles) · intrinsically [adjective] — the adverb
entries.variants: inherent in is the near twin with a different preposition; essential to is the plainer word; built into is the everyday phrase; of its very nature is the formal paraphrase. The antonym extrinsic takes to as well.
entries.contrast: Intrinsic to versus inherent in is a preposition split with no meaning behind it — the two adjectives cover nearly the same ground and simply take different prepositions, which is exactly why writers cross them. Against integral to, which is about being one of the parts, intrinsic to is about belonging to the nature of the thing. In finance the attributive use is a term of art: intrinsic value is what the thing is worth apart from what the market says. ✗ intrinsic in is a slip, though it appears; ✗ intrinsic of is not English.
entries.see also: inherent in, integral to, essential to, peculiar to, to

entries.meaning: Taking part in something, or connected with someone or something.
examples: Three departments were involved in drafting the policy.
She's been involved with the food bank since it opened.
He got involved in a dispute that had nothing to do with him.
They were involved in running the whole festival for eleven years.
Nobody wanted to be involved with that firm after the settlement.
entries.русский: участвующий в, замешанный в
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after in and with (involved in running the campaign) — never a to-infinitive. ✗ involved to run it is an error.
entries.pattern: be involved in [activity / verb-ing] · be involved with [person / organization] · get involved in [situation] · involve [someone] in [something] — the verb · deeply / heavily involved in [noun]
entries.variants: engaged in is the formal equivalent for activities; mixed up in is the disapproving informal one; caught up in is the passive one.
entries.contrast: Involved in an activity; involved with a person or an organization. Involved in the merger describes what you were doing; involved with the company describes an ongoing connection; and involved with someone is a standard American euphemism for a romantic relationship, which is why the two prepositions are worth keeping apart. Note the verb frame involve someone in something and the noun frame involvement in / with, which follow the same split. ✗ involved on is an error.
entries.see also: engaged to, concerned about, interested in, in

entries.meaning: Having exactly the same structure as something else, so that one can be mapped onto the other point for point.
examples: That group is isomorphic to the integers under addition.
Any two cyclic groups of the same order are isomorphic to each other.
The two graphs look different but are isomorphic to one another.
The new org chart is isomorphic to the one they abandoned in 2016.
He showed the puzzle is isomorphic to a problem already solved in 1974.
entries.русский: изоморфный чему-л. — мат., имеющий в точности ту же структуру
entries.register: technical — mathematics above all (group theory, graph theory), then linguistics, crystallography, and, as a borrowed metaphor, organizational theory
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the other structure — a group, a graph, a system — never a gerund and never a clause. The two things compared must be structures of the same kind.
entries.pattern: [structure] is isomorphic to [structure] · isomorphic with [noun] — the variant, commoner outside mathematics · an isomorphism between [X] and [Y] — the noun frame, with between · isomorphic [noun] — attributive
entries.variants: isomorphic with is standard in the looser social-science use; homomorphic to is the weaker mathematical relation; structurally identical to is the paraphrase; congruent to is geometry's version of the same instinct.
entries.contrast: In mathematics isomorphic to is exact and technical: two structures are isomorphic when a one-to-one mapping preserves all the relevant operations, which is a far stronger claim than similarity. The borrowed use in organizational theory (the new agency is isomorphic to the one it replaced) means only that the shapes match, and specialists find it loose. Against analogous to, which says reasoning carries over, isomorphic to says the structures match exactly. Note the noun's different preposition: an isomorphism between two groups, not ✗ of them. ✗ isomorphic of is an error.
entries.see also: congruent to, congruent with, analogous to, equivalent to, identical to, to

entries.meaning: Wanting what someone else has — or fiercely protective of something you have.
examples: He's jealous of anyone who gets to work from home.
She's jealous of her Sundays and won't schedule anything.
The younger one is jealous of every minute the baby takes.
Small firms are jealous of their independence.
I'm jealous of the way he can sleep through anything.
entries.русский: завидующий кому-л.; ревниво оберегающий своё
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (jealous of having to share the office) — never a to-infinitive and never a clause.
entries.pattern: be jealous of [person / thing] · be jealous of [someone's] [possession or advantage] · jealously guard [something] · jealous of [something one protects]: jealous of her privacy
entries.variants: envious of is the formal twin for the wanting sense only; possessive of and protective of cover the guarding sense.
entries.contrast: Jealous does two jobs with one preposition. Jealous of her sister's job wants what someone else has — that is envious of territory. Jealous of her own time guards what it already has, and envious cannot mean that. A third use covers romantic insecurity: jealous of the new coworker can mean either wanting his position or fearing he is a rival, and only context separates them. ✗ jealous about and ✗ jealous with are errors; the noun keeps of: jealousy of his success.
entries.see also: envious of, suspicious of, proud of, of

entries.meaning: Enthusiastic about something — most often heard, in America, in the negative.
examples: I'm not too keen on driving all that way for one meeting.
He's keen on anything involving a boat.
The board wasn't keen on the timing.
She's keen to get started before the permits expire.
They were keen on the location and cool on the price.
entries.русский: увлечённый чем-л. — в амер. англ. чаще в отрицании: not keen on
entries.register: neutral in British English; in American English it reads as mildly British or bookish, and survives mainly in the negative
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after on (keen on hiking) — never a to-infinitive after on. The adjective takes a bare to-infinitive directly (keen to start), which is the frame American writers reach for when they use the word at all.
entries.pattern: be keen on [noun / verb-ing] · be keen to [verb] · not too keen on [noun] · keen alone, meaning sharp or intense: a keen eye, keen interest
entries.variants: into, crazy about, and enthusiastic about are the American everyday equivalents; eager to replaces keen to.
entries.contrast: Keen on + -ing versus keen to + verb is the same split as eager for / eager to: on takes the thing, to takes the action. The American usage note matters here — a sentence like She's keen on the idea is understood everywhere but sounds imported in the United States, while the negative I'm not too keen on that is thoroughly naturalized American understatement. ✗ keen about and ✗ keen of are errors; the intensifier sense (a keen sense of smell) takes no preposition.
entries.see also: enthusiastic about, crazy about, eager for, fond of, on

entries.meaning: Treating someone with warmth and consideration.
examples: She was kind to every nervous first-year who came through the door.
Be kind to the guy at the counter; it's his second day.
It was kind of you to wait.
The years have been kind to that house.
The new surface is kind to runners' knees.
entries.русский: добрый, внимательный к кому-л.
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: a person or animal after to — never a gerund, never a to-infinitive, never a clause. The judgment frame takes of plus a doer plus an infinitive: It was kind of you to call.
entries.pattern: be kind to [person / animal] · it is kind of [someone] to [verb] · be kind enough to [verb] · kind about [something] — tolerant regarding · kind to [a surface or a body part]: kind to your knees
entries.variants: nice to, good to, and decent to are the everyday equivalents; considerate of and thoughtful toward are the formal ones.
entries.contrast: To names who receives the kindness; of names who supplied it. Kind to me and kind of you are both correct and mean different things, and the second is a fixed politeness frame in American English: That's kind of you. ✗ kind with is an error, which is worth flagging because gentle with and patient with sit right next door and take with. The extended sense — a shampoo that's kind to color-treated hair — keeps to.
entries.see also: nice to, polite to, cruel to, generous with, to

entries.meaning: Recognized by other people — for something, as something, or to someone.
examples: The neighborhood is known for its stubborn holdout houses.
He's known as the only person who can fix that machine.
The car was already known to the county sheriff.
Storms like that are known to strand traffic for hours.
She's known for returning calls the same day, which is rarer than it should be.
entries.русский: известный чем-л.; known as — как кто-л., known to — кому-л. известный
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after for (known for showing up early) — never a to-infinitive after for. After as, a noun naming a role or a name (known as the Iron Range). After to, a person who knows it. The passive known to + infinitive (known to happen) is a separate frame meaning reported to.
entries.pattern: be known for [quality / verb-ing] · be known as [role / name] · be known to [person] · be known to [verb] · make [something] known to [someone] · little known outside [place]
entries.variants: famous for is the strong version; notorious for the negative one; renowned for the formal one; recognized as the credential version.
entries.contrast: Four prepositions, four jobs, and this is one of the busiest words in the file. For = what you do or have: known for her sourdough. As = what you are called or counted as: known as Big Jim, known as a hard grader. To + person = who knows it: known to the police. To + infinitive = reported to do it: bears are known to open car doors. Substituting one for another goes wrong immediately: ✗ known as her sourdough. ✗ known of is an error, though unknown to and known by (with an agent) are both correct.
entries.see also: famous for, notorious for, familiar with, as, for

entries.meaning: Short of some quality that ought to be there.
examples: The proposal is not lacking in ambition, only in numbers.
His apology was conspicuously lacking in any actual apology.
The building is lacking in the kind of light the studio needs.
She's never been lacking in nerve.
The report is lacking several attachments referenced in the index.
entries.русский: лишённый качества, которого следовало бы ожидать
entries.register: neutral to formal
