entries.complement: an abstract quality after in (lacking in imagination) — never a gerund and never a to-infinitive. The bare participle also takes a direct object with no preposition (lacking any evidence), and the plain verb lack takes a direct object and never a preposition.
entries.pattern: be lacking in [quality] · be lacking [noun] · be sadly / conspicuously lacking in [quality] · lack [something] — the verb, with no preposition · a lack of [noun] — the noun, with of
entries.variants: deficient in is the technical version; short on and low on the informal ones; devoid of and wanting in the formal ones.
entries.contrast: The three related forms take three different structures, and this is the trap. ✓ The plan lacks detail (verb, no preposition — ✗ lacks of detail). ✓ The plan is lacking in detail (adjective, in). ✓ There is a lack of detail (noun, of). Learners who have met the noun first tend to write ✗ lacks of detail, which is the single commonest error involving this word; see the zero-preposition entry for lack. Lacking in prefers abstract qualities, so lacking in courage is natural and lacking in a hammer is not.
entries.see also: lack, short of, absent from, free of, in

entries.meaning: Arriving or acting after the time you were supposed to.
examples: She was late for the interview and got the job anyway.
He's late with the rent for the third month running.
The district was late in notifying families about the closure.
Don't be late to your own party.
I'm always late for things that start on the half hour.
entries.русский: опоздавший на что-л.
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: a noun naming an appointment or event after for (late for the meeting) — never a gerund after for and never a to-infinitive. After in, a gerund naming what was done late (late in filing), which is the formal frame. After with, the thing owed (late with the rent).
entries.pattern: be late for [event] · be late to [event or place] · be late in [verb-ing] · be late with [something owed] · run late · late alone, of time: it's getting late
entries.variants: late to is increasingly common in American English before an event, and late to the party is a fixed idiom. Behind on covers the "late with" sense: behind on the rent.
entries.contrast: For takes the event you failed to reach on time; with takes the thing you failed to hand over; in takes the action you were slow to perform. Late for the hearing, late with the filing, late in filing — three frames, three grammatical shapes. The opposite is on time for or punctual for, both with for; there is no ✗ early for / late of symmetry, since early for is correct and late of means something else entirely (Ann Reilly, late of Cleveland is the obituary formula for "formerly of").
entries.see also: punctual for, ready for, prepared for, for

entries.meaning: Legally answerable for something, answerable to somebody — or, in the everyday sense, likely to do something.
examples: The contractor is liable for any damage to the sidewalk.
Partners are jointly and severally liable for the firm's debts.
She's liable to the tenants for the deposit, whatever the manager did.
That pipe is liable to freeze if the crawlspace door stays open.
He's liable to say something he can't take back.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˈlaɪəbəl fər/ and /ˈlaɪəbəl tə/; two syllables, LY-bul, is a common casual reduction
entries.русский: юр. отвечающий за (for) перед кем-л. (to); разг. — склонный, того и гляди сделает
entries.register: legal in the for frame, neutral to informal in the "likely" frame — and the informal one is thoroughly American
entries.complement: after for, a noun phrase naming the harm or debt you must answer for (liable for the damages) — never a gerund in the legal sense. After to, either a noun naming the person owed or a person harmed (liable to the buyer), or a bare infinitive in the entirely separate "likely to" sense (liable to break). The infinitive frame is the informal one: ✗ liable to breaking.
entries.pattern: be liable for [damages / debt] · be liable to [person] for [amount] · be liable to [verb] — the "likely" sense · hold [someone] liable for [noun] · jointly and severally liable for — the standard American formula
entries.variants: responsible for is the everyday equivalent of the legal sense; on the hook for is the slang one; apt to and likely to replace the informal sense; answerable for is the formal one.
entries.contrast: Three frames, three meanings. Liable for the repairs names what you owe. Liable to the landlord names whom you owe it to. Liable to freeze tonight means likely, has nothing to do with law, and is only ever followed by a bare verb — a use that strikes British ears as folksy and is unremarkable in America. There is also the older liable to + noun meaning "exposed to" (liable to prosecution, liable to a fine), which survives in statutes. ✗ liable of is an error, and ✗ liable to pay in the legal sense should be liable for payment unless you mean it is likely to happen.
entries.see also: responsible for, accountable to, accountable for, answerable to, subject to, for

entries.meaning: Anticipate something with pleasure.
examples: I look forward to hearing from you at your convenience.
She's looking forward to three weeks with no email.
We look forward to working with your team on the next phase.
He looks forward to Thursdays the way other people look forward to Fridays.
Nobody is looking forward to explaining this to the board.
entries.русский: с нетерпением ждать — после to герундий, не инфинитив
entries.register: neutral; the standard sign-off of American business correspondence
entries.type: verb + preposition — included here because it is the classic case of the fixed to
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (look forward to hearing from you) — never a to-infinitive. ✗ I look forward to hear from you is the single most-corrected error in professional English, and the noun test proves the point: look forward to the weekend ✓, so to is a preposition.
entries.pattern: look forward to [noun / verb-ing] · look forward to [someone] -ing (look forward to your joining us) · be looking forward to [noun / verb-ing] · much / greatly looking forward to [noun]
entries.variants: look ahead to is the neutral news-writing version; anticipate takes a direct object with no preposition at all (anticipate the results).
entries.contrast: The whole difficulty is that forward to looks like an infinitive and is not. Compare the three: ✓ look forward to seeing you, ✓ hope to see you, ✗ look forward to see you. The same fixed to governs object to, be opposed to, be accustomed to, be used to, be committed to, be dedicated to, confess to, admit to, and resort to — a list worth learning as a set, because every one of them takes -ing: ✓ object to being asked, ✓ confessed to taking it, ✓ resorted to calling her at home. In the progressive, I'm looking forward to is warmer and more personal than the simple I look forward to, which is the formal sign-off. This is the one verb phrase given a full entry here rather than next door; the rest of the look family — look at, look for, look after, look into — is treated with the verbs.
entries.see also: accustomed to, used to, opposed to, committed to, look at / for / after / into, to

entries.meaning: Steadfast in supporting a person, a group, or a cause when it would be easy not to be.
examples: She stayed loyal to the shop through two changes of ownership.
He's loyal to the people who hired him, not to the company that bought it.
Customers loyal to the old formula complained for a year.
They remained loyal to a candidate everyone else had written off.
Nobody in that district is loyal to a party for its own sake.
entries.русский: верный, преданный кому-л. или чему-л.
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: a noun phrase or pronoun naming the person, group, or cause you stand by — never a gerund (✗ loyal to showing up) and never a clause. The abstract complement (loyal to the idea, loyal to a fault — the fixed phrase) is a noun in every case.
entries.pattern: be loyal to [person / institution / cause] · remain / stay loyal to · fiercely / doggedly loyal to · loyal to a fault — the frozen phrase · loyalty to [noun] — the noun keeps to
entries.variants: faithful to is the near twin and covers marriage and duty; devoted to stresses feeling; true to covers principles and one's word; committed to is the workplace version.
entries.contrast: Against devoted to, which is about attachment and effort, loyal to is about not defecting — it presupposes that leaving was an option. Against faithful to, the difference is mostly domain: faithfulness belongs to promises and marriages, loyalty to people, teams, and brands. Note that loyal rarely takes a complement at all in advertising (loyal customers), where the noun follows the adjective instead. ✗ loyal with and ✗ loyal for are errors.
entries.see also: devoted to, committed to, dedicated to, married to, to

entries.meaning: Angry — the everyday American word, informal but universal.
examples: She's still mad at me for telling her mother.
He got mad about the parking situation and wrote three emails.
Don't be mad at the dog; you left the gate open.
They were mad that the meeting had been moved without notice.
I'm not mad at you, I'm mad about how it was handled.
entries.русский: злящийся на кого-л. — разг., обычное американское слово
entries.register: informal; the American conversational default for anger
entries.complement: a person after at; a noun phrase or gerund after about (mad about being left out) — never a to-infinitive. A that-clause attaches to the bare adjective: mad that nobody told her.
entries.pattern: be mad at [person] · be mad about [thing] · get mad at [person] · be mad at [person] for [verb-ing] · be mad about [someone] — the British "in love with" sense · mad alone, meaning insane
entries.variants: angry with / at is the neutral version; ticked off at and pissed at are the escalating informal ones.
entries.contrast: The American and British senses of mad about are opposites, and this is a genuine transatlantic trap. In American English, mad about the schedule means angry about it; in British English, mad about the boy means crazy about him. Americans use crazy about for affection and reserve mad for anger, so a British sentence like She's mad about him will be misread in the United States. Within American usage the split is clean: at takes the person, about takes the situation. ✗ mad with is an error in American English except in the fixed mad with grief, meaning driven insane.
entries.see also: angry with, furious with, annoyed with, crazy about, at

entries.meaning: Joined in marriage to someone — or, figuratively, bound to something.
examples: She's been married to the same man since 1994.
He got married to his high-school lab partner twenty years later.
They're married with three kids and a dog nobody planned on.
The department is married to a process that stopped working years ago.
She married a man from Duluth — the verb, with no preposition.
entries.русский: женатый на, замужем за; перен. — намертво привязанный к
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: a person after to; in the figurative sense, an idea or an institution (married to the job) — never a gerund and never a to-infinitive.
entries.pattern: be married to [person] · get married to [person] · marry [person] — the verb, with no preposition · be married (alone) · married with children — a fixed idiom about having them, not about whom you married · married into [a family]
entries.variants: wed to is the headline and literary version and takes the same to.
entries.contrast: Married to, not ✗ married with. This is one of the most common errors made by speakers of Romance and Slavic languages, whose equivalents use "with," and it is worth drilling: ✓ She's married to a pilot, ✗ She's married with a pilot. The one place with is correct is the fixed phrase married with two kids, where with introduces the children, not the spouse. Note also that the verb takes no preposition at all — ✓ He married her, ✗ He married with her, ✗ He married to her — so the adjective and the verb differ; see the zero-preposition entry for marry. Married into means joining a family by marriage.
entries.see also: marry, engaged to, committed to, related to, to

entries.meaning: Important enough to a decision or an outcome that it could change it.
examples: The lawsuit is material to the buyer's decision and has to be disclosed.
Whether the roof leaked is material to the price, not just to the mood.
Auditors flagged an error material to the quarter's results.
Nothing in the correspondence is material to the jurisdictional question.
Any change material to the coverage must be reported within ten days.
entries.русский: существенный для решения или исхода — юр./книжн.
entries.register: legal and accounting; in those fields it is a precise term (material to the decision, a material misstatement), and it is nearly the only place the adjective takes a complement
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the question, decision, or outcome that the fact could affect, or a gerund (material to deciding the motion). Never a to-infinitive: ✗ material to decide the motion. A wh-clause is fine: material to what the buyer agreed to pay.
entries.pattern: be material to [issue / decision] · a fact material to [noun] · not material to [noun] — the common denial · a material breach / material weakness — attributive terms of art, no preposition
entries.variants: relevant to is the broader everyday word; germane to is about topical fit; pertinent to is the formal synonym of relevant; significant to is the plain paraphrase.
entries.contrast: Relevant is the low bar and material the high one. Evidence is relevant to a case if it bears on it at all; a fact is material to a decision only if it could have changed the outcome — which is why American securities law defines materiality by whether a reasonable investor would want to know. Against dispositive of, which settles the question outright, material to only means the fact could matter. Watch the unrelated senses of material: the noun (building material), and the adjective meaning physical (material evidence in the sense of tangible), neither of which takes to. ✗ material for and ✗ material in are errors here.
entries.see also: relevant to, germane to, pertinent to, dispositive of, to

entries.meaning: Keeping something in mind and letting it shape what you do.
examples: Be mindful of the neighbors when you run the saw before eight.
The court was mindful of the burden this places on small towns.
Ever mindful of the budget, she priced three options before calling.
He wrote the memo mindful of how it would read in six months.
We're mindful of being guests in somebody else's building.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˈmaɪn(d)fəl əv/ — the d is usually dropped: "MYNE-ful-uv"
entries.русский: помнящий о чём-л. и сообразующий с этим свои действия
entries.register: formal to neutral; common in official statements and in careful speech, and quite separate from the wellness sense of mindfulness
entries.complement: a noun phrase or a gerund (mindful of being the newest person in the room) — never a to-infinitive: ✗ mindful of to be the newest. A that-clause attaches to the bare adjective with no preposition: mindful that the deadline is Friday ✓.
entries.pattern: be mindful of [noun / verb-ing] · be mindful (that) [clause] · ever / always / painfully mindful of · bear [something] in mind — the idiom, with a different shape
entries.variants: conscious of and aware of are the neutral equivalents; cognizant of the formal one; alert to points forward at a risk; heedful of is the literary version.
entries.contrast: Mindful of means you are letting the fact govern how you act, which is more than aware of claims: a driver aware of the ice knows about it, a driver mindful of the ice slows down. Against conscious of, which reports what is present in your mind, mindful of reports what is guiding your conduct — which is why it fits instructions and public statements so well. Note the separate modern noun mindfulness, a meditation practice, which takes of only in its older sense. ✗ mindful about and ✗ mindful to are errors, though the imperative mind the gap is a different construction entirely.
entries.see also: aware of, conscious of, cognizant of, careful with, of

entries.meaning: Originating in a particular place and belonging there naturally.
examples: The shrub is native to the dry side of the mountains.
These beetles aren't native to North America and have no predators here.
The nursery stocks only plants native to the watershed.
Cynicism about zoning is native to this county.
The format is native to the older software and has to be converted.
entries.русский: родом из, исконно обитающий или произрастающий в
entries.register: neutral to technical — biology, gardening, and geography; also used figuratively of habits and instincts
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a place, a region, or a habitat — native to the Pacific Northwest, native to alkaline soils. Never a gerund and never a clause. When the complement is a person rather than a place, the frame changes: native speaker of Spanish, a native of Ohio — both with of.
entries.pattern: [species] be native to [place] · plants native to [region] · a native of [place] — the noun frame, with of · native [noun] — attributive (native grasses, native speaker)
entries.variants: indigenous to is the formal equivalent and is the preferred word for peoples; endemic to is stronger and means found nowhere else; originating in is the neutral paraphrase; the opposites are introduced, nonnative, and invasive.
entries.contrast: Native to says it originated here; endemic to says it is found only here. Douglas fir is native to the Northwest and also grows elsewhere; an island snail may be endemic to one valley. Note the switch between adjective and noun: a species is native to Ohio, but a person is a native of Ohio — ✗ he is native to Ohio is not how Americans say it about people. In computing, native to has a live technical sense (an app native to the platform), meaning built for it rather than ported. ✗ native of after the adjective and ✗ native in are errors.
entries.see also: endemic to, peculiar to, specific to, common to, to

entries.meaning: Uneasy about something that is coming.
examples: He's nervous about the presentation on Monday.
She gets nervous about driving in snow after what happened.
Everyone was nervous about how the vote would go.
I'm nervous about leaving the house empty for three weeks.
He's nervous around horses, which makes them nervous too.
entries.русский: нервничающий из-за предстоящего
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after about (nervous about flying) — never a to-infinitive after about. The adjective takes a bare to-infinitive directly (nervous to ask), less commonly. After of, a thing feared — a usage that is British-flavored and rarer in the United States.
entries.pattern: be nervous about [noun / verb-ing] · get nervous about [noun] · be nervous of [thing] — chiefly British · make [someone] nervous (no preposition on the object)
entries.variants: anxious about is the more formal twin; worried about the more consequential one; jittery about and antsy about the informal American ones.
entries.contrast: Nervous about is about an upcoming event; afraid of is about a standing fear. Nervous about the flight is one flight; afraid of flying is every flight. In American English, ✗ nervous of dogs sounds foreign — the American choice is afraid of dogs or nervous around dogs. Note the useful fourth frame nervous around, which names the company that produces the feeling rather than the event.
entries.see also: anxious about, worried about, afraid of, scared of, about

entries.meaning: Recently arrived at something and not yet used to it — or, of a thing, not previously encountered.
examples: He's new to the route and still checking addresses twice.
I'm new to keeping bees and have already been stung twice.
That objection is new to me — nobody raised it in committee.
She's new to the city but not new to the work.
Anyone new to the building gets a badge on the first day.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /nu tə/ — American English says NOO, not the British NYOO
entries.русский: новичок в чём-л., ещё не освоившийся; о вещи — впервые встреченный кем-л.
entries.register: neutral and everyday
entries.complement: a noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (new to managing people) — never a to-infinitive: ✗ new to manage people. The noun test settles it: new to the job ✓.
entries.pattern: be new to [place / job / activity] · new to [someone] — meaning unfamiliar to them: that idea is new to me · brand new to [noun] · fairly / relatively new to
entries.variants: unfamiliar with looks at the same fact from the other end; a newcomer to is the noun phrase; green at is the informal one for inexperience; just starting out is the plain paraphrase.
entries.contrast: The subject decides which way the phrase points. With a person as subject, new to means inexperienced at something: she's new to the department. With a thing as subject, it means unfamiliar to somebody: this rule is new to me. The two are the same construction pointed in opposite directions, and only context tells them apart. Against unfamiliar with, which reports what you do not know, new to reports how recently you arrived. ✗ new in is used of places in some varieties (new in town is the fixed American exception) and ✗ new at survives only in new at this.
entries.see also: familiar with, accustomed to, used to, acquainted with, to

entries.meaning: Behaving pleasantly toward someone.
examples: Be nice to your sister; she's had a long week.
The staff there is nice to everybody, which is not nothing.
It was nice of him to drive all that way.
She was nice about the whole misunderstanding.
The weather has been nice to us for three straight weekends.
entries.русский: любезный, приветливый с кем-л.
entries.register: informal to neutral
entries.complement: a person or animal after to — never a gerund, never a to-infinitive, never a clause. The judgment frame takes of plus a doer and an infinitive (nice of you to come), and the evaluative frame takes an infinitive with no preposition (nice to meet you).
entries.pattern: be nice to [person] · it is nice of [someone] to [verb] · it is nice to [verb] · be nice about [something] — gracious regarding · play nice with [someone]
entries.variants: kind to, good to, pleasant to, and decent to are the same frame at different temperatures.
entries.contrast: The three nice frames say three different things. Nice to meet you evaluates the meeting. Nice of you to come praises the person for coming. Be nice to your brother instructs about treatment. The last is the one that takes the fixed preposition, and it patterns with kind to, polite to, rude to, and cruel to. ✗ nice with is an error except in the informal play nice with, and ✗ nice for you to come changes the meaning to convenience rather than kindness.
entries.see also: kind to, polite to, friendly with, rude to, to

entries.meaning: Widely known for something bad.
examples: That intersection is notorious for fender-benders.
He's notorious for rewriting the agenda ten minutes before the meeting.
The permit office is notorious for losing paperwork.
She was notorious as the toughest grader in the department.
August is notorious for thunderstorms that arrive exactly at rush hour.
entries.русский: печально известный чем-л.
entries.register: neutral to journalistic
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after for (notorious for showing up late) — never a to-infinitive. After as, a noun naming a role (notorious as a bad tipper).
entries.pattern: be notorious for [fault / verb-ing] · be notorious as [role] · notoriously [adjective] — the adverb frame · notorious among [group]
entries.variants: infamous for is the same idea with a stronger moral charge; known for is the neutral one; famous for is the positive one.
entries.contrast: Notorious is always negative. Famous for its pies and notorious for its pies are opposite reviews. The word cannot be used approvingly without irony, which is why ✗ notorious for her generosity reads as a joke. The adverb frame is often the neater choice — a notoriously slow intersection beats an intersection notorious for slowness. ✗ notorious of and ✗ notorious about are errors.
entries.see also: famous for, known for, popular with, for

entries.meaning: Bound by duty or by law to do something — or, in the older sense, indebted to someone for a kindness.
examples: The landlord is obligated to give twenty-four hours' notice.
Nobody is obligated to answer a question at the counter.
She felt obligated to say something before the vote.
We're obligated to the bondholders first and to everyone else after.
I'm much obliged to you for driving out here in this weather.
entries.русский: обязанный сделать что-л. по долгу или закону; в старом смысле — признательный кому-л.
entries.register: obligated to is the standard American form; obliged to is commoner in Britain and survives in America in the courteous much obliged
entries.type: adjective (past participle) + preposition or infinitive marker
entries.complement: two frames, and the to is a different word in each. Before a person or body, to is a preposition: obligated to the bank, obliged to her for the introduction. Before a duty, to is an infinitive marker and a bare verb follows: obligated to notify the tenant. What is impossible is the gerund: ✗ obligated to notifying the tenant. The noun test tells you which frame you are in — obligated to the bank ✓ is prepositional, obligated to notify is not.
entries.pattern: be obligated to [verb] · be obligated to [person] to [verb] — both slots at once · feel obligated to [verb] · be under an obligation to [verb] · much obliged — the fixed courtesy, no complement
entries.variants: required to and bound to fill the duty frame; indebted to and beholden to fill the person frame in the "owe a favor" sense; have to is the plain everyday verb.
entries.contrast: Obligated for duties, obliged for favors is the working American split: I'm obligated to file by the fifteenth is a duty, I'm obliged to you for the ride is thanks. British English uses obliged for both and finds obligated heavy. Against beholden to, which always implies a constraining debt, obligated to is neutral about how you feel. Note that this entry is one of the few in the file where a bare infinitive is required — the fixed to here is not always a preposition, which is exactly why the gerund error does not occur with it.
entries.see also: beholden to, bound by, incumbent on, incumbent upon, liable for, liable to, to

entries.meaning: Not noticing something that is right there, and usually blamed for it.
examples: He walked into the meeting oblivious to what everyone else had heard.
She's oblivious to how loud that laugh is.
Drivers seem oblivious to the new signal at the crosswalk.
The kids played on, oblivious to the fact that it was pouring.
He was oblivious to being the only one still arguing.
entries.русский: не замечающий того, что прямо перед ним — обычно с укором
entries.register: neutral, with a critical edge — to call someone oblivious is not a compliment
entries.complement: a noun phrase or a gerund (oblivious to being watched) — never a to-infinitive: ✗ oblivious to be watched. A that-clause is impossible; use unaware that instead.
entries.pattern: be oblivious to [noun / verb-ing] · oblivious of [noun] — the older variant · completely / blissfully / cheerfully oblivious to · oblivious — used alone, with the complement understood
entries.variants: unaware of is the neutral equivalent; blind to is the metaphorical one; heedless of is literary; out of it is the slang paraphrase.
entries.contrast: Oblivious to and oblivious of are both correct, with to now dominant in American English and of the older and more literary choice; usage guides once insisted the word meant only "forgetful of" (from Latin oblivisci), but that battle ended a century ago. Against unaware of, which is neutral, oblivious to implies the person should have noticed — the word carries a judgment. Against impervious to, which means it does not get through, oblivious to means it never registered at all. ✗ oblivious about is an error.
entries.see also: aware of, conscious of, indifferent to, impervious to, to

entries.meaning: Unable to stop thinking about something.
examples: She's obsessed with getting the drainage right before the spring rains.
He's been obsessed with that band since eighth grade.
The department is obsessed with metrics that measure nothing.
I'm obsessed with this bread and I'm not going to apologize.
He was obsessed by the idea that the file had been altered.
entries.русский: одержимый чем-л., не могущий перестать думать о
entries.register: neutral in the clinical sense; heavily used as hyperbole in American speech
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (obsessed with getting it right) — never a to-infinitive and never a clause.
entries.pattern: be obsessed with [noun / verb-ing] · become obsessed with [noun] · obsessed by [an idea that pursues you] · an obsession with [noun] — the noun keeps with
entries.variants: fixated on takes on; preoccupied with takes with; consumed by takes by. The casual American can't stop thinking about is the plain paraphrase.
entries.contrast: Obsessed with is the ordinary choice; obsessed by casts the idea as the agent that pursues the person — obsessed by the thought that he'd forgotten something is more literary and slightly more sinister than obsessed with. ✗ obsessed about is an error, although the verb obsess takes about correctly (stop obsessing about it), which is the source of the mistake. ✗ obsessed on borrows from fixated on.
entries.see also: addicted to, hooked on, crazy about, intent on, with

entries.meaning: Against something — a plan, a policy, a course of action.
examples: The council is opposed to rezoning the whole block at once.
She's not opposed to working weekends, within reason.
Most residents are opposed to the highway extension.
He's firmly opposed to anything that lengthens the meeting.
We're talking about a lease, as opposed to a purchase.
entries.русский: выступающий против чего-л. — после to герундий
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (opposed to raising the fee) — never a to-infinitive. ✗ opposed to raise the fee is the error, and it is common in policy writing; the noun test settles it (opposed to the increase ✓).
entries.pattern: be opposed to [noun / verb-ing] · be strongly / firmly / bitterly opposed to [noun] · oppose [something] — the verb, with no preposition · as opposed to [noun] — the comparison idiom
entries.variants: against is the plain preposition that says the same thing and takes the same complement (against raising the fee). Averse to is the formal near-synonym and also takes a gerund.
entries.contrast: The verb and the adjective take different structures. ✓ They oppose the plan (no preposition), ✓ They are opposed to the plan — and ✗ They oppose to the plan is a frequent error. Note the separate idiom as opposed to, which is a comparison marker rather than a statement of opposition: hourly as opposed to salaried simply contrasts two categories; see as opposed to. Not opposed to is standard American understatement for mildly in favor.
entries.see also: committed to, reluctant to, against, as opposed to, to

entries.meaning: At right angles to something — literally, in geometry, and figuratively, of questions that do not bear on each other.
examples: The two vectors are orthogonal to each other, so their dot product is zero.
Choose a basis in which each axis is orthogonal to the others.
The two treatment factors were made orthogonal to one another by design.
Cost is orthogonal to the question of whether the thing works at all.
His objection is orthogonal to the motion on the floor.
entries.русский: перпендикулярный (мат.); перен. — лежащий в другой плоскости, не относящийся к делу
entries.register: technical in mathematics and statistics; borrowed as jargon into engineering, economics, and American office talk, where orthogonal to means "beside the point"
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the other vector, factor, dimension, or question — never a gerund and never a clause.
entries.pattern: [vector] be orthogonal to [vector] · orthogonal to [the question at hand] — the jargon use · mutually orthogonal · orthogonality — the noun
entries.variants: perpendicular to is the geometric equivalent in two and three dimensions; at right angles to is the plain phrase; independent of and unrelated to are what the jargon use actually means; uncorrelated with is the statistician's term.
entries.contrast: Perpendicular to is about lines you can draw; orthogonal to generalizes the idea to any number of dimensions — and to statistics, where orthogonal factors vary independently. The office use (that's orthogonal to what we're deciding) is a borrowed metaphor meaning "unrelated, and let's not conflate them"; some readers find it affected, and unrelated to says the same thing. Against independent of, which is the plain word for the same relation, orthogonal to claims the two things can be varied without touching each other. ✗ orthogonal with and ✗ orthogonal from are errors.
entries.see also: perpendicular to, parallel to, independent of, tangent to, to

entries.meaning: Running alongside something at a constant distance, in space or in development.
examples: The service road runs parallel to the highway for about four miles.
Draw a line parallel to the base through the midpoint.
Her research is parallel to what the Michigan group published last spring.
The bike path is parallel to the river the whole way.
The two investigations proceeded parallel to each other for months.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˈpærəˌlɛl tə/ — note the spelling, one r and two l's in the middle
entries.русский: параллельный чему-л. — в пространстве или в развитии
entries.register: neutral to technical; geometry, road directions, and analytical writing about resemblances
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the line, path, course, or case that runs alongside — never a gerund and never a clause. The variant parallel with takes the same complement.
entries.pattern: [line / street] be parallel to [line] · run parallel to [noun] · parallel with [noun] — the equally standard variant · a parallel to / a parallel with [noun] — the noun frame, both prepositions available · draw a parallel between [X] and [Y]
entries.variants: parallel with is fully standard and slightly commoner when the two things move together in time; alongside is the plain preposition; analogous to covers the figurative sense more precisely.
entries.contrast: Parallel to and parallel with are both correct, and no American reader will notice which you used; if there is a tendency, to suits fixed geometric relations (a line parallel to the base) and with suits things developing side by side (her career ran parallel with his). Against analogous to, which claims corresponding relations, parallel to claims that two courses run alongside without meeting. The noun takes between in the draw a parallel frame, which is a third pattern worth keeping separate. ✗ parallel of is an error, except in the geographic noun (the 49th parallel).
entries.see also: perpendicular to, adjacent to, analogous to, orthogonal to, to

entries.meaning: Caring intensely about something over a long stretch, not just at the moment.
examples: She's passionate about getting the trail finished before the fall.
He's passionate about barbecue in a way that has cost him a garage.
The whole staff is passionate about the work and underpaid for it.
I'm not passionate about spreadsheets, but I'm good at them.
They're passionate about keeping the pool open year-round.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˈpæʃənət əˈbaʊt/, and in fast speech the preposition reduces to "'BOWT"
entries.русский: страстно увлечённый чем-л. — не на минуту, а надолго
entries.register: neutral; a fixture of American cover letters, mission statements, and dating profiles, to the point of being a cliché in all three
entries.complement: a noun phrase or a gerund (passionate about getting kids outdoors) — never a to-infinitive: ✗ passionate about to teach, ✗ passionate to teach in this sense. The noun test is immediate: passionate about the work ✓.
entries.pattern: be passionate about [noun / verb-ing] · deeply / genuinely passionate about · a passion for [noun] — the noun frame, which switches to for · passionate [noun] — attributive (a passionate defense)
entries.variants: enthusiastic about is the neutral equivalent; crazy about and nuts about are the informal ones; devoted to and committed to take to; keen on is British-leaning.
entries.contrast: Adjective about, noun for. ✓ passionate about food, ✓ a passion for food, ✗ a passion about food, ✗ passionate for food. That switch is the only structural trap here. The register trap is larger: American hiring managers have read passionate about so many thousand times that the phrase now carries almost no information, and a concrete verb usually beats it. Against enthusiastic about, which is about visible energy, passionate about claims a deeper and more durable commitment.
entries.see also: enthusiastic about, crazy about, serious about, committed to, about

entries.meaning: Willing to put up with delay, difficulty, or slowness without getting angry.
examples: She's endlessly patient with students who ask the same question twice.
Be patient with the software; it takes a minute to index.
He was never patient with anyone who hadn't read the material.
The coach is patient with mistakes and hard on carelessness.
Everyone lost patience with the process about six months in.
entries.русский: терпеливый с кем-л., не раздражающийся
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: a person, animal, or process after with — never a gerund, never a to-infinitive. The adjective also appears bare (be patient) and with about naming the matter (patient about the delay).
entries.pattern: be patient with [person / process] · be patient about [matter] · be patient (alone) · lose patience with [person] — the noun keeps with
entries.variants: tolerant of takes of; forbearing toward is the formal one; easy on is the informal one.
entries.contrast: Patient takes with, not to, which puts it with gentle with and against kind to, nice to, and polite to. The reason is the same: with marks the manner of dealing, to marks the direction of treatment. Note that the noun follows the adjective — patience with the process, out of patience with him — and that the medical noun patient is a different word entirely, taking of only in the possessive sense (a patient of Dr. Reyes). ✗ patient at is an error.
entries.see also: gentle with, kind to, annoyed with, indifferent to, with

entries.meaning: Belonging to one group, place, or thing and to no other.
examples: The vowel is peculiar to speakers born east of the river.
That kind of feud is not peculiar to small towns, whatever people say.
The bookkeeping method is peculiar to this one branch of the business.
There's a stubbornness peculiar to people who have farmed dry land.
The defect is peculiar to units built in the first two months.
entries.русский: свойственный только кому-л. или чему-л. и никому больше
entries.register: formal to neutral; standard in scholarly and technical writing, where it means "belonging exclusively to" and carries none of the "odd" sense
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the group, place, or thing that alone has the feature — never a gerund and never a clause.
entries.pattern: [feature] be peculiar to [group / place] · not peculiar to [noun] — a common frame for denying that a problem is local · a usage peculiar to [dialect] · peculiar — the everyday adjective meaning strange, with no complement
entries.variants: specific to is the neutral modern equivalent; unique to is the strongest; characteristic of stresses typicality rather than exclusivity; endemic to covers species and diseases.
entries.contrast: Peculiar to means found only there; the bare adjective peculiar means odd, and the presence of the complement is what tells the two apart: a custom peculiar to the valley is exclusive, a peculiar custom is strange. Against characteristic of, which says the trait is typical of a thing but may appear elsewhere, peculiar to claims exclusivity. Against common to, the two are near opposites: common to several, peculiar to one. ✗ peculiar for and ✗ peculiar of are errors.
entries.see also: specific to, characteristic of, endemic to, common to, to

entries.meaning: Meeting something at a right angle.
examples: The new wing is perpendicular to the original building.
Set the fence perpendicular to the blade before you cut.
The cross street runs perpendicular to the avenue for two blocks.
Drop a line perpendicular to the base from the opposite vertex.
Park perpendicular to the curb here, not at an angle.
entries.русский: перпендикулярный чему-л.
entries.register: neutral to technical — geometry, construction, and directions
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the line, surface, or direction — never a gerund and never a clause.
entries.pattern: [line] be perpendicular to [line / plane] · run / sit / set [something] perpendicular to [noun] · the perpendicular — the noun, meaning a vertical line · at right angles to — the plain equivalent
entries.variants: at right angles to is the everyday paraphrase; orthogonal to is the generalized mathematical term; normal to is the physicist's word for perpendicular to a surface; square to is the carpenter's.
entries.contrast: Against orthogonal to, which generalizes to any number of dimensions and to statistics, perpendicular to stays concrete and geometric. Note that in physics and engineering the word for the same relation to a surface is normal to, which is the term a reader will meet in optics and mechanics. In carpentry, square to does the same job. ✗ perpendicular with and ✗ perpendicular from are errors.
entries.see also: parallel to, orthogonal to, adjacent to, tangent to, to

entries.meaning: Bearing directly on the matter at hand.
examples: Please produce every email pertinent to the September order.
That fact is interesting but not pertinent to the claim she filed.
The manual's third chapter is the only part pertinent to our setup.
Keep the questions pertinent to the position, not to her family.
Anything pertinent to safety goes in the first section of the report.
entries.русский: относящийся к делу, имеющий прямое касательство к
entries.register: formal; the natural home is a document request, a policy memo, or a records search — all documents pertinent to the transaction
entries.complement: a noun phrase or a gerund (pertinent to deciding whether to appeal) — never a to-infinitive: ✗ pertinent to decide. A wh-clause is fine: pertinent to what the committee has to vote on.
entries.pattern: be pertinent to [matter] · [documents / facts] pertinent to [noun] · directly / hardly pertinent to · pertain to [noun] — the verb, catalogued with the verb patterns
entries.variants: relevant to is the neutral everyday word and will replace it anywhere; germane to is the parliamentary one; material to is the legal one; applicable to covers rules rather than facts; appertaining to is the archaic legal form.
entries.contrast: Pertinent to and relevant to are close to interchangeable, with pertinent the more formal and slightly narrower of the two — it suggests the thing bears directly on the matter rather than merely touching it. Against material to, which in law asks whether the fact could change the outcome, pertinent to asks only whether it belongs to the subject. Do not confuse the adjective with impertinent, whose everyday meaning is "rude," though its older sense — not pertinent — survives in the legal phrase scandalous and impertinent matter. ✗ pertinent for and ✗ pertinent with are errors.
entries.see also: relevant to, germane to, material to, probative of, to

entries.meaning: Satisfied and glad about something.
examples: The client was pleased with the revised layout.
She's pleased about getting the earlier slot.
Everyone was pleased by how smoothly the move went.
We are pleased to offer you the position.
He looked far too pleased with himself for someone who'd just been lucky.
entries.русский: довольный чем-л.
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: noun phrase after with, about, and by; a gerund after about (pleased about being asked) — never a to-infinitive after a preposition. The adjective takes a bare to-infinitive directly (pleased to announce) and a that-clause (pleased that it worked out).
entries.pattern: be pleased with [thing assessed] · be pleased about [situation] · be pleased by [the cause] · be pleased to [verb] · be pleased (that) [clause] · pleased with oneself
entries.variants: happy with is the everyday equivalent; satisfied with the more measured one; delighted with the warmer one.
entries.contrast: With takes what you are judging; about takes the situation; by takes the cause. Pleased with the results is a verdict; pleased about the outcome is a mood; pleased by her reaction points at what produced it. The infinitive frame is a formality marker — We are pleased to inform you — and never takes a preposition. Pleased with himself is fixed and means smug, not merely satisfied. ✗ pleased of is an error.
entries.see also: happy about, satisfied with, delighted with, content with, with

entries.meaning: Showing good manners toward someone.
examples: Be polite to the inspector even if he's wrong.
She was polite to everyone and warm to almost no one.
It's polite to let the host start eating first.
It was polite of him to pretend not to notice.
The clerk stayed polite to the very end of a long afternoon.
entries.русский: вежливый с кем-л.
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: a person after to — never a gerund and never a to-infinitive. The judgment frame takes of plus a doer and an infinitive: It was polite of him to ask first.
entries.pattern: be polite to [person] · it is polite to [verb] · it is polite of [someone] to [verb] · polite about [something] — gracious regarding
entries.variants: courteous to, civil to, and respectful toward are the formal ladder; nice to is the everyday one.
entries.contrast: Polite to joins kind to, nice to, rude to, and cruel to in taking to for the person treated. ✗ polite with is an error. The difference from nice to is one of temperature: politeness is a matter of form and can be cold — He was perfectly polite to her often implies he was nothing more — while nice to implies warmth. Polite about names the matter one is gracious concerning: polite about the burned dinner.
entries.see also: rude to, nice to, kind to, friendly with, to

entries.meaning: Not good at something — or, in the other sense, short of some substance.
examples: He's poor at estimating how long anything will take.
The topsoil here is poor in organic matter.
She's poor at delegating and knows it.
The team is poor at closing out games it should win.
Most of the district's schools are poor in everything but enthusiasm.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /pʊr ət/; also /pɔr/, rhyming with pore
entries.русский: слабый в чём-л. (о навыке); poor in — бедный чем-л. (о ресурсе)
entries.register: formal to neutral; bad at is the everyday version
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after at (poor at estimating time) — never a to-infinitive. After in, a resource lacked (poor in mineral content), which is a different sense and the direct opposite of rich in.
entries.pattern: be poor at [skill / verb-ing] · be poor in [resource] · a poor [noun] — attributive, no preposition · poor showing / poor judgment
entries.variants: bad at, weak at, not strong at, and terrible at run from neutral to blunt; deficient in is the formal counterpart of poor in.
entries.contrast: Poor at a skill; poor in a resource. Poor at math is unskilled; soil poor in nitrogen is lacking a substance, and the second sense is the exact mirror of rich in. ✗ poor on and ✗ poor with are errors for the skill sense, though poor with money does occur informally on the model of good with money. Note the register split: American writing prefers bad at in speech and poor at in evaluations and reports.
entries.see also: bad at, terrible at, hopeless at, rich in, at

entries.meaning: Liked by a lot of people in some group or place.
examples: The evening section is popular with students who work days.
That policy was never popular with the people who had to enforce it.
Sardines are popular in parts of the coast and nowhere else.
The trail is popular among trail runners on weekday mornings.
Telling them at the last minute will not be popular with anyone.
entries.русский: популярный среди, пользующийся любовью у
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: a person or group after with and among — never a gerund and never a to-infinitive. After in, a place: popular in the Midwest.
entries.pattern: be popular with [group] · be popular among [group] · be popular in [place] · prove popular with [group] · not popular with [group] — the standard understatement
entries.variants: popular among is the formal equivalent and is preferred when the group is large or statistical; a hit with is the informal one; well liked by is the passive one.
entries.contrast: With takes the audience; in takes the territory; among takes a group considered as a set. Popular with teachers and popular among teachers differ only in formality, but popular in Texas means something else — geography, not audience. ✗ popular by is an error (that would be the passive liked by), and ✗ popular to is an error, though popular with and appeal to cover the same ground with different words.
entries.see also: famous for, friendly with, known for, with

entries.meaning: Having something — a quality, a faculty, or an estate — in the formal register.
examples: The testator was possessed of three properties at the time of death.
She is possessed of a memory that makes note-taking look optional.
Anyone possessed of the least common sense would have called first.
He remained possessed of his faculties to the end.
The trust is possessed of assets that have never been appraised.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /pəˈzɛst əv/, and before a consonant often /pəˈzɛs ə/ — the t drops: "puh-ZESS-uh"
entries.русский: обладающий чем-л. — качеством, способностью, имуществом; книжн./юр.
entries.register: formal and literary, with a legal survival; an American meets possessed of in wills, in older fiction (a single man in possession of a good fortune is the same idea), and in judicial prose
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming what is held — a quality, a fortune, an estate, a faculty. Never a gerund and never a clause. The related but opposite frames take other prepositions and are set out under Contrast.
entries.pattern: be possessed of [quality / property] · seized and possessed of [land] — the old conveyancing pair · possessed of [one's faculties] · in possession of [noun] — the noun frame, with of
entries.variants: in possession of is the ordinary modern phrase and is what a police report uses; endowed with covers qualities given rather than held; have is the plain verb that replaces all of them.
entries.contrast: Possessed of means holding; possessed by means owned or controlled by; possessed with means gripped by an idea. A landowner is possessed of a hundred acres, a character in a horror film is possessed by a demon, and an obsessive is possessed with the notion that the neighbors are listening. Only the first is this entry. Against endowed with, which implies a giver, possessed of says only that the thing is held. The whole pattern is formal: in ordinary American English, write has. ✗ possessed to is not English.
entries.see also: endowed with, vested with, seized of, seised of, replete with, of

entries.meaning: Useful for forecasting something else, whether or not it causes it.
examples: Attendance in the first two weeks is predictive of whether a student finishes.
The marker is only weakly predictive of recurrence.
Nothing in the interview turned out to be predictive of performance.
Rainfall in March is predictive of the fire season by August.
Late payments are predictive of default about a year out.
entries.русский: позволяющий предсказать что-л., прогностический в отношении
entries.register: technical — statistics, medicine, and evaluation research; the everyday phrase is predicts or is a good sign of
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the outcome predicted, or a gerund (predictive of dropping out) — never a to-infinitive: ✗ predictive of to drop out. A wh-clause is fine: predictive of who will renew.
entries.pattern: be predictive of [outcome] · highly / only weakly predictive of · predict [outcome] — the verb, direct object, no preposition · predictive value / predictive model — attributive
entries.variants: a predictor of is the noun phrase and takes of as well; associated with is the weaker and more careful claim; diagnostic of concerns present conditions rather than future ones; prognostic of is the clinical word for outcome.
entries.contrast: Predictive of points forward; indicative of points at what is already the case. A test result indicative of infection says something about now; a score predictive of relapse says something about later. Statisticians are careful with the word because prediction is not causation — predictive of claims only that knowing one improves your guess about the other. Note the verb takes no preposition at all: ✓ the model predicts turnover, ✗ the model predicts of turnover. ✗ predictive for is an error, though a predictor for turns up in clinical writing.
entries.see also: indicative of, symptomatic of, suggestive of, proportional to, of

entries.meaning: Damaging to someone's rights, position, or case, and unfairly so.
examples: The photographs were ruled unfairly prejudicial to the defendant.
Delay of this length is prejudicial to the tenants' ability to respond.
The transfer would be prejudicial to creditors who filed on time.
Conduct prejudicial to good order carries its own charge.
Nothing in the amendment is prejudicial to rights already vested.
entries.русский: наносящий ущерб правам или позиции, притом несправедливо — юр.
entries.register: legal; an American meets it in a courtroom objection (unfairly prejudicial to the defendant) and in employment and military discipline (conduct prejudicial to good order and discipline)
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the person, party, or interest harmed — never a gerund and never a clause. The complement is the victim, never the cause.
entries.pattern: be prejudicial to [party / interest] · unfairly prejudicial to [noun] — the evidentiary standard · conduct prejudicial to [noun] · without prejudice to [rights] — the fixed phrase, catalogued with the legal prepositions
entries.variants: detrimental to is the neutral equivalent; damaging to the plain one; adverse to points at interests; harmful to covers people and bodies.
entries.contrast: Prejudicial to adds unfairness to harm. In American evidence law all damaging evidence hurts one side — that is the point of it — so the question is never whether evidence is prejudicial but whether it is unfairly prejudicial, meaning it invites the jury to decide on the wrong basis. Against detrimental to, which is neutral about fairness, and adverse to, which describes a position rather than an effect, prejudicial to is the strongest of the three. Note the noun phrase without prejudice to, which means "without giving up," and the everyday sense of prejudice as bias, which takes against. ✗ prejudicial for and ✗ prejudicial of are errors.
entries.see also: detrimental to, adverse to, harmful to, material to, to

entries.meaning: Done in order to get ready for something that follows.
examples: The crew shut off the water preparatory to replacing the main.
Files were boxed and indexed preparatory to the move.
She resigned from the board preparatory to filing her own suit.
Soil samples were taken preparatory to any grading work.
The rehearsal is preparatory to Thursday's walkthrough with the inspector.
entries.русский: предваряющий что-л., совершаемый в порядке подготовки к — книжн.
entries.register: formal and somewhat stiff — corporate minutes, engineering reports, and older prose; in speech an American says before or to get ready for
entries.type: adjective functioning as a complex preposition
entries.complement: a noun phrase or a gerund (preparatory to filing the petition) — the gerund is the commoner of the two — and never a to-infinitive: ✗ preparatory to file the petition.
entries.pattern: [action] preparatory to [noun / verb-ing] · steps preparatory to [noun] · preparatory [noun] — attributive (preparatory work, a preparatory school)
entries.variants: prior to and in advance of are the neutral formal equivalents; in preparation for is the noun phrase and takes for; before is the plain word and beats all of them in most sentences.
entries.contrast: The phrase implies purpose, not just sequence. Preparatory to says the first action was done in order to make the second possible, where prior to says only that it came first. Note the switch of preposition in the noun frame: preparatory to the audit but in preparation for the audit. American style guides treat the whole phrase as a candidate for cutting — before the audit usually says it better. For the plain time prepositions, see time. ✗ preparatory for is an error in this frame.
entries.see also: previous to, antecedent to, prepared for, ready for, to

entries.meaning: Made ready in advance — for what is coming, or to do what is asked.
examples: The crew was prepared for a two-day outage and got a five-day one.
She's prepared to testify if it comes to that.
Nobody was prepared for how quiet the building would be.
Are you prepared for the questions they're going to ask?
We came prepared for rain and got sun the whole week.
entries.русский: готовый к чему-л.; с инфинитивом — готовый сделать что-л.
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: a noun naming what is coming after for (prepared for the storm) — a gerund after for is possible but heavy. The adjective takes a bare to-infinitive directly (prepared to leave), which is the frame for willingness and is very common. Never a to-infinitive after for.
entries.pattern: be prepared for [event / eventuality] · be prepared to [verb] · prepare for [event] — the verb · prepare [someone] for [event] · be well prepared for [noun]
entries.variants: ready for / ready to runs exactly parallel and is the everyday version; braced for is the version reserved for something bad.
entries.contrast: Prepared for is readiness; prepared to is willingness. I'm prepared for a long meeting means I have the coffee; I'm prepared to stay late means I'm willing. This is the same split as ready for / ready to, and the pair is worth learning as one lesson. ✗ prepared of is an error, and note that the verb prepare takes for the same way (prepare for the worst) but prepare + object takes no preposition (prepare dinner).
entries.see also: ready for, late for, suitable for, for

entries.meaning: Coming before something in time — a formal way of saying before.
examples: Previous to the merger, the two firms shared a single supplier.
She had no experience with grant work previous to joining the office.
Nothing in the file is dated previous to March.
Previous to that season, the team had never sold out a weeknight game.
Any claim arising previous to closing stays with the seller.
entries.русский: предшествующий чему-л., до — книжн. вместо before
entries.register: formal and slightly dated; prior to has largely displaced it in American writing, and before beats both
entries.type: adjective functioning as a complex preposition
entries.complement: a noun phrase or a gerund (previous to joining the firm) — never a to-infinitive: ✗ previous to join the firm. No clause follows; for a clause use before.
entries.pattern: [event] previous to [event] · previous to [verb-ing] · the previous [noun] — the ordinary attributive adjective, which is far commoner · previously — the adverb
entries.variants: prior to is the living formal twin and is what American business writing uses; before is the plain word; ahead of covers sequence in queues and schedules; antecedent to and anterior to are the archaic-formal versions.
entries.contrast: Everything previous to can do, before can do more simply, which is why usage guides on both sides of the Atlantic single the phrase out: before the hearing is shorter than previous to the hearing and loses nothing. Where it survives is in formal narrative and in older legal prose. Against preparatory to, which implies purpose, previous to claims nothing but sequence. Note that the attributive adjective (the previous tenant) is entirely ordinary modern English and is not this pattern. For the plain time prepositions, see time.
entries.see also: antecedent to, preparatory to, anterior to, posterior to, subject to, to

entries.meaning: Let in on something private — a conversation, a plan, or a contract.
examples: I wasn't privy to whatever they decided in that meeting.
Only three people were privy to the offer before it was announced.
Staff privy to the numbers signed confidentiality agreements.
The subcontractor was never privy to the owner's contract.
She was privy to the discussions but had no vote.
entries.русский: посвящённый во что-л. — допущенный к тайне, плану, договору; не просто знающий
entries.register: formal to neutral; common in journalism and in speech about secrets (not privy to those conversations), and a technical term in contract law
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the information, discussion, or agreement you are inside of — never a to-infinitive (✗ privy to know), and a gerund is awkward enough that careful writers avoid it: prefer privy to the discussions over ✗ privy to their discussing it.
entries.pattern: be privy to [information / discussion] · not privy to [noun] — the commonest frame by far · privy to the contract — the legal sense · privity of contract / privity with [party] — the noun frame
entries.variants: in on is the informal equivalent (in on the plan); party to is the legal near-twin and is catalogued with the noun patterns; aware of is weaker; in the loop is the office idiom.
entries.contrast: Privy to means admitted to something private, not merely aware of it — the word implies you were let in. Against aware of, which reports knowledge from any source, privy to reports access. The legal sense is narrower still: parties in privity have a direct contractual relationship, which is why a subcontractor is generally not privy to the owner's contract. Note the unrelated noun privy meaning an outhouse, a homograph that gives the word a faint comic edge in speech. ✗ privy of and ✗ privy with are errors, though in privity with is the correct legal phrase.
entries.see also: aware of, cognizant of, apprised of, acquainted with, to

entries.meaning: Tending to prove a fact that is actually in dispute.
examples: The receipt is probative of when he was in the building, not of why.
Counsel argued the tattoo was not probative of membership in anything.
Prior repairs are probative of notice, which is the whole issue here.
The court found the recording highly probative of intent.
Testimony about her reputation is not probative of what happened that night.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˈproʊbədəv əv/, with the t flapped
entries.русский: доказывающий спорный факт — юр., доказательственный
entries.register: legal, narrowly — evidence law; the word is essentially confined to briefs, rulings, and evidence classrooms
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the fact to be proved — probative of intent, probative of knowledge, probative of identity. Never a gerund and never a clause.
entries.pattern: be probative of [fact at issue] · highly / marginally probative of · probative value — the noun phrase weighed against unfair prejudice under the American rules of evidence · more probative than prejudicial
entries.variants: tending to prove is the plain paraphrase; evidence of is the everyday noun phrase; indicative of is the general word; dispositive of is the strongest.
entries.the whole american law of evidence turns: evidence must be relevant, its probative value is then weighed against the risk of unfair prejudice, and only rarely is anything dispositive of the question. So probative of claims that the item tends to prove a fact — no more. Against indicative of, which is the general-purpose word for a sign, probative of is a term of art with a legal test behind it. ✗ probative to and ✗ probative for are errors.
entries.see also: dispositive of, material to, indicative of, suggestive of, of

entries.meaning: Standing in a constant ratio to something else — or, loosely, sized to fit it.
examples: The force is proportional to the square of the current.
Brightness falls off inversely proportional to the square of the distance.
Each partner's share is proportional to what they put in.
Staffing should be proportional to the number of beds, not to the square footage.
The fine is proportional to the tonnage, so the big haulers pay most.
entries.русский: пропорциональный чему-л.; разг. — соразмерный
entries.register: technical in the mathematical sense, neutral in the everyday one about fairness
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the other quantity — never a gerund and never a clause. Where the relation is inverse, the fixed phrase is inversely proportional to, with the same complement.
entries.pattern: [quantity] be proportional to [quantity] · directly proportional to · inversely proportional to — as one quantity rises the other falls · in proportion to [noun] — the prepositional phrase · proportionate to [noun] — the variant adjective, commoner in law and about fairness
entries.variants: proportionate to is the near-identical alternative and is the usual word in legal and ethical writing (a punishment proportionate to the offense); in proportion to is the phrase for informal comparisons; scales with is the working-scientist's verb; commensurate with is the formal near-synonym.
entries.contrast: Proportional to is a claim about a constant ratio: if y is proportional to x, doubling x doubles y, and inversely proportional to means doubling x halves y. The everyday sense is looser and means only "appropriately sized," which is where proportionate to usually sits. Against equivalent to, which claims equal value, proportionality claims a fixed relationship between two changing quantities. The noun switches preposition: in proportion to, never ✗ in proportional to. ✗ proportional with is an error.
entries.see also: equivalent to, equal to, predictive of, related to, to

entries.meaning: Feeling satisfaction at something you or someone connected to you has done.
examples: She's proud of every one of those students.
He's proud of having built the whole deck himself.
They were proud of their daughter for saying something.
I'm proud to be part of the project.
The town takes pride in the fact that nothing here has ever burned down.
entries.русский: гордящийся чем-л.
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (proud of having finished it alone) — never a to-infinitive after of. The adjective takes a bare to-infinitive directly (proud to serve) and a that-clause (proud that she'd asked).
entries.pattern: be proud of [person / thing / verb-ing] · be proud of [someone] for [verb-ing] · be proud to [verb] · be proud (that) [clause] · take pride in [noun] — the noun frame uses in
entries.variants: pleased with is the cooler version; boastful about the negative one; take pride in the formal noun frame.
entries.contrast: Proud of doing looks back at something accomplished; proud to do looks forward or reports an honor. I'm proud of serving recalls the service; I'm proud to serve accepts it now. Note that the noun changes preposition: ✓ proud of her work, ✓ pride in her work, ✗ pride of her work — a good example of why these patterns cannot be reasoned out from meaning. ✗ proud for and ✗ proud about are errors.
entries.see also: ashamed of, pleased with, grateful to, of

entries.meaning: Nearer to the point of attachment, or farther from it, along a limb or a tube.
examples: The fracture is just proximal to the wrist.
The stent sits distal to the narrowing.
Sensation is intact everywhere distal to the injury.
The elbow is proximal to the forearm and distal to the shoulder.
Bleeding was found distal to the anastomosis.
entries.русский: проксимальный / дистальный по отношению к — анат., ближе к месту прикрепления или дальше
entries.register: technical — anatomy, surgery, dentistry, and gastroenterology; an American meets them in an operative report or a physical-therapy note and nowhere else
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the reference point on the body or along a structure — never a gerund and never a clause. The pair is relative: everything is proximal or distal to something, so the complement is obligatory unless the reference point is understood (the distal end).
entries.pattern: [structure] be proximal to [structure] · [structure] be distal to [structure] · just proximal to / immediately distal to · the proximal / distal end — attributive, complement understood
entries.variants: nearer to and farther from are the plain equivalents; upstream of and downstream of do the same job for vessels, bowel, and pipelines; central and peripheral cover the same idea for the body as a whole.
entries.contrast: Proximal means nearer the trunk or the point of origin; distal means farther from it, so the elbow is proximal to the wrist and the wrist is distal to the elbow. The pair runs along a limb or a tube, unlike anterior to, posterior to, which runs front to back. Outside anatomy, proximal has a live use in psychology (proximal cause, the zone of proximal development), and in law the near-homophone is proximate cause — a different word with an -ate ending. ✗ proximal from and ✗ distal from are errors: both take to.
entries.see also: anterior to, posterior to, adjacent to, close to, native to, to

entries.meaning: Arriving or acting exactly at the appointed time.
examples: He is unfailingly punctual for every shift.
The trains here are punctual for about eight months of the year.
She's punctual in answering even the tedious emails.
Guests are asked to be punctual for the six o'clock seating.
Being punctual for the first meeting bought him a lot of goodwill.
entries.русский: приходящий точно к назначенному времени
entries.register: formal; American speech says on time
entries.complement: a noun naming an appointment or event after for (punctual for appointments) — never a gerund, never a to-infinitive, never a clause. After in, a gerund naming what is done on time (punctual in paying).
entries.pattern: be punctual for [event] · be punctual in [verb-ing] · be punctual about [noun / verb-ing] · punctual alone: she is always punctual
entries.variants: on time for is the ordinary American equivalent and is far commoner; prompt about / in covers the same ground in business writing.
entries.contrast: Punctual for an event; punctual in or about an activity. The word is the positive counterpart of late for and takes the same for. In American English it is markedly formal — a manager writes punctual and dependable in a review but says she's always on time out loud — so choosing it in casual writing sounds stiff. ✗ punctual to is an error, and ✗ punctual at is an error except with a clock time: punctual at nine is possible but odd.
entries.see also: late for, ready for, prepared for, for

entries.meaning: Prepared, willing, or on the point of something.
examples: The field won't be ready for play until Thursday.
She's ready to sign as soon as the numbers come back.
Get the kids ready for school; the bus moved up ten minutes.
He was ready with an answer before anyone finished asking.
That transmission looks ready to give out any day now.
entries.русский: готовый к чему-л. — подготовленный, согласный или вот-вот приступающий
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: a noun naming what is coming after for (ready for the season) — a gerund after for is uncommon and reads as heavy. The adjective takes a bare to-infinitive directly (ready to go), which is the frame for willingness or imminence. Never a to-infinitive after for.
entries.pattern: be ready for [event / thing] · be ready to [verb] · get ready for [event] · be ready with [something prepared in hand] · ready when you are
entries.variants: prepared for / to is the formal twin and splits the same way; set for and all set to are the informal ones.
entries.contrast: Ready for takes a thing; ready to takes an action. ✓ ready for the interview, ✓ ready to answer, ✗ ready for answering in most contexts. Note that ready to has a second, non-volitional sense meaning on the point of — ready to collapse does not mean the building is willing. Ready with is a third frame naming something held in reserve: ready with an excuse. ✗ ready of is an error.
entries.see also: prepared for, eager for, late for, for

entries.meaning: Connected — by family, by cause, or by subject matter.
examples: She's related to half the families on that road.
The two outages turned out not to be related to each other.
Anything related to payroll goes through the third floor.
Costs related to running the second location doubled in a year.
Sales are up, though not for any reason related to the campaign.
entries.русский: связанный с — родством, причинно или по теме
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or pronoun; a gerund where an activity is meant (costs related to running the shop) — never a to-infinitive and never a clause.
entries.pattern: [X] is related to [Y] · closely / distantly related to [noun] · [noun]-related: weather-related delays · relate to [something] — the verb, meaning to identify with · in relation to [noun]
entries.variants: connected to / with, linked to, and tied to are the neighbors; akin to is the loose literary one.
entries.contrast: Related to covers kinship, causal connection, and topical relevance with one preposition. ✗ related with is an error, and it is a common one because connected with is correct. Keep the adjective apart from the verb relate to meaning to sympathize (I can relate to that), which is informal American English and says something about the speaker rather than the two things. The compound suffix -related has become the compact newsroom form: a heat-related death.
entries.see also: relevant to, similar to, married to, based on, to

entries.meaning: Bearing on the matter under discussion, in a way that matters.
examples: None of that is relevant to whether the permit was filed on time.
The judge ruled the testimony relevant to the second count.
Half the syllabus is no longer relevant to how the work is actually done.
Anything relevant to the audit should be flagged.
Her earlier experience is directly relevant to this job.
entries.русский: имеющий значение для, относящийся к обсуждаемому
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: noun phrase or pronoun; a gerund where an activity is meant (relevant to deciding the appeal) — never a to-infinitive and never a clause.
entries.pattern: [X] is relevant to [Y] · directly / hardly / no longer relevant to [noun] · relevance to [noun] — the noun keeps to · relevant for [purpose] — less common
entries.variants: pertinent to and germane to are the formal equivalents, both with to; bear on is the verb version (that bears on the question).
entries.contrast: Relevant takes to, never for in the ordinary sense and never with. ✗ relevant with the discussion is an error; ✗ relevant of is an error. Relevant to the case means bearing on it; relevant for the case is used occasionally to mean useful for that purpose, but to is the safe default. Compare related to, which asserts a connection of any kind, against relevant to, which asserts that the connection matters for the question at hand.
entries.see also: related to, essential to, subject to, to

entries.meaning: Needing something in order to function.
examples: The region is heavily reliant on a single employer.
The whole system is reliant on one aging server.
Rural clinics are reliant on volunteers for weekend coverage.
She's reliant on the bus until the car is fixed.
We've become reliant upon forecasts that were never that accurate.
entries.русский: зависящий от чего-л., полагающийся на
entries.register: formal to neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (reliant on getting the grant renewed) — never a to-infinitive and never a clause.
entries.pattern: be reliant on [noun / verb-ing] · be reliant upon [noun] · heavily / increasingly / overly reliant on [noun] · self-reliant (no complement) · rely on [someone] to [verb] — the verb frame
entries.variants: reliant upon is the formal equivalent; dependent on is the everyday twin and is far commoner.
entries.contrast: Reliant on, like dependent on, takes on — never ✗ reliant of or ✗ reliant to. The difference from dependent on is one of tone: dependent can suggest weakness or need, while reliant is neutral about the relationship and is the word chosen in policy and technical writing (reliant on imported grain). Note the verb rely on takes an infinitive after a person — rely on him to lock up — and that this frame belongs to the verb, not the adjective: ✗ reliant on him to lock up is odd.
entries.see also: dependent on, independent of, based on, on

entries.meaning: Unwilling to do something, and showing it.
examples: The bank was reluctant to extend the line of credit.
She's reluctant to commit before seeing the final numbers.
Witnesses were reluctant to say anything on the record.
He was reluctant about the whole arrangement from the start.
Nobody is reluctant to take the credit once it works.
entries.русский: неохотно делающий что-л., не желающий — после to инфинитив, а не герундий
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.type: adjective + infinitive marker — the counterexample in this file
entries.complement: a bare to-infinitive (reluctant to sign) — and here the to is not a preposition, so ✗ reluctant to signing is the error. Apply the noun test: ✗ reluctant to the signature fails, which proves the to is an infinitive marker. The adjective takes about + gerund for the prepositional frame: reluctant about signing.
entries.pattern: be reluctant to [verb] · be reluctant about [noun / verb-ing] · reluctantly [verb] — the adverb is commoner than the about frame
entries.variants: unwilling to, hesitant to, loath to, and disinclined to all take the infinitive the same way; averse to takes a gerund and is the odd one out of that set.
entries.contrast: This entry exists to mark the boundary. Reluctant to, hesitant to, unwilling to, ready to, able to, likely to, and about to all take a bare verb — the to is an infinitive marker. Accustomed to, used to, opposed to, averse to, committed to, dedicated to, devoted to, subject to, and look forward to all take a gerund — the to is a preposition. There is no way to tell from the spelling, and the noun test is the only reliable check: if to the noise is grammatical, write -ing. Note the near-pair averse to doing versus reluctant to do, which mean the same thing and take opposite complements.
