entries.see also: opposed to, accustomed to, used to, ready for, to

entries.meaning: Abundantly supplied with something — filled up with it.
examples: The record is replete with warnings the agency chose to ignore.
Her first novel is replete with the kind of detail only a nurse would know.
The manual is replete with diagrams and short on plain instructions.
That period of the archive is replete with letters from the same three families.
The report is replete with qualifications, which is how you know it was lawyered.
entries.русский: изобилующий чем-л., до краёв полный — книжн.
entries.register: formal to literary; a reviewer's and a judge's word (the record is replete with examples), and it sounds ornate in speech
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming what the thing is full of, usually plural or mass — never a gerund and never a clause. The complement may be good or bad, which is what separates the word from fraught with.
entries.pattern: be replete with [examples / detail / errors] · the record is replete with [noun] — the standing judicial phrase · replete — the rare bare use, meaning full up
entries.variants: full of is the plain everyday word; rife with is negative and journalistic; fraught with is negative and about danger; teeming with is about living things; abounding in is the literary variant with a different preposition.
entries.contrast: Against fraught with, which is always negative, replete with is neutral and often admiring — a book replete with detail is a compliment, a process fraught with detail is not. Against full of, the difference is register alone: replete with is what full of wears to a hearing. Note the older sense of replete meaning "having eaten enough," which survives in repletion in clinical writing. ✗ replete of and ✗ replete in are errors.
entries.see also: fraught with, full of, crowded with, endowed with, with

entries.meaning: Standing in for a larger whole because it resembles it in the relevant ways.
examples: The sample isn't representative of the district's actual age spread.
These three cases are representative of the hundred we reviewed.
That painting is not representative of his later work at all.
Weekend traffic is not representative of what the intersection sees at rush hour.
The panel was chosen to be representative of the counties, not of the parties.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˌrɛprəˈzɛnədəv əv/, with both t's flapped in fast speech
entries.русский: показательный для, представляющий собой целое в миниатюре
entries.register: neutral to technical; standard in survey research, sampling, and criticism
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the whole that the sample or example stands for — never a gerund and never a clause. What follows of is the population, not the trait.
entries.pattern: be representative of [population / body of work] · broadly / hardly representative of · a representative sample of [noun] · a representative of [organization] — the noun, which looks identical and means a delegate
entries.variants: typical of is the everyday equivalent; illustrative of claims only that it makes the point; emblematic of is the loaded literary word; characteristic of looks at the trait rather than the sample.
entries.contrast: Representative of claims the example resembles the whole in the ways that matter — which is a statistical claim when the whole is a population, and a critical judgment when it is a body of work. Against typical of, which says something is what you would expect from a group, representative of says it can stand in for the group. Watch the identical-looking noun: a representative of the union is a person, and confusion between the two is easy in a sentence like she is a representative of the district versus her district is representative of the state. ✗ representative for is an error in this sense, though a representative for the company exists as a job title.
entries.see also: typical of, illustrative of, characteristic of, indicative of, of

entries.meaning: Irreconcilable with a higher rule — or, in the everyday sense, deeply offensive to somebody.
examples: A local ordinance repugnant to state law cannot be enforced.
The clause is repugnant to the granting language earlier in the deed.
The practice was repugnant to every doctor who testified.
Nothing in the settlement is repugnant to the court's earlier order.
He found the whole arrangement repugnant to his sense of the job.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /rəˈpʌɡnənt tə/ — the g is pronounced, unlike in impugn
entries.русский: противоречащий высшей норме (юр.); разг. — глубоко отвратительный кому-л.
entries.register: two registers, and both are formal: a legal one meaning "inconsistent with and therefore void" (a statute repugnant to the Constitution), and a moral one meaning "disgusting to"
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the higher authority or the offended party — never a gerund in the legal sense; the moral sense allows a gerund as subject rather than complement (being asked to lie was repugnant to her). No clause follows.
entries.pattern: [statute / clause] be repugnant to [constitution / statute] · [conduct] be repugnant to [person / conscience] · morally repugnant to · repugnant — the bare adjective, meaning disgusting
entries.variants: inconsistent with and contrary to are the neutral legal equivalents; offensive to and abhorrent to cover the moral sense; incompatible with is the general word.
entries.contrast: In law the word means "cannot stand with," not "disgusting" — Marbury's famous formula is that a law repugnant to the Constitution is void, and no revulsion is implied. In ordinary use the moral sense has taken over so completely that the legal one now reads as a term of art. Against consonant with and compatible with, repugnant to is the direct opposite in the legal sense. Note that the bare adjective needs no complement at all in the moral sense: a repugnant argument. ✗ repugnant with and ✗ repugnant for are errors.
entries.see also: consonant with, adverse to, compatible with, opposed to, to

entries.meaning: Having a duty for something, having caused something, or answering to someone.
examples: She's responsible for everything that leaves the loading dock.
Faulty wiring was responsible for the outage.
The director is responsible to a seven-member board.
Each department is responsible for keeping its own inventory.
Nobody wanted to be held responsible for the decision afterward.
entries.русский: ответственный за; виновник чего-л.; responsible to — подотчётный кому-л.
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after for (responsible for closing up) — never a to-infinitive after for. ✗ responsible to close up changes the meaning entirely, because responsible to takes a person you answer to.
entries.pattern: be responsible for [duty / outcome / verb-ing] · be responsible to [person or body one answers to] · hold [someone] responsible for [noun] · personally responsible for [noun] · responsibility for [noun] — the noun keeps for
entries.variants: accountable for a result and accountable to a person split exactly the same way; in charge of covers the duty sense; to blame for covers the fault sense.
entries.contrast: Responsible for names the job or the fault; responsible to names the boss. She's responsible for scheduling is her duty; She's responsible to the board is her reporting line. Mixing them produces a real misunderstanding rather than a stylistic slip. Note the two senses of the for frame — duty (responsible for the night shift) and culpability (responsible for the leak) — which are distinguished only by context, and the bare adjective meaning trustworthy (a responsible adult), which takes no preposition at all.
entries.see also: guilty of, innocent of, subject to, for

entries.meaning: Containing a great deal of something.
examples: Kale is rich in vitamin K and nobody is happy about it.
The valley is rich in iron ore and short of everything else.
Her account is rich in the kind of detail that can't be invented.
The soil along the creek is rich in organic matter.
The town's history is rich in feuds and thin on documents.
entries.русский: богатый чем-л., с высоким содержанием чего-л.
entries.register: neutral to formal; common in nutrition, geology, and description
entries.complement: a mass noun naming what there is a lot of (rich in iron, rich in detail) — never a gerund, never a to-infinitive, never a clause.
entries.pattern: be rich in [substance / quality] · [noun] rich in [noun] · [noun]-rich: protein-rich, nutrient-rich · rich with [something abundant and sensory] · rich alone: a rich family
entries.variants: high in is the everyday nutrition version (high in sodium); abundant in and replete with are the formal ones; loaded with is the informal one.
entries.contrast: Rich in is the standard; rich with is possible when the abundance is sensory or atmospheric — air rich with woodsmoke — and it is the more literary choice. ✗ rich of and ✗ rich on are errors. The exact opposite is poor in (soil poor in nitrogen), which is worth learning as a pair, since the antonym keeps the same preposition. Note that the plain sense of rich — having money — takes no preposition.
entries.see also: full of, poor at, crowded with, lacking in, in

entries.meaning: Behaving in a way that offends ordinary good manners.
examples: He was rude to the receptionist and wondered why the appointment slipped.
It's rude to check your phone while someone is answering your question.
She was rude about the neighbors within earshot of the neighbors.
It was rude of them to leave before the toast.
Nobody there was rude to us; they were just impossible to reach.
entries.русский: грубый с кем-л., невежливый
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: a person after to — never a gerund and never a to-infinitive. The judgment frame takes of plus a doer and an infinitive: It was rude of her to interrupt.
entries.pattern: be rude to [person] · it is rude to [verb] · it was rude of [someone] to [verb] · rude about [something] — insulting concerning
entries.variants: impolite to, discourteous to, and disrespectful toward are the formal ladder; nasty to and short with are the informal ones — note that short with takes with.
entries.contrast: Rude to the person, rude about the subject. She was rude to the waiter is how she treated him; She was rude about the food is what she said concerning it. The of-frame assigns blame to the doer: It was rude of him to leave without saying goodbye. ✗ rude with is an error, though short with and sharp with, which mean something close, both take with.
entries.see also: polite to, cruel to, nice to, kind to, to

entries.meaning: Unhappy about something.
examples: She's sad about leaving the house more than about leaving the town.
Everyone was sad about the way the season ended.
I'm sad for him; he put four years into that program.
It was sad to see the place boarded up.
He's sad about not having asked more questions while he could.
entries.русский: огорчённый чем-л., которому грустно из-за
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after about (sad about leaving) — never a to-infinitive after about. The adjective takes a bare to-infinitive directly (sad to see it go) and a that-clause (sad that nobody came).
entries.pattern: be sad about [noun / verb-ing] · be sad to [verb] · be sad (that) [clause] · be sad for [someone] · sad alone, of a thing: a sad story
entries.variants: upset about is the more agitated version; sorry about the apologetic one; heartbroken over the intensified one, which takes over.
entries.contrast: Sad about names the situation; sad for names the person you feel it on behalf of; sad to + verb reports the reaction as it happens. Sad about the closing is the fact; sad for the staff is on their behalf; sad to hear it is the moment of learning. ✗ sad of and ✗ sad with are errors. Note the useful distinction from sorry about, which carries either apology or sympathy — I'm sorry about your father is condolence, while I'm sad about your father would be an odd thing to say to a mourner, because it centers the speaker.
entries.see also: upset about, sorry for, disappointed with, happy about, about

entries.meaning: Out of reach of some danger.
examples: The files are safe from anything short of a fire.
Nothing on that block was safe from the reassessment.
Keep the seedlings safe from frost for another two weeks.
It's safe to assume the meeting will run long.
Your secret is safe with me, which people say and rarely mean.
entries.русский: защищённый от, вне досягаемости опасности
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: a noun naming the danger escaped after from — a gerund is possible but rare. The adjective takes a bare to-infinitive in a different frame (safe to drink, safe to assume), which describes the thing rather than the person. Never a to-infinitive after from.
entries.pattern: be safe from [danger] · be safe to [verb] · keep [someone] safe from [danger] · safe for [a use or a group]: safe for kids · safe with [a person entrusted]: the secret is safe with me
entries.variants: secure from and protected from / against are the formal equivalents; out of reach of is the concrete one.
entries.contrast: Four frames, four jobs. Safe from the threat; safe for the user or purpose (safe for pets); safe with the person you trusted; safe to + verb about what may be done (safe to eat). Substituting one changes the sentence: safe for children means it will not hurt them, while safe from children means they cannot get at it — and both sentences occur in real life. ✗ safe of is an error.
entries.see also: free of, vulnerable to, independent of, from

entries.meaning: Content with what was received or done — or, in the formal sense, convinced.
examples: The customer was satisfied with the replacement and dropped the complaint.
She wasn't satisfied with the first three explanations.
The inspector was satisfied that the repairs met code.
He seems satisfied with the arrangement, or at least done arguing about it.
Nobody is ever entirely satisfied with a compromise, which is how you know it worked.
entries.русский: удовлетворённый чем-л.; в офиц. смысле — убеждённый в чём-л.
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after with (satisfied with letting it stand) — never a to-infinitive after with. A that-clause attaches to the bare adjective in the "convinced" sense: satisfied that the accounts were in order.
entries.pattern: be satisfied with [thing assessed] · be satisfied (that) [clause] · be satisfied by [the thing that satisfies] · satisfy [someone] — the verb, no preposition · satisfaction with [noun] — the noun keeps with
entries.variants: happy with and pleased with are the everyday twins; content with is the quieter one; okay with is the conversational one.
entries.contrast: Satisfied with means content; satisfied that means convinced. The second sense is the language of inspectors and judges: satisfied that the requirements have been met is a finding, not a mood. Satisfied by points at the cause, and it is also the frame used for requirements: the condition was satisfied by the second payment. ✗ satisfied of is an error in modern American English, though satisfied of the truth of it survives in legal prose.
entries.see also: pleased with, content with, happy about, disappointed with, with

entries.meaning: Feeling fear.
examples: He's scared of heights and took the job on the ninth floor anyway.
She was scared by how quickly the water came up.
I was scared to ask what the estimate was.
They were scared for the crew still out on the water.
Everybody's a little scared of the first day.
entries.русский: боящийся, испуганный чем-л.
entries.register: informal to neutral; the everyday American word
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (scared of falling) after of; a noun after by — never a to-infinitive after a preposition. The adjective takes a bare to-infinitive directly (scared to look), a separate frame.
entries.pattern: be scared of [noun / verb-ing] · be scared by [the event that caused it] · be scared to [verb] · be scared for [someone] · scared stiff / scared to death · scare [someone] (no preposition on the object)
entries.variants: afraid of is the neutral twin; frightened of the slightly formal one; terrified of and petrified of the intensified ones.
entries.contrast: Scared of is the standing fear, scared by the single event, scared to the hesitation to act. Scared of the dark is general; scared by the noise was one moment; scared to open it is not doing something. All three are correct and they are not interchangeable. ✗ scared from is an error. Register is the only thing separating scared of from afraid of: the first is what Americans say, the second is what they write.
entries.see also: afraid of, frightened of, nervous about, worried about, of

entries.meaning: Lawfully holding an estate in land — or, of a tribunal, having a matter properly in hand.
examples: The grantor was seized of an estate in fee simple at the time of the conveyance.
Title showed the decedent seised of the eastern half only.
The tribunal is seized of the dispute and has set a briefing schedule.
Anyone seized of land subject to the covenant takes it with the burden.
The abstract recites that she died seized of the property.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /sizd əv/ — both spellings are pronounced the same
entries.русский: юр. владеющий недвижимостью на законном праве; о суде — принявший дело к рассмотрению
entries.register: legal and archaic-legal; the seised spelling is the traditional one in real-property law, and an American meets either only in a deed, a title opinion, or a court's statement that it has a matter in hand
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming land, an estate, or a matter before a tribunal — never a gerund and never a clause.
entries.pattern: be seized of [land / estate] — the property sense · be seised of [an estate in fee simple] — the conveyancing spelling · the court is seized of [the matter] — the jurisdiction sense, borrowed from international practice · seized with [a matter] — a variant of the second sense
entries.variants: seised of is the same phrase in the older spelling kept by property lawyers to distinguish it from ordinary seizing; possessed of is the neighboring formal phrase; in possession of is the modern equivalent; have jurisdiction over replaces the tribunal sense in American courts, which more often say the matter is before the court.
entries.contrast: Seized of means lawfully holding, which is nearly the opposite of what the everyday verb suggests — police seize property from you, but a landowner is seized of an estate in it. The tribunal sense (the court is seized of the matter) is common in international and European practice and is used in America chiefly by arbitrators and by writers with a foreign audience. Against possessed of, which covers qualities as well as property, seized of is confined to estates in land and to matters before a tribunal. ✗ seized to is not English, and seized by means the ordinary taking.
entries.see also: possessed of, vested with, appurtenant to, entitled to, of

entries.meaning: Reacting readily to something — physically, emotionally, or considerately.
examples: The film is sensitive to even a few seconds of daylight.
He's sensitive about how long it took him to finish school.
The proposal is sensitive to small changes in the discount rate.
She's sensitive to the fact that half the staff has been here longer.
Some patients are sensitive to the dye used in the scan.
entries.русский: чувствительный к — физически, эмоционально или деликатный по отношению к
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or pronoun after to; noun phrase or gerund after about (sensitive about being asked her age) — never a to-infinitive after either.
entries.pattern: be sensitive to [stimulus / concern] · be sensitive about [a personal sore point] · sensitive to [substance] — the allergic sense · a sensitive [noun] — attributive, meaning delicate or confidential
entries.variants: responsive to covers the neutral technical sense; touchy about is the informal version of sensitive about; allergic to is the medical one.
entries.contrast: Sensitive to points outward; sensitive about points inward. Sensitive to criticism means it affects you; sensitive about your accent means you don't want it mentioned. A third sense is purely physical — sensitive to light, sensitive to penicillin — and a fourth is approving: sensitive to the concerns of the neighborhood means considerate, not fragile. ✗ sensitive of is an error, though sensitive of you to notice appears occasionally and is better rendered thoughtful of you.
entries.see also: vulnerable to, aware of, harmful to, indifferent to, to

entries.meaning: Genuinely intending something, and not joking about it.
examples: She's serious about moving the whole operation to the coast.
If you're serious about the offer, put it in writing.
They finally got serious about fixing the drainage.
He's serious about her, which surprised everyone including him.
The county is serious about enforcing the ordinance this time.
entries.русский: всерьёз настроенный на что-л., не шутящий
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (serious about going back to school) — never a to-infinitive. ✗ serious to go back is an error.
entries.pattern: be serious about [noun / verb-ing] · get serious about [noun] · be serious (alone): are you serious? · dead serious about [noun] · serious about [someone] — in a relationship
entries.variants: in earnest about is the formal one; committed to takes to and a gerund; not kidding about is the conversational one.
entries.contrast: Serious about + -ing versus determined to + verb is the usual pairing: same idea, opposite complements. Note the relationship sense — serious about her, meaning committed romantically — which is one of the few cases where the object of about is a person. Do not confuse the adjective with serious meaning grave (a serious injury), which takes no preposition at all. ✗ serious in is an error, though serious in tone and serious in intent are correct phrases where in names the respect.
entries.see also: committed to, intent on, enthusiastic about, about

entries.meaning: Startled and upset by something unexpected, usually something bad.
examples: Neighbors were shocked at how fast the building came down.
She was shocked by the tone of the letter.
I was shocked to find out he'd been gone since March.
The board was shocked at the size of the shortfall.
He was shocked into silence, which for him was remarkable.
entries.русский: потрясённый, шокированный чем-л. неожиданным
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after at and by (shocked at finding the door open) — never a to-infinitive after a preposition. The adjective takes a bare to-infinitive directly (shocked to learn) and a that-clause (shocked that nobody objected).
entries.pattern: be shocked at [noun / verb-ing] · be shocked by [the cause] · be shocked to [verb] · be shocked (that) [clause] · shocked into [verb-ing] · shock [someone] (no preposition on the object)
entries.variants: appalled at / by and horrified at / by are the stronger versions with the same split; taken aback by is the milder one.
entries.contrast: Same at / by split as surprised and astonished: at frames it as your reaction, by frames it as the thing acting on you. Shocked at the price is a judgment; shocked by the news is an effect. Shocked to learn reports the moment. The literal electrical sense takes by only (shocked by a live wire), which is a useful anchor for remembering which preposition means "acted on by." ✗ shocked of and ✗ shocked with are errors.
entries.see also: surprised at, astonished at, upset about, at

entries.meaning: Not having enough of something — or, in the second sense, anything other than.
examples: We're short of volunteers for the Saturday shift.
He's short on patience and long on opinions.
Short of rebuilding the retaining wall, there's no permanent fix.
The count came up two short of what the manifest said.
The performance fell short of what the reviews had promised.
entries.русский: испытывающий нехватку чего-л.; во втором значении — кроме, разве что не (+ герундий)
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase after of in the "lacking" sense; noun phrase or gerund in the "except" sense (short of rebuilding the whole thing) — never a to-infinitive. After on, a noun naming the supply that is low.
entries.pattern: be short of [something needed] · be short on [supply] · short of [verb-ing] — meaning "except by" · fall short of [standard] · nothing short of [noun] · stop short of [verb-ing]
entries.variants: low on and out of are the everyday American versions of short on and short of; wanting in and deficient in are the formal ones and take in.
entries.contrast: Short of has two distinct senses in the same shape. The first is lacking: short of cash. The second is "anything except": Short of selling the building, I don't see a way out — and this second sense takes a gerund and is genuinely useful. Short on is the near-twin used with supplies and qualities: short on patience. ✗ short in is an error for both senses, though short in stature is a fixed phrase about height. The idioms fall short of, stop short of, and nothing short of all keep of.
entries.see also: lacking in, free of, full of, absent from, of

entries.meaning: Thoroughly tired of something and out of patience with it.
examples: I'm sick of explaining the same policy every August.
She got sick of waiting and drove herself.
They're sick and tired of being told the parts are on order.
He was sick with something all week and blamed the flight.
Everyone is sick of the construction noise by now.
entries.русский: которому надоело что-л. — разг., сыт по горло
entries.register: informal to neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (sick of hearing about it) — never a to-infinitive and never a clause.
entries.pattern: be sick of [noun / verb-ing] · get sick of [noun] · sick and tired of [noun / verb-ing] · be sick with [an illness] · be sick to death of [noun]
entries.variants: tired of is the calmer twin; fed up with the equivalent with a different preposition; done with the flat American one.
entries.contrast: Sick of is impatience; sick with is illness; sick from is the cause of illness. Sick of the flu would mean weary of it; sick with the flu means having it; sick from the shot means it made you ill. Keep them apart. Note also that fed up takes with, so ✗ sick with waiting and ✗ fed up of waiting are mirror errors. The fixed sick and tired of is a set phrase and cannot be rearranged.
entries.see also: tired of, fed up with, bored with, of

entries.meaning: Resembling something without being identical to it.
examples: The new layout is similar to the old one with two extra exits.
Her symptoms are similar to what the first patient described.
The two contracts are similar in structure to the one we signed in June.
The taste is similar to buckwheat, if buckwheat had been left in the sun.
Their approach is similar to ours and their timeline is not.
entries.русский: похожий на, сходный с — но не тождественный
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (similar to working from home, but with worse coffee) — never a to-infinitive and never a that-clause. A free relative works: similar to what we saw last year.
entries.pattern: [X] is similar to [Y] · broadly / strikingly similar to [noun] · similar in [respect] to [noun] · similarly [adjective] · similarity to / between — the noun takes both
entries.variants: like is the everyday equivalent and takes the same kind of complement; comparable to is the measured one; akin to the literary one; close to the loose one.
entries.contrast: Similar takes to, never with and never as. ✗ similar with the original and ✗ similar as the original are both errors, the second borrowed from the same as. Note the noun's double life: similarity to compares one thing to another, while similarity between treats them as a pair — the similarity between the two accounts. See similar to for the word treated as a comparison preposition.
entries.see also: identical to, different from, equal to, related to, similar to

entries.meaning: Having developed ability in some practice or field.
examples: She's skilled at getting two departments to agree on a date.
He's skilled in both civil and criminal procedure.
The crew is skilled at working around weather delays.
We need someone skilled in structural inspection, not just licensed.
He's skilled at the part of the job nobody writes down.
entries.русский: умелый в чём-л., владеющий навыком
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after at (skilled at defusing arguments) and after in (skilled in negotiation) — never a to-infinitive. ✗ skilled to negotiate is an error.
entries.pattern: be skilled at [practice / verb-ing] · be skilled in [field or discipline] · highly skilled at [verb-ing] · skilled labor (no preposition)
entries.variants: proficient in, adept at, practiced at, accomplished in, and versed in fill out the same range; good at is the plain everyday version.
entries.contrast: At takes the practice, in takes the field. Skilled at soldering is what you do with your hands; skilled in electrical engineering is a body of knowledge. The distinction is soft — both are correct in most sentences — but in sounds credentialed and at sounds practical, which is why résumés prefer in and recommendations prefer at. ✗ skilled on and ✗ skilled of are errors. The parallel adjectives expert, good, bad, hopeless, and terrible all take at for practices.
entries.see also: expert at, good at, capable of, successful in, at

entries.meaning: Taking longer than others do — at a task, or in reacting.
examples: He's slow at mental arithmetic and unbeatable on paper.
She's slow to take offense, which is why people tell her things.
The office was slow in processing the refund.
I'm slow at anything involving a keyboard shortcut.
The county has been slow to release the inspection reports.
entries.русский: медлительный в чём-л. (о навыке); slow to — не спешащий сделать что-л.
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after at (slow at reading music) and after in (slow in responding, the formal frame). The adjective also takes a bare to-infinitive meaning "not quick to" (slow to anger, slow to respond), which is the commoner frame in writing. Never a to-infinitive after at.
entries.pattern: be slow at [skill / verb-ing] · be slow to [verb] · be slow in [verb-ing] · slow on the uptake · slow alone, of business: sales are slow
entries.variants: not quick to is the plain paraphrase of slow to; behind on covers the schedule sense.
entries.contrast: Slow at names a skill you perform slowly; slow to names a reaction you are late in having. Slow at arithmetic is about ability; slow to complain is about temperament, and it is one of the small set of adjectives — with quick to, ready to, eager to — where an infinitive follows directly. Slow in + -ing is the formal alternative to slow to: slow in acknowledging receipt. ✗ slow of is an error except in the fossil slow of speech.
entries.see also: bad at, poor at, late for, good at, at

entries.meaning: Regretful about something you did, or sympathetic about something that happened.
examples: I'm sorry for keeping you waiting; the earlier meeting ran long.
She was sorry about the whole misunderstanding.
Don't feel sorry for him; he chose every part of this.
I'm sorry to hear about the diagnosis.
He was sorry that he'd ever mentioned it.
entries.русский: виноватый, сожалеющий о своём поступке; sorry for someone — жалеющий кого-л.
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: a person after for in the pity sense; a noun phrase or gerund after for and about in the apology sense (sorry for keeping you waiting) — never a to-infinitive after a preposition. The adjective takes a bare to-infinitive directly (sorry to bother you) and a that-clause (sorry that it came to this).
entries.pattern: be sorry for [person] — pity · be sorry for [verb-ing] — apology · be sorry about [thing] · be sorry to [verb] · be sorry (that) [clause] · feel sorry for [person] · sorry alone, as an apology
entries.variants: apologize for + gerund is the formal verb frame; regret takes a direct object or a gerund with no preposition at all (regret saying it).
entries.contrast: The three frames say three different things, and mixing them is a genuine social error. Sorry for you is pity — often unwelcome. Sorry about your father is condolence. Sorry for interrupting is an apology for something you did. And sorry to hear that is a reaction to news. So I'm sorry for you and I'm sorry about that are not interchangeable, and the first can insult where the second consoles. ✗ sorry of is an error; sorry for + gerund and sorry about + gerund are both fine for apologies, with for slightly the more contrite.
entries.see also: ashamed of, guilty of, sad about, grateful to, for

entries.meaning: Belonging to one context, group, or case and not to others.
examples: The error is specific to the Windows build and doesn't appear on a Mac.
That rule is specific to districts with fewer than five hundred students.
The training is specific to the machines on this floor.
Symptoms like these are not specific to any one condition.
The permit conditions are specific to the parcel and don't travel.
entries.русский: характерный только для данного случая, специфичный для
entries.register: neutral to technical; the modern workhorse for "belonging only to," common in medicine, software, and policy writing
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the group, place, context, or case — or a gerund where the context is an activity (specific to running the night shift). Never a to-infinitive: ✗ specific to run the night shift.
entries.pattern: be specific to [group / context] · [noun] specific to [noun] · not specific to [noun] — the common denial · site-specific, species-specific, context-specific — the hyphenated compounds, where the complement moves in front · be specific about [noun] — the unrelated sense, "give details"
entries.variants: peculiar to is the formal equivalent; unique to is the strongest; particular to is a close synonym; restricted to and confined to say the same thing about range.
entries.contrast: Two different adjectives share this spelling. Specific to + noun means "belonging only to": a symptom specific to the disease. Specific about + noun means "giving detail": be specific about the dates. The prepositions keep them apart and are not interchangeable — ✗ be specific to the dates asks for something else entirely. Against peculiar to, which is formal and slightly literary, specific to is the neutral modern choice. In medicine the pair sensitive and specific are terms of art about tests, and there specific takes no complement at all.
entries.see also: peculiar to, native to, endemic to, common to, to

entries.term: stuck with, stuck in, stuck on
entries.respell: STUCK with, STUCK in, STUCK on
entries.meaning: Unable to get free of something — a burden, a place, or a problem, depending on the preposition.
examples: We got stuck with the catering bill when the sponsor pulled out.
She's been stuck in traffic on the bridge for forty minutes.
I'm stuck on the third question and the rest went fine.
He's stuck in a job he outgrew four years ago.
They were stuck with explaining the whole thing to the board twice.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /stʌk wəθ/, /stʌk ən/, /stʌk ən/ — in and on both reduce to /ən/, so stuck in traffic and stuck on a problem sound alike in the unstressed syllable and are told apart by the noun
entries.русский: застрявший — with с обузой, in в месте, on на задаче
entries.register: informal to neutral; thoroughly American conversational English, and common in writing that wants a spoken texture
entries.complement: after with, a noun phrase naming the burden you cannot get rid of — and a gerund (stuck with paying for it). After in, a noun naming the place or condition you cannot get out of, or a gerund (stuck in waiting for approval is possible but marginal). After on, a noun naming the problem you cannot get past or the person you are infatuated with. No to-infinitive after any of the three: ✗ stuck with to pay. The bare frame stuck + -ing with no preposition (stuck waiting an hour) is also standard.
entries.pattern: be stuck with [bill / responsibility / verb-ing] · be stuck in [traffic / a job / a rut] · be stuck on [a problem / question / person] · get stuck [verb-ing] — no preposition · be stuck at [a number] — a fourth, quantitative frame
entries.variants: saddled with and left holding the bag replace stuck with; bogged down in replaces stuck in; hung up on is the near twin of stuck on in both its senses.
entries.contrast: The three prepositions carve up the idea cleanly. Stuck with is about a burden you did not want (stuck with the bill); stuck in is about a place or state you cannot leave (stuck in traffic, stuck in a bad contract); stuck on is about a point you cannot get past (stuck on question four) or, in the older slang, a person you cannot stop thinking about (he's been stuck on her since high school). Note that stuck with takes people too, and then it is rude: stuck with my brother-in-law for the weekend. ✗ stuck to means physically adhering (gum stuck to the seat) and is a different pattern altogether.
entries.see also: fed up with, tired of, involved in, encumbered by, encumbered with, with

entries.meaning: Conditional on something, liable to undergo it, or under its authority.
examples: All prices are subject to change without notice.
The sale is subject to a satisfactory inspection.
Flights out of that airport are subject to fog delays all spring.
Contractors are subject to the same background checks as employees.
The award is subject to being reviewed after the first year.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˈsʌbdʒɪkt tə/ — the adjective stresses the first syllable, unlike the verb subject /səbˈdʒɛkt/
entries.русский: при условии чего-л.; подверженный чему-л.; подчинённый чему-л.
entries.register: formal; the standard idiom of contracts, notices, and regulation
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (subject to being called back) — never a to-infinitive. ✗ subject to be reviewed is the error; write subject to review or subject to being reviewed.
entries.pattern: be subject to [condition / authority / liability] · [noun], subject to [condition] · subject to change without notice · subject [someone] to [something] — the verb, stressed on the second syllable
entries.variants: contingent on and conditional on cover the "depending on" sense and take on; liable to covers the "likely to suffer" sense; governed by covers the authority sense.
entries.contrast: Subject to carries three related senses, all with the same preposition. Conditional: the offer is subject to financing. Liable to undergo: prices subject to change, subject to delays. Under the authority of: subject to state law. Distinguish the verb, which is spelled the same and stressed differently: they subjected him to three hours of questions. ✗ subject of is a different word entirely — the noun, meaning topic.
entries.see also: dependent on, based on, responsible for, vulnerable to, to

entries.respell: suh-BOR-duh-nit too; the verb is suh-BOR-duh-nayt
entries.meaning: Ranking below something else in authority, priority, or importance.
examples: The regional offices are subordinate to the state director.
The second lien is subordinate to the bank's mortgage.
Everything else in the plan is subordinate to keeping the plant open.
She refuses to be subordinate to a committee that never meets.
In this design, style is subordinate to legibility.
entries.русский: подчинённый чему-л., стоящий ниже по власти или значимости
entries.register: formal; standard in organizational writing, in finance (subordinated debt), and in grammar (a subordinate clause)
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming what ranks higher — a person, a body, an interest, a lien. A gerund is possible where the higher thing is an activity (subordinate to keeping the lights on), and a to-infinitive is impossible: ✗ subordinate to keep the lights on.
entries.pattern: be subordinate to [person / interest] · make [something] subordinate to [noun] · subordinate [a lien] to [another] — the verb, in finance · subordinated debt / a subordination agreement — the terms of art
entries.variants: secondary to is the neutral equivalent; inferior to ranks quality rather than authority; junior to is the finance and military word for priority; beneath and under are the plain prepositions.
entries.contrast: Against inferior to, which judges quality (an inferior copy), subordinate to describes rank and authority and implies no judgment about worth. In American lending the term is precise: a subordinated lien is paid after the senior one, and a subordination agreement is what makes it so — which is why a second mortgage is subordinate to the first regardless of when it was recorded. Note that in grammar a subordinate clause is one that cannot stand alone, another use with no preposition. ✗ subordinate of is an error, though a subordinate of the director exists as a noun.
entries.see also: inferior to, ancillary to, incidental to, superior to, to

entries.meaning: Achieving what was intended.
examples: She was successful in getting the deadline moved twice.
The clinic has been successful at reaching families the old program missed.
He's been successful in every business he's touched except restaurants.
The campaign was successful in raising the money and useless at spending it.
They were successful with the first group and are repeating it in the fall.
entries.русский: добившийся успеха в чём-л., достигший задуманного
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after in (successful in raising the money) and after at (successful at getting people to show up) — never a to-infinitive. ✗ successful to raise the money is an error; use succeeded in raising or managed to raise.
entries.pattern: be successful in [field / verb-ing] · be successful at [practice / verb-ing] · be successful with [a particular case or group] · succeed in [verb-ing] — the verb keeps in · success in / at — the noun follows suit
entries.variants: effective in / at, productive in, and does well at cover the same ground; manage to + verb is the everyday paraphrase with an infinitive.
entries.contrast: In leans toward the field or the endeavor; at leans toward the repeated practice. Successful in business names a domain; successful at raising money names something done more than once. Both are correct with a gerund. The verb takes only in: ✓ succeeded in convincing them, ✗ succeeded to convince them — a very common error, since manage and try both take infinitives. ✗ successful of is an error.
entries.see also: skilled at, good at, expert at, in

entries.meaning: Pointing toward a conclusion without establishing it.
examples: The films show changes suggestive of an old fracture.
The pattern of withdrawals is suggestive of something other than payroll.
Her account is suggestive of a much longer delay than the log shows.
Wear on the threshold is suggestive of daily use, not occasional.
The findings are suggestive of, though not diagnostic of, the disorder.
entries.русский: наводящий на мысль о — намекающий, но не доказывающий
entries.register: formal; the natural home is a radiology report or a clinical note (findings suggestive of pneumonia), and by extension any careful analytical writing
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming what is hinted at, or a gerund (suggestive of having been repaired before) — never a to-infinitive: ✗ suggestive of to be repaired.
entries.pattern: [finding] be suggestive of [condition] · strongly / only mildly suggestive of · suggestive — used alone, where the modern meaning is risqué · suggest [conclusion] — the verb, direct object, no preposition
entries.variants: indicative of is the stronger word; consistent with is the radiologist's hedge that claims even less; symptomatic of names the condition outright; reminiscent of is the aesthetic cousin (a style reminiscent of the thirties).
entries.contrast: A ladder of confidence runs consistent with → suggestive of → indicative of → diagnostic of, and American clinicians choose among them deliberately: findings consistent with pneumonia would fit it, findings suggestive of pneumonia point toward it, findings diagnostic of it settle the matter. Watch the bare adjective: suggestive with no complement now means sexually suggestive, so the photograph was suggestive and the photograph was suggestive of an earlier repair are two different sentences and only the second is this pattern. ✗ suggestive to and ✗ suggestive for are errors.
entries.see also: indicative of, symptomatic of, illustrative of, predictive of, of

entries.meaning: Right for a particular purpose, use, or audience.
examples: The lot isn't suitable for anything heavier than a shed.
The material is suitable for outdoor use in freezing weather.
The film is not suitable for younger viewers.
That soil is suitable for almost nothing but blueberries.
She's better suited to the research side than the client side.
entries.русский: подходящий для — для цели, применения или аудитории
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: a noun naming a purpose, use, or group after for; a gerund is possible (suitable for freezing) — never a to-infinitive after for. The adjective also takes a bare to-infinitive in the passive-ish frame suitable to serve, which is rarer.
entries.pattern: be suitable for [purpose / group] · be suitable to [a standard or occasion] · suitable for framing · not suitable for [group]
entries.variants: appropriate for and right for are the everyday equivalents; fit for is the blunter one; suited to is the close twin and takes to.
entries.contrast: Suitable for a purpose; suited to a role or a person. A car suitable for city driving and a candidate well suited to the job — the pair differs by preposition and by what fills the slot, and ✗ suitable to city driving and ✗ suited for the job both drift. Note the fixed phrases: suitable for all ages, not suitable for children, suitable for framing. ✗ suitable of is an error.
entries.see also: available to, useful for, essential to, ready for, for

entries.meaning: Higher in quality or rank than something else.
examples: The older tooling is superior to anything available now at that price.
She was superior to every other applicant on paper and in person.
The second route is superior in every respect to the one we took.
He has a way of sounding superior to the people he's asking for help.
Nothing about the newer model is superior to the one it replaced.
entries.русский: превосходящий что-л. — выше по качеству или рангу
entries.register: formal to neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or pronoun — never a gerund, never a to-infinitive, never a clause.
entries.pattern: [X] is superior to [Y] · superior in [respect] to [noun] · vastly / demonstrably superior to [noun] · a superior [noun] — attributive, no preposition · feel superior to [person]
entries.variants: better than is the everyday equivalent and takes than, which is exactly the source of the error this entry warns about.
entries.contrast: Superior takes to, never than. ✗ superior than the original is a persistent error, and it happens because the word means "better" while behaving like a Latin comparative. The same rule covers inferior to, senior to, junior to, prior to, preferable to, anterior to, and posterior to — a family worth learning together. Note also that superior takes no more: ✗ more superior to is redundant, though it is common in speech.
entries.see also: inferior to, equal to, similar to, than, to

entries.meaning: Free of doubt — or, in the infinitive frames, bound to happen or expected to be done.
examples: I'm sure of the date; the receipt is right here.
She wasn't sure about moving the whole family in January.
Make sure of the measurement before you cut.
Be sure to turn off the water at the street.
That corner is sure to flood again in the spring.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ʃʊr əv/, and in fast speech /ˈʃʊrə/
entries.русский: уверенный в чём-л.; в инфинитивных оборотах — непременно случится или ожидается
entries.register: neutral; the everyday twin of certain
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, gerund (sure of getting the spot), or a wh-clause after about (sure about what she wants) — never a to-infinitive after the preposition. A that-clause attaches to the bare adjective (sure that he'd locked it), and a bare to-infinitive attaches directly with a different meaning: sure to happen means bound to happen.
entries.pattern: be sure of [noun / verb-ing] · be sure about [matter] · be sure (that) [clause] · be sure to [verb] — an instruction or a prediction · make sure of [noun] · for sure
entries.variants: certain of / about is the more formal twin and covers every frame; positive about is the emphatic conversational one.
entries.contrast: Sure of is confidence; sure to is inevitability or instruction. He's sure of a spot means he feels confident; He's sure to get a spot means it will happen; Be sure to lock up is an order. Three different things from one adjective. Of takes a fact or an outcome, about takes a matter under consideration, and about is the one that takes wh-clauses. ✗ sure for is an error.
entries.see also: certain of, confident of, aware of, of

entries.meaning: Reacting to something you did not expect.
examples: I was surprised at how empty the place was on a Friday.
She was surprised by the second call, which came at midnight.
He was surprised to find the office already unlocked.
Nobody was surprised that the vote was postponed again.
I'm surprised at you — you know better than that.
entries.русский: удивлённый чем-л. неожиданным
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after at and by (surprised at finding it unlocked) — never a to-infinitive after a preposition. The adjective takes a bare to-infinitive directly (surprised to learn) and a that-clause (surprised that anyone remembered).
entries.pattern: be surprised at [noun / verb-ing] · be surprised by [the cause] · be surprised to [verb] · be surprised (that) [clause] · surprise [someone] (no preposition on the object) · take [someone] by surprise
entries.variants: surprised at and surprised by are both standard American English; by is the commoner of the two in writing and points harder at the cause.
entries.contrast: At frames the reaction; by frames the cause. Surprised at how little it cost is your reaction to a figure; surprised by the phone call is the call acting on you — which is why an event that arrives takes by and a fact you consider takes at. The infinitive frame is different again: surprised to see her there reports the moment. Note the reproachful idiom I'm surprised at you, which is a mild rebuke and cannot be rebuilt with by. ✗ surprised of and ✗ surprised from are errors.
entries.see also: astonished at, shocked at, impressed with, at

entries.meaning: Open to being affected by something, in the to frame; capable of admitting something, in the of frame.
examples: Older patients are more susceptible to the complication than the trial suggested.
Galvanized fittings are susceptible to corrosion where they meet copper.
He's susceptible to flattery from anyone who mentions the boat.
The sentence is susceptible of at least two readings.
The claim is not susceptible of proof one way or the other.
entries.русский: подверженный чему-л. (to); допускающий что-л., поддающийся (of); книжн.
entries.register: susceptible to is neutral and everyday in medicine and engineering; susceptible of is formal and now largely legal and literary
entries.complement: after to, a noun phrase naming the harm or influence you are open to, or a gerund (susceptible to being talked into things). After of, a noun naming what the thing admits — susceptible of proof, susceptible of two readings — and a gerund is not used there. Never a to-infinitive after either: ✗ susceptible to be persuaded.
entries.pattern: be susceptible to [disease / influence / damage] · be susceptible of [proof / interpretation / improvement] · particularly / especially susceptible to · susceptibility to [noun] — the noun frame keeps to
entries.variants: vulnerable to and prone to replace the to frame; open to and capable of replace the of frame; liable to covers both loosely; at risk of is the public-health phrase.
entries.contrast: To for what can happen to it; of for what it will admit. Old pipe is susceptible to corrosion (it can be attacked); a clause is susceptible of two readings (it will bear them). The of frame is the older and rarer one, and it is nearly always followed by an abstract noun like proof, interpretation, division, or improvement. Against vulnerable to, which stresses harm and defenselessness, susceptible to is neutral enough for engineering and for personality (susceptible to flattery). ✗ susceptible for is an error.
entries.see also: vulnerable to, immune from, immune to, amenable to, sensitive to, to

entries.meaning: Not trusting someone or something, and having reasons.
examples: The bank was suspicious of three transfers in one afternoon.
She's suspicious of anyone who volunteers to take the minutes.
Investigators grew suspicious about the timing of the sale.
He was suspicious of being sent on an errand at that hour.
Everyone was suspicious of the offer and nobody said so.
entries.русский: относящийся с подозрением к, не доверяющий
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (suspicious of being followed) — never a to-infinitive. A that-clause attaches to the bare adjective only in the sense "suspecting": suspicious that something had been moved.
entries.pattern: be suspicious of [person / thing] · be suspicious about [a matter] · grow / become suspicious of [noun] · look suspicious (no complement) · suspicion of [noun] — the noun keeps of
entries.variants: wary of and leery of are the cautious versions; skeptical of / about is the intellectual one; distrustful of is the formal one.
entries.contrast: Suspicious of is what you feel about someone; suspicious about is what you feel about a matter; and suspicious alone means looking guilty. The last is the ambiguity worth naming: He was suspicious can mean either that he suspected something or that he seemed suspect, and only context decides — the second sense usually appears as He looked suspicious. ✗ suspicious to and ✗ suspicious from are errors.
entries.see also: critical of, jealous of, confident of, of

entries.meaning: Feeling or showing understanding for someone, or favorably disposed toward a cause.
examples: The committee was sympathetic to the tenants but bound by the ordinance.
She's sympathetic toward anyone trying to get a permit out of that office.
The paper has always been sympathetic to the union's position.
He was sympathetic to the argument without agreeing with the conclusion.
I sympathize with the family — the verb, with with.
entries.русский: сочувствующий кому-л.; благосклонный к делу, идее
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: a noun naming a person, group, or cause after to and toward — never a gerund and never a to-infinitive.
entries.pattern: be sympathetic to [cause / person] · be sympathetic toward [person] · be sympathetic with [a position] — less common · sympathize with [person] — the verb takes with
entries.variants: toward is the American spelling and towards the British; both are read as ordinary in the United States, with toward the house style of most American publishers. Sympathetic to is the commoner of the two in American writing.
entries.contrast: The adjective takes to or toward; the verb takes with. ✓ sympathetic to the strikers, ✓ sympathize with the strikers, ✗ sympathize to the strikers. That split is the whole difficulty. A second sense of the adjective means favorably disposed rather than compassionate — a judge sympathetic to the defense — and it is the one used in political writing. The unrelated technical sense (the sympathetic nervous system) takes no preposition.
entries.see also: sensitive to, kind to, sorry for, to

entries.meaning: Serving as a sign of a larger condition lying underneath.
examples: The rash is symptomatic of the reaction, not of the infection itself.
Three resignations in a month are symptomatic of something nobody wants to name.
The backlog is symptomatic of a system built for half the volume.
His answer was symptomatic of how the department handles complaints.
Late shipments were symptomatic of a supplier who had already given up.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˌsɪmptəˈmædək əv/, with the t flapped: "simp-tuh-MAD-ik-uv"
entries.русский: симптоматичный для — служащий признаком более глубокой причины
entries.register: formal; medical in origin and now at least as common in commentary about institutions (symptomatic of a deeper problem)
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the underlying condition or problem, or a gerund (symptomatic of having grown too fast) — never a to-infinitive: ✗ symptomatic of to grow too fast.
entries.pattern: [sign] be symptomatic of [condition] · symptomatic of a larger / deeper / wider [noun] — the commentary cliché · symptomatic — the clinical bare use, meaning showing symptoms (symptomatic patients) · asymptomatic — the negative, a word every American learned in 2020
entries.variants: indicative of is the neutral evidential word; a symptom of is the noun phrase and takes of too; emblematic of is the loaded version; a sign of is the plain one.
entries.contrast: Symptomatic of names the sign of a condition that lies underneath, which is why the figurative use is so common and so lazy: symptomatic of a deeper problem is a way of not naming the problem. Against indicative of, which points at any conclusion, symptomatic of implies a whole disease behind the sign. Note the clinical bare use, where symptomatic means "having symptoms" and takes no complement at all — symptomatic patients were tested first — which is a different construction from this one. ✗ symptomatic to and ✗ symptomatic for are errors.
entries.see also: indicative of, suggestive of, illustrative of, characteristic of, of

entries.meaning: Meaning the same thing as something else — or, of a name, so associated with a quality that it stands for it.
examples: In everyday speech, begin is synonymous with start, though the registers differ.
The family name became synonymous with the mill and closed with it.
That neighborhood was for decades synonymous with cheap rent.
Speed is not synonymous with haste, whatever the schedule says.
His byline is synonymous with stories nobody else would take.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /səˈnɑnəməs wəθ/ — note that the adjective stresses the second syllable while the noun synonym stresses the first
entries.русский: синонимичный чему-л.; об имени — ставший символом какого-л. качества
entries.register: neutral to formal; a linguistic term and, far more often, a journalistic idiom about reputations
entries.complement: a noun phrase, or a gerund (synonymous with cutting corners) — never a to-infinitive: ✗ synonymous with cut corners.
entries.pattern: be synonymous with [word / thing] · practically / virtually / now synonymous with · a synonym for [word] — the noun, which switches to for
entries.variants: interchangeable with is the strict linguistic claim; equivalent to claims equal value; identified with is the reputational sense stated plainly; a byword for is the idiom for the journalistic use.
entries.contrast: Adjective with, noun for. ✓ synonymous with, ✓ a synonym for, ✗ a synonym with, ✗ synonymous for. In strict use the word claims two expressions mean the same thing; in the commoner journalistic use it claims that a name has come to stand for a quality — a town synonymous with steel. Against equivalent to, which is quantitative, synonymous with is about meaning and reputation. ✗ synonymous to is an error and a frequent one.
entries.see also: equivalent to, identical to, tantamount to, similar to, with

entries.meaning: Touching a curve or surface at exactly one point without crossing it.
examples: Draw the line tangent to the circle at the point where they meet.
The derivative gives the slope of the line tangent to the curve.
A plane tangent to the sphere touches it at a single point.
The road runs tangent to the reservoir for a quarter mile.
His question was tangential to the agenda, which is the figurative form.
entries.русский: касательный к — мат., касающийся кривой в одной точке
entries.register: technical — geometry and calculus, where a line tangent to a curve touches it at exactly one point; the figurative work is done by the noun tangent and by tangential to
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the curve or surface touched — never a gerund and never a clause.
entries.pattern: [line] be tangent to [curve] · a plane tangent to [surface] · the tangent line at [point] · go off on a tangent — the idiom, with no complement · tangential to [noun] — the figurative adjective
entries.variants: tangential to is the form for the figurative sense, meaning only slightly connected (a question tangential to the motion); touching is the literal paraphrase; osculating is the specialist's word for a closer contact in differential geometry.
entries.contrast: Tangent to stays mathematical; tangential to carries the figurative sense. A line is tangent to a circle; a remark is tangential to the discussion, and using tangent to for the second reads as an error to anyone who took calculus. Against perpendicular to and parallel to, which describe fixed relations between straight lines, tangent to describes contact at a single point on a curve. The related American idiom go off on a tangent keeps the image: you leave the curve along the line that just touched it.
entries.see also: perpendicular to, parallel to, orthogonal to, adjacent to, to

entries.meaning: Equal in effect to something graver than what it was called.
examples: Saying nothing at that point was tantamount to agreeing.
Refusing the inspection is tantamount to an admission.
The transfer was tantamount to a gift, whatever the paperwork called it.
Cutting the route is tantamount to stranding half the riders.
Her memo was tantamount to accusing the vendor of padding the invoices.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˈtænəˌmaʊnt tə/ — the first t after n often drops in speech: "TAN-uh-mownt"
entries.русский: равносильный чему-л. — книжн., по сути то же, но названное мягче
entries.register: formal to journalistic; almost always used to characterize an act as something worse than it was called
entries.complement: a noun phrase or a gerund — tantamount to admitting the whole thing ✓ — and never a to-infinitive: ✗ tantamount to admit the whole thing. The gerund is the commoner complement, which makes this one of the highest-value entries in the file for the -ing rule.
entries.pattern: be tantamount to [noun / verb-ing] · amount to [noun / verb-ing] — the near-identical verb · tantamount to a [confession / declaration / admission] — the standard collocations
entries.variants: amounts to is the plain verb and does the same work in ordinary prose; equivalent to is neutral; in effect is the adverbial paraphrase (in effect a confession); no better than is the blunt version.
entries.contrast: Tantamount to is a judgment, not a measurement. Where equivalent to says two things are equal in value, tantamount to says an act has the force of something graver — which is why the complement is nearly always negative: tantamount to fraud, tantamount to a threat, tantamount to giving up. The word has no attributive use: ✗ a tantamount admission is not English. And the to is a preposition every time, so the -ing form is obligatory: ✗ tantamount to say nothing, ✓ tantamount to saying nothing.
entries.see also: equivalent to, synonymous with, equal to, amenable to, to

entries.meaning: Very bad at something, or very bad for something.
examples: I'm terrible at estimating how much paint a room takes.
That schedule is terrible for anyone with a second job.
He's terrible with names and excellent with faces.
She's terrible about checking the shared calendar.
We're both terrible at saying no to a weekend project.
entries.русский: ужасно плохой в чём-л. (at); terrible for вредный, terrible with не умеющий обращаться с
entries.register: informal to neutral; emphatic
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after at (terrible at keeping secrets) — never a to-infinitive. After for, a person or thing harmed (terrible for morale). After with, a category handled badly.
entries.pattern: be terrible at [skill / verb-ing] · be terrible for [person / thing] · be terrible with [category] · be terrible about [verb-ing] — chronically negligent · terrible alone: a terrible mistake
entries.variants: awful at, horrible at, bad at, and hopeless at are the same word at different volumes; no good at is the flat one.
entries.contrast: Terrible at / for / with splits exactly as good at / for / with and bad at / for / with do — skill, harm, and category respectively — so learning one of the three learns all three. ✗ terrible in math is an error in American English. Note the about frame, which reports a chronic failure to do something rather than a lack of skill: terrible about returning calls means you can, but don't.
entries.see also: bad at, hopeless at, poor at, good at, at

entries.meaning: Feeling relief and gratitude that something is the case.
examples: We're thankful for every dry day this month.
She's thankful for having had those last two summers with him.
I'm thankful to be back in a house with working heat.
They were thankful that the storm turned before the harbor.
Be thankful for small mercies and a short agenda.
entries.русский: благодарный за, с облегчением радующийся тому, что
entries.register: neutral to warm
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after for (thankful for having somewhere to go) — never a to-infinitive after for. The adjective takes a bare to-infinitive directly (thankful to be home) and a that-clause (thankful that nobody was hurt).
entries.pattern: be thankful for [thing] · be thankful to [verb] · be thankful (that) [clause] · be thankful to [a benefactor] — restricted · thankfully as a sentence adverb
entries.variants: grateful for is the close twin and additionally takes a person with to; appreciative of is the formal one.
entries.contrast: Thankful takes for, and, unlike grateful, it does not comfortably take a person. ✓ grateful to the neighbors, and ✗ thankful to the neighbors is odd — the exception is thankful to God, a fixed religious phrase. That is the whole difference between the two words grammatically; in tone, thankful is warmer and more personal, grateful more likely to acknowledge a specific debt. ✗ thankful of and ✗ thankful about are errors.
entries.see also: grateful to, glad about, happy about, for

entries.meaning: Out of patience with something, or physically worn out by it.
examples: She's tired of explaining why the office closes at four.
He was tired from three days of moving furniture.
I'm tired of being the only one who reads the agenda.
They were tired from the flight and useless until noon.
Voters are tired of hearing about a bridge that never gets built.
entries.русский: которому надоело что-л.; tired from — физически утомлённый чем-л.
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund after of (tired of waiting) and after from (tired from standing all day) — never a to-infinitive after either. ✗ tired to wait is an error; too tired to wait is a different, correct construction.
entries.pattern: be tired of [noun / verb-ing] — fed up · be tired from [noun / verb-ing] — physically worn out · get tired of [noun] · sick and tired of [noun] · too tired to [verb]
entries.variants: sick of and fed up with are the impatience versions; worn out from and exhausted from are the physical ones.
entries.contrast: Tired of is impatience; tired from is exhaustion. Tired of the drive means you'd rather not do it again; tired from the drive means you need to sit down. The two are constantly confused and the difference is total. A third frame, too tired to + verb, uses an infinitive and belongs to too … to, not to this adjective. ✗ tired with is an error in American English, though it appears in older British prose.
entries.see also: sick of, fed up with, bored with, of, from

entries.meaning: Showing the usual qualities of a person, group, or kind — often said with a sigh.
examples: The long lead-in is typical of his later work.
Rain like this is typical of early spring here.
It's typical of her to have read the whole file before the meeting.
That kind of answer is typical of the whole department.
Snow in October is typical for this elevation, if not for this state.
entries.русский: типичный для, характерный для — часто со вздохом: «как всегда»
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or pronoun; a gerund where a behavior is meant (typical of showing up unannounced is possible but heavy) — never a to-infinitive and never a clause. The it-frame takes an infinitive: It's typical of him to volunteer.
entries.pattern: be typical of [person / group / period] · [noun] typical of [noun] · it is typical of [someone] to [verb] · typically [adjective / verb] · That's typical.
entries.variants: characteristic of is the neutral formal twin; representative of is the statistical one; par for the course is the idiomatic complaint.
entries.contrast: Typical of is very often a complaint; characteristic of almost never is. That's typical of them usually means they have let you down again, and the bare That's typical is a pure grumble. Note also the difference from representative of: a typical case is an ordinary one, while a representative sample is one chosen to stand for the whole. ✗ typical for is an error in this sense, though typical for this time of year is correct and means normal for that period — a genuinely different frame worth knowing.
entries.see also: characteristic of, similar to, known for, of

entries.meaning: Distressed or annoyed — the general-purpose word covering everything from mild irritation to real grief.
examples: Parents are upset about how late the schedule was announced.
She's upset with her brother and won't say why.
He was visibly upset by the question.
The whole neighborhood is upset over the tree removal.
Don't get upset about something you can't change before Friday.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ʌpˈsɛt əˈbaʊt/ — the adjective stresses the second syllable, unlike the noun upset /ˈʌpsɛt/
entries.русский: расстроенный, огорчённый чем-л. — от лёгкой досады до настоящего горя
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after about, over, and by (upset about being left out) — never a to-infinitive after a preposition. A person follows with. A that-clause attaches to the bare adjective: upset that nobody called.
entries.pattern: be upset about [situation / verb-ing] · be upset with [person] · be upset by [the cause] · be upset over [situation] · be upset (that) [clause] · get upset about [noun]
entries.variants: bothered by, rattled by, and thrown by are the milder ones; distraught over is the intensified one and prefers over.
entries.contrast: The familiar split, with one extra option. About and over take the situation, with takes the person, by takes the cause acting on you. Upset with her sister about the will fills two slots at once. Over is slightly more emotional than about and is the newspaper's choice for grief and grievance. ✗ upset of is an error, and the medical an upset stomach is a different use with no preposition at all.
entries.see also: angry with, annoyed with, sad about, worried about, about

entries.meaning: Accustomed to something — or, in the identical-looking semi-modal, in the habit of doing something in the past.
examples: She's used to the noise from the interstate by now.
I'm not used to getting up before the alarm.
He got used to driving on the left in about a week.
We used to eat there every Friday before it closed.
There didn't use to be a light at that intersection.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /just tə/, in ordinary speech /ˈjustə/ — note the adjective is /just/ with the s of loose, not /juzd/ with the z of used a pencil
entries.русский: привыкший к (прилагательное, дальше герундий); либо «раньше, бывало» — о прошлой привычке
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: adjective + preposition — and, spelled identically, a semi-modal of the habitual past
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (used to working nights) — never a to-infinitive after the adjective. ✗ I'm used to work nights is the error. The semi-modal used to, by contrast, takes a bare infinitive and no be: I used to work nights, meaning I no longer do.
entries.pattern: be / get / become used to [noun / verb-ing] · used to [bare verb] — habitual past · didn't use to [verb] · never used to [verb] · not used to [noun / verb-ing]
entries.variants: accustomed to is the formal equivalent of the adjective and behaves identically. Would covers part of the habitual-past sense, but only for repeated actions, not for states: ✓ We used to live there, ✗ We would live there.
entries.preceded by a bare subject and followed: the semi-modal, meaning a discontinued habit — I used to smoke. The negative and interrogative of the semi-modal drop the d in American writing: didn't use to, did he use to — though never used to is commoner in speech. And there is no present tense of the semi-modal: ✗ I use to smoke for a current habit is an error; say I usually smoke.
entries.contrast: This is the most consequential ambiguity in the file. Look at what precedes and what follows. Preceded by be, get, or become, and followed by a noun or -ing: the adjective, meaning accustomed — I'm used to the noise, She got used to driving in it.
entries.see also: accustomed to, familiar with, comfortable with, look forward to, to

entries.meaning: Serving a purpose, or being of help to someone.
examples: That attachment is useful for getting into corners.
Her notes were useful to everyone who came after her.
The old map turned out to be useful in ways nobody expected.
It's useful to know which door they actually unlock at seven.
A second set of hands is useful for about an hour of this job.
entries.русский: полезный для (цели); useful to — полезный кому-л., useful in — в какой-л. обстановке
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: a noun naming a purpose, or a gerund (useful for getting into tight corners) after for; a person after to — never a to-infinitive after a preposition. The adjective takes a bare to-infinitive in the frame useful to know, which describes what may be done, not who benefits.
entries.pattern: be useful for [purpose / verb-ing] · be useful to [person] · be useful in [a situation or process] · it is useful to [verb] · make oneself useful
entries.variants: helpful for / to splits the same way; handy for is the informal one; of use to is the formal noun frame.
entries.contrast: For names the purpose; to names the person who benefits; in names the setting. Useful for removing rust, useful to anyone with an old car, useful in a pinch. The infinitive frame is a fourth thing: It's useful to know the code means knowing it helps, and its subject is the impersonal it, not a person. ✗ useful of is an error.
entries.see also: suitable for, essential to, good at, available to, for

entries.meaning: Formally granted a power, an authority, or an interest.
examples: The commission is vested with authority to subpoena records.
By the power vested in me by the state — the converse frame, with in.
The trustee is vested with discretion over distributions.
No single office is vested with the power to waive the requirement.
The council is vested with everything the charter took from the mayor.
entries.русский: наделённый чем-л. — полномочием, властью, правом; юр./офиц.
entries.register: formal and legal; the natural home is a statute, a charter, or a ceremony — by the power vested in me
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the power, authority, or interest conferred — never a gerund and never a clause. The recipient goes in the subject, and the source, if named, in a by-phrase.
entries.pattern: be vested with [authority / power] · vest [power] in [person] — the converse frame, where the power is the object and the person takes in · by the power vested in me by [authority] — the wedding formula · a vested interest in [noun] · fully vested — the retirement-plan sense, with no complement
entries.variants: endowed with covers qualities and funds; invested with is the same word in its longer form and is used of dignity and symbolism (invested with meaning); granted and conferred on are the plain verbs.
entries.contrast: Vested with takes the power; vested in takes the person. The board is vested with authority to set rates; authority to set rates is vested in the board — same fact, mirrored. Against endowed with, which suits qualities and gifts, vested with suits offices and legal powers. Note the American benefits sense, where an employee becomes vested after a period of service and takes no complement at all, and the idiom a vested interest in, which means a stake worth protecting.
entries.see also: endowed with, possessed of, entitled to, seized of, seised of, with

entries.meaning: Open to being harmed by something.
examples: Older homes on that street are vulnerable to basement flooding.
The system was vulnerable to a fairly obvious attack for two years.
Seedlings are vulnerable to a late frost for another month.
The company is vulnerable to any real change in fuel prices.
The change left part-time staff vulnerable to being cut first.
entries.русский: уязвимый для, беззащитный перед
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: a noun naming the threat after to; a gerund where a process is meant (vulnerable to being outvoted) — never a to-infinitive. ✗ vulnerable to be attacked is an error; write vulnerable to attack.
entries.pattern: be vulnerable to [threat] · leave [someone] vulnerable to [threat] · particularly / especially vulnerable to [noun] · vulnerable alone: a vulnerable population
entries.variants: susceptible to, exposed to, prone to, open to, and at risk of are the neighbors; all but the last take to.
entries.contrast: Vulnerable to names what can hurt you; at risk of names what might happen to you. Vulnerable to flooding and at risk of flooding are close, but the first says the defenses are weak and the second says the odds are high. Note the related prone to, which takes both a noun and, unusually, sometimes a bare verb (prone to overreact alongside prone to overreacting) — a rare crossover in this family. ✗ vulnerable for and ✗ vulnerable from are errors.
entries.see also: sensitive to, safe from, subject to, harmful to, to

entries.meaning: Anxious about something that might go wrong.
examples: She's worried about the second mortgage more than the first.
Doctors were worried by the pattern in the second scan.
He's worried for his parents, who haven't left the house all winter.
I'm worried about signing anything before the survey comes back.
Nobody was worried that the vote would fail; they were worried about the margin.
