entries.русский: беспокоящийся о том, что может пойти не так
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund after about (worried about losing the deposit) and after by — never a to-infinitive after a preposition. A that-clause attaches to the bare adjective: worried that the check hadn't cleared.
entries.pattern: be worried about [noun / verb-ing] · be worried by [the thing causing the worry] · be worried for [someone's welfare] · be worried (that) [clause] · get worried about [noun] · worry [someone] (no preposition on the object)
entries.variants: concerned about is the more formal twin; anxious about the more clinical one; nervous about the version reserved for a specific upcoming event.
entries.contrast: About names the topic of the worry; by names what produced it; for names the person you fear for. Worried about the results is ordinary; worried by the results means the results themselves disturbed you and is what a doctor says; worried for her is on her behalf. The by frame is the one that reports an active cause, exactly as with annoyed by and bored by. ✗ worried of and ✗ worried with are errors.
entries.see also: concerned about, anxious about, nervous about, afraid of, about

entries.meaning: Good enough or important enough to deserve something.
examples: The proposal is worthy of a closer look than it got.
Two findings in the audit are worthy of mention in the cover letter.
That's a performance worthy of the room it was played in.
Her record is worthy of being read aloud at the ceremony.
Nothing in the complaint is worthy of the attention it has drawn.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˈwɜrði əv/, and before a consonant often /ˈwɜrði ə/ — "WUR-thee-uh-note"
entries.русский: достойный чего-л., заслуживающий
entries.register: neutral to formal; ordinary in reviews, recommendations, and argument
entries.complement: a noun phrase or a gerund (worthy of being taken seriously) — never a to-infinitive after of: ✗ worthy of to be considered. A separate and much older frame takes a bare infinitive with no of at all (worthy to be called a son), which survives in scripture and in deliberate archaism.
entries.pattern: be worthy of [noun / verb-ing] · hardly / richly / well worthy of · worthy of note / worthy of mention / worthy of consideration — the fixed collocations · worth [noun / verb-ing] — the different adjective, with no preposition
entries.variants: deserving of is the close twin and stresses what conduct has earned; meriting is the participial version; worth replaces the whole phrase in ordinary speech and takes no of.
entries.contrast: Worthy of takes of; worth takes nothing. ✓ worth a look, ✓ worthy of a look, ✗ worth of a look, ✗ worthy a look except in the frozen literary worthy a second glance. That is the trap, and it catches native writers. Against deserving of, which is about desert earned by conduct, worthy of can simply weigh quality: a sequel worthy of the original has met a standard, not earned a reward. Note the common compound suffix -worthy — newsworthy, trustworthy, seaworthy — where the complement has moved in front and the of disappears.
entries.see also: deserving of, entitled to, suitable for, capable of, of

entries.meaning: Faulty, or mistaken — the preposition decides which.
examples: Something is wrong with the compressor again.
What's wrong with leaving an hour earlier?
He was wrong about the closing date by two weeks.
There's nothing wrong with the plan except that nobody will fund it.
It was wrong of them to announce it before telling the staff.
entries.русский: не в порядке с — wrong with о неисправности или недомогании, wrong about об ошибке во мнении
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: a noun or pronoun naming what has the fault after with; a noun phrase or gerund after about (wrong about assuming they'd call) — never a to-infinitive after either. The it-frame takes an infinitive: It's wrong to say that.
entries.pattern: there is something wrong with [noun] · what's wrong with [noun] · be wrong about [matter / verb-ing] · it is wrong to [verb] · go wrong with [noun] · nothing wrong with [noun / verb-ing]
entries.variants: the matter with is the exact equivalent of wrong with in the fault frame: what's the matter with the car. Mistaken about is the formal twin of wrong about.
entries.contrast: Wrong with locates a fault; wrong about assigns a mistaken belief. Something's wrong with him means he is unwell or acting oddly; He's wrong about the date means he has the wrong information. These two do not overlap at all, and only the preposition separates them. Note the very common defensive frame nothing wrong with + -ing, which is a standard American way of defending a choice: There's nothing wrong with taking the long way. ✗ wrong of names the doer instead: It was wrong of him to ask, which is correct in that frame only.
entries.see also: bad at, guilty of, responsible for, with

entries.meaning: Give a reply to a question, a letter, a call, or a door — with the thing replied to as a direct object.
examples: She answered every question without looking at her notes.
Nobody answered the door, so we left the package on the porch.
Would you answer the phone if it rings while I'm out?
He answers to a board of nine people, none of whom agree.
Somebody is going to have to answer for how this was budgeted.
entries.pronunciation note: the object attaches with no preposition and no pause: answer the question /ˈænsər ðə ˈkwɛstʃən/ — the only weak form in the phrase is the article /ðə/, because no preposition intervenes
entries.русский: отвечать на — без предлога: answer the question, не ✗ answer to the question
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: a direct object — a question, a letter, a phone, a door, a person. ✗ answer to the question and ✗ answer at the phone are errors. The verb does take to and for in other senses, described below.
entries.pattern: answer [question / letter / phone / door] · answer [someone] · answer to [a person or body you report to] · answer for [something you are held accountable for] · answer back · an answer to [question] — the noun takes to
entries.variants: reply to and respond to both require to, which is exactly where the confusion starts: ✓ answer the letter, ✓ reply to the letter, ✗ answer to the letter.
entries.contrast: The verb takes no preposition; the noun takes to; and the two idiomatic frames take to and for. ✓ She answered the question. ✓ That's not an answer to my question. ✓ He answers to the regional director. ✓ Somebody has to answer for the delay. Four different structures from one word, and only the first is the plain transitive use.
entries.see also: discuss, contact, request, responsible for

entries.meaning: Come near to something, or raise a matter with someone.
examples: The storm approached the coast faster than forecast.
Temperatures are approaching ninety by mid-morning.
She approached the whole problem from the accounting side.
Nobody had approached him about taking over the route.
Two hikers approached the ranger station just before dark.
entries.pronunciation note: the object attaches directly: approach the building /əˈproʊtʃ ðə ˈbɪldɪŋ/ — weak /ðə/, and nothing else in the phrase to reduce
entries.русский: подходить к, обращаться к — без предлога: approach the problem, не ✗ approach to
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: a direct object — a place, a person, a figure, a subject. ✗ approach to the building and ✗ approach at the deadline are errors. The verb takes about when a person is approached regarding something: approach her about the job, which is a second object slot, not a substitute for the first.
entries.pattern: approach [place / person / number] · approach [someone] about [matter] · approach [a problem] · an approach to [problem] — the noun takes to
entries.variants: come up to and go up to are the everyday physical equivalents and do take prepositions; get in touch with replaces the "approach someone about" sense in casual speech.
entries.contrast: The verb takes a bare object; the noun takes to. ✓ We approached the problem differently. ✓ That's a new approach to the problem. ✗ We approached to the problem. The about frame is fully correct and worth knowing, because it is what you actually want when raising a subject with someone: I approached her about covering the shift.
entries.see also: reach, contact, enter, close to

entries.meaning: Be present at something — with the event as a direct object.
examples: About forty people attended the hearing.
He attended the same high school as both his parents.
She couldn't attend the funeral and sent her brother.
I'll attend to the invoices as soon as the phones stop — a different verb.
Everyone on the crew is expected to attend the safety briefing.
entries.pronunciation note: the object attaches directly: attend the meeting /əˈtɛnd ðə ˈmitɪŋ/ — weak /ðə/, with no preposition between verb and object
entries.русский: присутствовать на, посещать — без предлога: attend the meeting
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: a direct object — a meeting, a school, a service, an event. ✗ attend to the meeting means something else entirely, and ✗ attend at the conference is an error. The separate phrasal verb attend to means to deal with or care for.
entries.pattern: attend [event / institution] · attend to [a matter or a patient] — a different verb · attendance at [event] — the noun takes at · in attendance
entries.variants: go to is the everyday equivalent and requires to: ✓ go to the meeting, ✓ attend the meeting, ✗ attend to the meeting in that sense. Be present at is the formal one.
entries.contrast: Attend an event; attend to a task. ✓ She attended the hearing (she was there). ✓ She attended to the paperwork (she handled it). ✓ A nurse attended to him (cared for him). The two are different verbs that happen to share a spelling, and choosing wrong changes the meaning rather than merely sounding foreign. Note that the noun takes at: attendance at the meeting was poor.
entries.see also: join, reach, absent from, late for

entries.meaning: Get in touch with someone.
examples: Contact the county clerk before you file anything.
She contacted three references and heard back from one.
Please contact us about any charge you don't recognize.
He hasn't been in contact with his sister since the spring.
We contacted every household on the affected block.
entries.pronunciation note: the object attaches directly: contact the office /ˈkɑntækt ði ˈɔfɪs/ — weak /ði/ before the vowel, and no preposition to reduce
entries.русский: связаться с кем-л. — без предлога: contact me, не ✗ contact with me
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: a direct object — a person or an organization. ✗ contact with the office and ✗ contact to the office are errors as verb frames. The noun contact does take with: contact with the family.
entries.pattern: contact [person / office] · contact [someone] about [matter] · be in contact with [someone] — the noun frame · make contact with [someone]
entries.variants: get in touch with and reach out to are the everyday American equivalents and both take prepositions, which is where the pull toward ✗ contact to comes from.
entries.contrast: The verb takes a bare object; every noun frame takes with. ✓ Contact the office before noon. ✓ We've had no contact with the office. ✗ Contact with the office before noon. The verb was coined from the noun in the twentieth century and was once condemned as business jargon; it is now entirely standard, but the noun's with still leaks into the verb frame.
entries.see also: phone, approach, answer, reach

entries.meaning: Talk about something in a considered way, with the topic as a direct object.
examples: The board discussed the budget for two hours and voted in five minutes.
We discussed the schedule with both crews before posting it.
She wants to discuss what happens if the grant isn't renewed.
Nobody had discussed the possibility of closing the second site.
There was a long discussion about pay — the noun, which does take about.
entries.pronunciation note: the object attaches directly: discuss the budget /dɪˈskʌs ðə ˈbʌdʒɪt/ — weak /ðə/, with no weak about /əˈbaʊt/ in between
entries.русский: обсуждать что-л. — без предлога: discuss the plan, не ✗ discuss about
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: a direct object or a wh-clause (discuss what to do next) — ✗ discuss about is an error, and it is the most common of all zero-preposition mistakes. A that-clause is not possible either: ✗ discuss that we should wait.
entries.pattern: discuss [topic] · discuss [topic] with [person] · discuss [wh-clause] · a discussion about / of [topic] — the noun takes a preposition
entries.variants: talk about and speak about both require about, which is exactly the source of the error: ✓ talk about the budget, ✓ discuss the budget, ✗ discuss about the budget.
entries.contrast: The verb takes no preposition for the topic and with for the person. ✓ I discussed the schedule with her. ✗ I discussed about the schedule. ✗ I discussed with her the problem is grammatical but awkward in American English; put the topic first. The noun takes about or of freely — a discussion about pay, a discussion of the evidence — and this asymmetry between verb and noun is what keeps the error alive.
entries.see also: mention, emphasize, answer, about

entries.meaning: Give special importance to something in speaking or writing.
examples: The chief emphasized that no decision had been made.
She emphasized the deadline three separate times.
The report emphasizes cost and says almost nothing about safety.
He stressed the same point in every meeting — stress, also with no preposition.
The curriculum places too much emphasis on memorization — the noun, with on.
entries.pronunciation note: the object attaches directly: emphasize the deadline /ˈɛmfəsaɪz ðə ˈdɛdlaɪn/ — weak /ðə/, with no weak on /ən/ in between
entries.русский: подчёркивать, особо отмечать — без предлога: emphasize the risk
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: a direct object or a that-clause (emphasized that the deadline was firm) — ✗ emphasize on is an error, though it is common in Indian and other South Asian English and is spreading. The related noun frames take on, which is where it comes from.
entries.pattern: emphasize [point] · emphasize (that) [clause] · place / put emphasis on [noun] — the noun frame takes on · lay stress on [noun] · stress [point] — also zero-preposition
entries.variants: stress and underscore behave identically and take no preposition; focus on and dwell on do take on and are not substitutes.
entries.contrast: The verb takes a bare object; the noun takes on. ✓ She emphasized the deadline. ✓ She placed great emphasis on the deadline. ✗ She emphasized on the deadline. The same asymmetry runs through the near-synonyms: ✓ stress the point / ✓ lay stress on the point. In American English the ✗ emphasize on form is corrected in every register, so it is worth eliminating deliberately.
entries.see also: discuss, mention, serious about, on

entries.meaning: Go into a place, or begin taking part in something.
examples: She entered the building through the loading dock.
Three of our people entered the contest and one placed.
He entered the profession the year the rules changed.
The two firms entered into an agreement in March — the abstract sense.
Enter the reading into the log before you leave the site.
entries.pronunciation note: the object attaches directly: enter the building /ˈɛntər ðə ˈbɪldɪŋ/ — weak /ðə/, and in the literal sense no into /ˈɪntə/ at all
entries.русский: входить в, вступать в — без предлога: enter the room, не ✗ enter into the room
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: verb + direct object (zero preposition) in the literal sense
entries.complement: a direct object — a place, a competition, a profession, data. ✗ enter into the room is an error in the literal sense. Enter into is correct and idiomatic in the abstract sense: enter into an agreement, enter into negotiations, enter into the spirit of the thing.
entries.pattern: enter [place / contest / profession] · enter [data] into [a system] · enter into [an agreement / negotiations / a discussion] · enter on / upon [a period or undertaking] — formal · entrance to [place] — the noun takes to
entries.variants: go into and come into are the everyday physical equivalents and require into: ✓ go into the room, ✓ enter the room, ✗ enter into the room.
entries.contrast: Literal movement takes a bare object; abstract commitment takes into. ✓ He entered the room. ✓ They entered into a five-year lease. ✓ Enter the figures into the spreadsheet — where into marks the destination of the data, not the thing entered. The formal enter upon a new phase survives in ceremonial writing. And the noun takes to: the entrance to the building.
entries.see also: approach, join, reach, into

entries.meaning: Become a member of something, or come together with someone.
examples: She joined the union her first week on the job.
Will you join us for dinner Thursday?
Two more agencies joined the search by Sunday morning.
He never joined in the complaining, which people noticed.
The city joined with the county to pay for the new intersection.
entries.pronunciation note: the object attaches directly: join the union /dʒɔɪn ðə ˈjunjən/ — weak /ðə/, and no preposition to reduce
entries.русский: вступать в, присоединяться к — без предлога: join the club
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: a direct object — an organization, a group, a person, a line. ✗ join to the union and ✗ join with the line are errors in this sense. Join in takes an activity (join in the singing) and join with takes a partner in a joint action (joined with the county to fund it), both of which are correct in their own frames.
entries.pattern: join [organization / group / person] · join [someone] for [a meal or an activity] · join in [an activity] · join with [a partner] to [verb] · join [X] to [Y] — physically connect
entries.variants: sign up for and become a member of are the everyday equivalents and take prepositions; take part in replaces join in.
entries.contrast: Four frames. ✓ She joined the union (became a member). ✓ Join us for dinner (accompany). ✓ He joined in the discussion (took part). ✓ Join the two pipes to each other (connect). Only the first is the bare transitive, and it is the one where an inserted preposition is wrong: ✗ She joined to the union.
entries.see also: attend, enter, involved in, engaged to

entries.meaning: Be without something that is needed or expected.
examples: The report lacks any discussion of what it would cost.
He doesn't lack confidence; he lacks a plan.
The building lacks a second exit on the top floor.
The proposal is lacking in specifics — the adjective, with in.
The case was dropped for lack of evidence — the noun, with of.
entries.pronunciation note: the object attaches directly: lack evidence /læk ˈɛvɪdəns/ — no article and no preposition, so the phrase carries no weak form at all; compare the noun frame a lack of evidence /ə ˈlæk əv/, with weak /ə/ and /əv/
entries.русский: не иметь чего-л., испытывать нехватку — без предлога: lack money
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: a direct object — usually an abstract or mass noun. ✗ lack of as a verb is an error: ✗ The report lacks of detail. The noun lack takes of (a lack of detail) and the adjective lacking takes in (lacking in detail), and those three shapes are the whole difficulty.
entries.pattern: lack [something] · be lacking in [quality] — the adjective frame · a lack of [noun] — the noun frame · for lack of [noun] · lacking [noun] — participle with a bare object
entries.variants: be short of and be without are the everyday equivalents and both take prepositions; want for is the literary one (want for nothing).
entries.contrast: Three related forms, three structures, and this is the most instructive case in the section. ✓ The plan lacks detail — verb, no preposition. ✓ The plan is lacking in detail — adjective, in. ✓ There is a lack of detail — noun, of. Learners who meet the noun first produce ✗ lacks of detail, which is the commonest error involving the word. Note also that lack has no progressive in careful writing: ✗ is lacking confidence is better as lacks confidence, though lacking in confidence is fine.
entries.see also: lacking in, short of, free of, full of

entries.meaning: Take someone as a husband or wife.
examples: They married in a courthouse two weeks after they met.
She married a man she'd known since middle school.
He got married to his college roommate's sister — the get frame, with to.
A judge married them on a Tuesday afternoon.
She married into a family that has farmed the same section since 1890.
entries.pronunciation note: the object attaches directly: marry her /ˈmɛri hər/, in ordinary speech with weak /ər/ — and no preposition to reduce
entries.русский: жениться на, выходить замуж за — без предлога: marry her, не ✗ marry with
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: a direct object — the person married. ✗ marry with and ✗ marry to are errors as verb frames: ✗ He married with her, ✗ He married to her. The adjective married takes to (married to a pilot), and get married to is correct, which is exactly what makes the verb frame confusing.
entries.pattern: marry [person] · get married to [person] · be married to [person] · marry into [a family] · marry [two people] — what the officiant does · marriage to [person] — the noun takes to
entries.variants: wed behaves identically and takes a bare object; get hitched is the informal one.
entries.contrast: The verb takes a bare object; every other form takes to. ✓ He married her in 1998. ✓ He got married to her in 1998. ✓ He's been married to her since 1998. ✗ He married to her. ✗ He married with her. The with error is produced by speakers of Spanish (casarse con), Italian, Polish, and Russian, among others, and is worth drilling because it is instantly noticeable. The fixed phrase married with two kids is about children, not spouses.
entries.see also: married to, engaged to, related to

entries.meaning: Refer to something briefly in speech or writing.
examples: Nobody mentioned the delay until the trucks were already loaded.
She mentioned it to her supervisor the same afternoon.
He mentioned that the road would be closed through Friday.
The report makes no mention of the second inspection — the noun, with of.
The rent went up twice, not to mention the new parking fee.
entries.pronunciation note: the object attaches directly: mention the delay /ˈmɛnʃən ðə dɪˈleɪ/ — weak /ðə/; the only weak preposition arrives with the person, as in mention it to her /tə hər/
entries.русский: упоминать о чём-л. — без предлога: mention the delay, не ✗ mention about
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: a direct object, a that-clause (mentioned that the road was closed), or a gerund (mentioned seeing him there) — ✗ mention about is an error, as is ✗ mention to the delay. The person told is introduced with to: mention it to her.
entries.pattern: mention [thing] · mention [thing] to [person] · mention (that) [clause] · mention [verb-ing] · not to mention [noun] · make mention of [noun] — the noun frame takes of
entries.variants: bring up and refer to are the everyday equivalents, and refer to requires to, which is part of the pull toward the error.
entries.contrast: The verb takes a bare object for the thing and to for the person. ✓ She mentioned the delay to the crew. ✗ She mentioned about the delay. ✗ She mentioned to the crew about the delay is doubly wrong. The noun takes of: no mention of the delay. Note the useful frozen phrases: not to mention, meaning "and also", and don't mention it, the reply to thanks.
entries.see also: discuss, emphasize, request, about

entries.meaning: Telephone someone.
examples: Phone the office before you drive all the way out there.
She called him twice and left one message.
Call me when you get in, no matter how late.
He phoned the clinic about the results.
Write me when you get settled — American, with no to.
entries.pronunciation note: the object attaches directly: phone the office /foʊn ði ˈɔfɪs/ — weak /ði/ before the vowel, and no preposition to reduce
entries.русский: звонить кому-л. — без предлога: phone her, не ✗ phone to her
entries.register: neutral; call is the American default and phone the slightly British-sounding alternative
entries.complement: a direct object — the person or place called. ✗ phone to the office and ✗ call to her are errors. American English also allows the double object call me back and, distinctively, write me without to.
entries.pattern: phone [person / place] · call [person] · phone [someone] about [matter] · give [someone] a call · a call to [person] — the noun takes to
entries.variants: call is the ordinary American verb; ring is British; reach covers the "get hold of" sense. All three take a bare object.
entries.contrast: The verb takes a bare object; the noun takes to. ✓ Phone the office. ✓ Make a call to the office. ✗ Phone to the office. A related American-versus-British point belongs here: Americans write write me with no preposition (write me when you land), while British English requires write to me. Both varieties agree on call me and phone me.
entries.see also: contact, answer, reach

entries.meaning: Object publicly or formally to something.
examples: Several hundred people protested the closure outside the county building.
Students protested the tuition increase through most of the spring.
She protested the charge in writing and got half of it reversed.
In London the same crowd would have protested against the bill.
He protested to the commissioner and was told to file a form.
entries.pronunciation note: the object attaches directly, with the article in its weak form and no preposition to reduce: protest the ruling /prəˈtɛst ðə ˈrulɪŋ/ — and note that the verb stresses the second syllable, unlike the noun protest /ˈproʊtɛst/
entries.русский: протестовать против — в амер. англ. без предлога: protest the ruling
entries.register: neutral; the bare transitive is the default of American news writing
entries.type: verb + direct object (zero preposition) in American English
entries.complement: a direct object naming what is objected to, or a that-clause (protested that no one had told him). In American English no preposition comes between: protest the verdict. British English requires protest against the verdict, which American readers accept without blinking. Protest to names the person the complaint is taken to and is standard in both varieties.
entries.pattern: protest [decision / policy / verdict] — American · protest against [noun] — British, and available in American writing · protest to [official] · protest (that) [clause] · protest (intransitive): they protested for three days · under protest · a protest against [noun] — the noun keeps against
entries.variants: object to and complain about are the everyday equivalents and both require their prepositions, which is part of what pulls against back into the verb frame. Demonstrate against covers the street sense only. Contest and challenge are the legal equivalents and are also bare transitives.
entries.contrast: This is the sharpest American-versus-British split in the section, and both forms are defensible. ✓ Thousands protested the ruling is standard in the United States and strikes many British ears as ungrammatical; ✓ Thousands protested against the ruling is the British requirement and passes everywhere, including American print. Keep both apart from protest to, which names the person you complain to — she protested to the commissioner — and from the that-frame, which introduces a denial (he protested that he'd never seen the form) and is where protest too much comes from. The noun keeps a preposition in either variety: ✗ a protest the closure, ✓ a protest against the closure.
entries.see also: opposed to, critical of, answer, request, against

entries.meaning: Arrive at something, extend to it, or get hold of someone.
examples: We reached the trailhead just before the rain started.
Temperatures reached ninety-four on Sunday.
The two sides reached an agreement at two in the morning.
I couldn't reach her all afternoon.
He reached for the railing and missed it — a different frame.
entries.pronunciation note: the object attaches directly: reach the airport /ritʃ ði ˈɛrpɔrt/ — weak /ði/ before the vowel, with nothing between verb and object
entries.русский: добираться до, дотягиваться до, дозваниваться кому-л. — без предлога: reach Tucson
entries.register: neutral
entries.complement: a direct object — a place, a figure, a decision, or a person you get hold of. ✗ reach to the airport and ✗ reach at the office are errors in these senses. Reach for is correct and different: it means to extend a hand toward something, whether or not you get it.
entries.pattern: reach [place / figure / agreement / person] · reach for [something] · reach out to [someone] · reach into [container] · within reach of [noun] — the noun frame takes of
entries.variants: get to and arrive at are the everyday equivalents for the travel sense and both require prepositions; get hold of replaces the contact sense.
entries.contrast: Reach the destination; reach for the object; reach out to the person. ✓ We reached Tucson by four. ✓ He reached for the light switch. ✓ She reached out to three former clients. Only the first is the bare transitive, and inserting a preposition there is the error: ✗ We reached to Tucson. Note that reach meaning "get hold of by phone" is also bare: ✓ I couldn't reach her all morning.
entries.see also: approach, contact, enter, attend

entries.meaning: Ask for something, in a formal register.
examples: She requested a full transcript of the hearing.
The office requested three references from each applicant.
They requested that the meeting be moved to the following week.
He requested to see the original file, not a copy.
The clerk denied the request for an extension — the noun, with for.
entries.pronunciation note: the object attaches directly: request a copy /rɪˈkwɛst ə ˈkɑpi/ — weak /ə/, and no weak for /fər/ after the verb
entries.русский: просить о чём-л., запрашивать — офиц., без предлога: request a transcript
entries.register: formal; ask for is the everyday equivalent
entries.complement: a direct object, a that-clause with a subjunctive (requested that she be present), or an infinitive (requested to see the file) — ✗ request for as a verb is an error: ✗ He requested for a copy. The noun takes for: a request for a copy.
entries.pattern: request [thing] · request [thing] from [source] · request that [subjunctive clause] · request to [verb] · a request for [thing] — the noun frame · at the request of [person]
entries.variants: ask for is the everyday equivalent and requires for, which is exactly the source of ✗ request for: ✓ ask for a copy, ✓ request a copy, ✗ request for a copy.
entries.contrast: The verb takes a bare object; the noun takes for. ✓ She requested a transcript. ✓ She submitted a request for a transcript. ✗ She requested for a transcript. The subjunctive frame is worth noting because American formal writing keeps it: We request that he be notified, not is notified. The same subjunctive follows ask, demand, insist, recommend, and suggest.
entries.see also: answer, mention, contact, for

entries.meaning: Look or be like something else.
examples: The second draft barely resembles the first.
He resembles his grandfather more every year.
The building resembles a filing cabinet with windows.
Their proposal closely resembles one we rejected in the spring.
There's a strong resemblance to the earlier design — the noun, with to.
entries.pronunciation note: the object attaches directly: resemble her mother /rɪˈzɛmbəl hər ˈmʌðər/, in ordinary speech with weak /ər/ — and no preposition to reduce
entries.русский: быть похожим на — без предлога: resemble his father
entries.register: neutral to formal
entries.complement: a direct object — the thing resembled. ✗ resemble to and ✗ resemble with are errors: ✗ She resembles to her mother. The related adjective takes to (similar to her mother), which is where the pull comes from.
entries.pattern: resemble [someone / something] · closely / strongly resemble [noun] · bear a resemblance to [noun] — the noun takes to · look like [noun] — the everyday equivalent, with like
entries.variants: look like and be like are the everyday versions and require like; take after is the family-specific one (she takes after her father).
entries.contrast: The verb takes a bare object; the noun and every synonym take a preposition. ✓ She resembles her mother. ✓ She bears a strong resemblance to her mother. ✓ She looks like her mother. ✗ She resembles to her mother. Note that resemble has no passive in careful usage — ✗ her mother is resembled by her is not English — and no progressive: ✗ she is resembling her mother.
entries.see also: similar to, identical to, related to, typical of
